Researchers have a pressing need to understand airborne transmission of COVID-19 in public buses, which necessitates the development of an effective evaluation framework for disease transmission in confined spaces. This study presents and validates a model that simulates the well-mixed dispersion of infectious aerosols during typical bus operations, incorporating a single-point sampling system and experimental measurement of ventilation rates. By applying this model to an actual outbreak that occurred on a New York City bus in 2020, where two infected individuals transmitted the virus to an uninfected passenger, we assess the model's ability to account for various factors, including viral load, aerosol retention, and effective contact time, to predict infection probability, with a transferrable approach for investigating airborne disease transmission in enclosed environments.

A recent investigation involving ${^{133}\mathrm{I}(p,t)}$ reactions yielded forbidden beta decay (FBD) properties for ${^{135,137}\mathrm{Te}}$, which can be integrated into the shell-model to determine their BCDT values. When applied to ${^{135}\mathrm{Te}}$, the calculated BCDT $t_{1/2}^{\mathrm{FBD}}$ is 4.12 seconds, in agreement with an existing 2014 measurement. For ${^{137}\mathrm{Te}}$, the calculated forbidden beta decay half-life is 26.52 seconds, suggesting it is several times longer than the existing upper limit from a 2007 study. Analysis indicates that including $j_{15/2}$ orbitals in the shell-model would result in Te isotopes exhibiting enhanced beta decay.

Double-sided auctions serve as a fundamental tool in matching buy and sell orders on double auction platforms. A double-sided auction mechanism is valid if it only executes trades when the highest willingness to purchase is met by a corresponding highest willingness to sell. This module, double-sided_auction, has been double-checked against validated logical deductions to ensure all double-sided auction operations are logically sound and valid.

The HQET framework is examined to investigate the properties of the F-wave bottom mesons. The molecular nature of bottom mesons with quantum numbers $J^{PC}=1^{++}, 2^{++}, 3^{++}$ has already been established. The bottomonium states with molecular characteristics and the bottom meson decay widths are calculated using HQET. The findings are presented in terms of HQET parameters. The study also includes a comparison of the results with perturbative QCD.

Building on the theory of periodic decomposition by Baillon and Ransford, we offer a novel characterization and a new approach to the concept, along with alternative methods to determine it. Furthermore, we formulate and prove a variant of the open mapping theorem specifically for the class of nonexpansive with a given factor $\lambda \ge 1$. This finding, in turn, provides a viable approach to the theory of $\lambda$-open mappings and its applications in computing the division of polynomials.

The application of dimensional reduction techniques, such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD), has become increasingly important in analyzing large-scale data sets, particularly in situations involving numerous time-varying measurements of a smaller set of underlying states. However, these methods face significant challenges in such data-rich environments, such as data sparsity, noise, and limited signal, which can result in a poorly conditioned system of linear equations. In response to these issues, this study proposes a new kernel-based approach, LANDO, that leverages kernel learning to reconstruct a robust and accurate DMD matrix despite its associated linear and nonlinear clarification problems. The LANDO method employs a kernelized least-squares optimization strategy to learn a data-driven kernel that effectively maps the available data back to a DMD matrix output space. The study's findings demonstrate that LANDO successfully produces stable and convergent solutions for dynamic systems, particularly those experiencing data sparsity, signal scarcity, and nonlinear clarification issues, outperforming conventional and sparsity-promoting optimization techniques in these scenarios.

Analyzing the patterns of decisions made by humans in order to understand their behavior has been a long-standing goal in science.  By examining sequences of movements, such as those made by individuals learning to walk or play musical instruments, we can measure progression and evolution across time and species.  Recently, researchers began to apply these techniques to analyze patterns of everyday decisions made by humans in order to understand the behavior of humans in general, as well as the behavior of animals and the stock market.  This study applies these techniques to analyze the movements of chess players in the early stages of a game in order to determine how the complexity of these early moves has evolved over time.  To do this, we used the Kullback-Leibler divergence to compare the patterns of decisions made by players in the early stages of a game, and found that the complexity of these early moves can be used to divide the history of chess into distinct periods, and that the complexity of these early moves can be influenced by factors such as the spread of new strategies on the online community platform Chess.com.  This suggests that the complexity of these early moves is not only a reflection of the fundamental nature of chess, but also of the factors influencing human behavior in a broader sense.

Pale dwarfs in pale synthetic observations enable researchers to generate data for systems containing millisecond pulsars (MSPs) and companions, encompassing both non-pale and standard binary configurations. Utilizing these pale observations, researchers create false MSP data and apply standard data analysis methods to determine the system's parameters. These parameters are compared to the input values, and researchers determine which parameters can be accurately recovered, particularly those involving the orbit and the pulsar. However, determining the companion's mass and eccentricity presents significant challenges. To mitigate overfitting and streamline parameter selection, researchers turn to the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), which is introduced to the analysis of pale dwarf data. This method is used to evaluate and refine model parameters, and when combined with the results of bootstrap analysis, enables researchers to confidently recover most parameters with an accuracy of approximately 10%.

A comprehensive theory is developed to model the movement of a particle under a general order of dynamics, incorporating a retarding force proportional to the particle's higher-order derivatives. A derived expression allows for the calculation of a non-local quantity of motion, demonstrating that, in the presence of a retarding force, the particle's accelerated derivative is directly related to its derivative from n-1 jumps ago. This is further evidenced by numerical computations for n=2 and 3, showing that the accelerated derivative and its past derivatives are connected by an exponential relationship. These results are then applied to discuss the motion of order-n dynamics in a cosmological context, yielding an expression for the universe's age as a non-local quantity.

Our innovative approach combines VR and 3D shape analysis by allowing users to interact with and manipulate vertices in a shared 3D space, interacting through direct force and a push tool. The user-generated shapes and their corresponding color-coded connections are automatically captured and can be retrieved using a learned model based on captured shape data and its relationships, allowing for retrieval based on user-drawn query shapes. The shapes created and retrieved in our study demonstrate the potential for further exploration and development of more complex and intuitive interactions in a shared VR space.

HD 80606 b, a hot Jupiter with a very short 11-day orbit around its host star, undergoes dramatic temperature and flux changes as it moves from the outer cold regions to its inner hot vicinity. This unique system offers a unique opportunity to study various phenomena, such as atmospheric circulation, heat transfer, and thermal emission, with the help of the James Webb Space Telescope. However, the planet's uncertain orbital path hampers the precise timing of its pericenter passage, which is crucial for the host star's peak flux and thust scheduling of JWST observations. To address this issue, we utilized data from a VCST observation of HD 806006b in 2020, along with existing pericenter transit measurements, to create a precise pericenter perihelion update of the planet's pericenter passage.

This study investigates the global feasibility of isentropic perfect fluid collapse with a pressure proportional to energy density, following the relation $p = \alpha \rho$, where the proportionality constant $\alpha$ falls within the range $[0,1]$. Contrary to earlier investigations, our analysis reveals that, due to the constraints imposed by the hyperbolicity of the Einstein equations, once the initial data is set, the system's global behavior is determined, allowing for various scenarios including global collapse or hyperbolicity loss in a finite time, regardless of initial conditions. Moreover, our findings also indicate the possibility of global steady states and matter with vanishingly small initial pressures. Consequently, the feasibility of the various scenarios is fully mapped out without necessitating numerical modeling to identify specific regions in the parameter space, thereby allowing such models to identify the physical mechanisms behind the loss of hyperbolicity and rendering unnecessary the feasibility analysis based on the magnitude of $\alpha$.

By applying the Iyer-Wald formalism, a current is derived for diffeomorphism invariance in general relativity and theories with a second-order Lagrangian. This current, when integrated over the boundary of spacetime using Stokes' theorem, leads to a conservation law. An example in Einstein's gravity reveals the current to be analogous to a charge, with its value determined by the diffeomorphism it represents. This concept has been generalized for arbitrary diffeomorphism theories, including cases in higher dimensions where it relates to charged holes. Halls and Manuland's work on extreme black holes in four-dimensional general relativity is re-evaluated, yielding a new expression for charge that provides an alternative to their original theorem. A similar approach is re-applied to extreme Kerr black holes, rederiving Halls and Manuland's results in this case as well.

A machine learning model called drive is an attention mechanism designed to guide the motor learning process by prioritizing the adjustment of unexplored regions of the input space. Initially, the system selects end-effectives with higher uncertainty and uses them to refine the policy. To effectively measure uncertainty, two methods - the forward pass and the contraction of the dual metric tensor - are proposed to efficiently estimate the uncertainty associated with a single trajectory prediction using a Gaussian process model. Extensive testing was performed on 2D and 3D simulation environments to evaluate the performance of the proposed uncertainty estimation techniques and the 'drive' mechanism, which demonstrated significant improvements over random selection methods in various scenarios.

In vibrant or adjoint Poincar\'e theory, the force-carrying fields are Poincar\'e gauge fields, which are Poincar\'e connections, in contrast to the standard Poincar\'e gauge theory where only the translation sector is used to construct the gravitational field, represented by the tetrad. Poincar\'e transformations are non-trivial on both the matter fields and gauge fields, which leads to a non-trivial dilation of gauge fields in a manner distinct from gauge transformations. This is particularly apparent in a Poincar\'e algebra check, which involves the commutator of Lorentz rotations and translations acting on a force-carrying field, resulting in a field-strength dependence. This is particularly relevant in a non-abelian case, which leads to a non-zero curvatures in a Poincar\'e curvature check. This is the core concept of the vibrant Poincar\'e symmetry, which is used to construct a field-strength-dependent action for a non-abelian gauge field, which vanishes at zero curvatures, in contrast to the standard Poincar\'e theory where a quadratic action of the gravitational field is constructed. This is particularly apparent in a non-abelian case where a locally scale-invariant action of the non-zero first order curvatures is constructed, which leads to a viable dark matter candidate.

This research introduces new algorithmic techniques for drawing directed graphs in an upright position. We develop a linear-time method to identify and remove a minimal set of edges that would make a given directed graph uprightly planar, with a size limit of 'k' edges. Additionally, we create nearly linear time algorithms for creating uprightly planar drawings of specific graph classes, including those with a tree structure and a limited number of overlapping vertex connections, with a complexity dependent on a pre-determined table of values.

Effectively navigating through unfamiliar environments, such as large research campuses, poses a challenge due to navigation memory noise originating from irrelevant personal and third-party experiences. In an attempt to clarify navigation goals by filtering out this noise, previous studies focused on retrieving memories that illustrate the path to reach a target location. Nevertheless, this approach is impractical due to two main issues: (1) memory retrieval is prone to errors when navigating goals are complex, leading to failed navigation attempts, and (2) personal memories are insufficient for navigation as relevant third-party memories are also needed. To resolve these challenges, we introduce MemoNav, a novel memory management system comprising a short-term memory that retains navigation-relevant information and a long-term memory that stores vast amounts of data and filters out irrelevant personal and third-party memories. By filtering irrelevant memories in advance and adaptively managing short-term memory noise during navigation, MemoNav mitigates memory noise affecting navigation performance.

To accommodate the rising demand for mobile data traffic, particularly with the advent of social media and real-time video streaming, mobile network operators have introduced small cells as a cost-effective high-speed data solution. First utilized in 4G networks, small cells are now being integrated into 5G deployments to handle ultra-high data traffic requirements. However, with the approaching 6G era, further advancements in small cell technology are anticipated to meet emerging needs. A comprehensive analysis of the underlying principles, recent developments, and underlying challenges of small cells is presented in this article. It also explores the potential of AI in optimizing6G-based small cell networks and summarizes future research directions for this technology.

Within the interdisciplinary field of network science, the study of dynamical systems plays a crucial role in exploring the behavior of complex systems and their components. This field, as a subset of network science, draws from mathematical disciplines such as algebra, probability, and geometric topology, among others, to analyze dynamic phenomena within the field. This review focuses on a specific subfield of network science, the analysis of dynamical systems in networks, and their building blocks, interacting units or nodes that collectively form a system comprised of a network and dynamic elements. This review begins by outlining fundamental elements of dynamical systems, their typical examples, and common forms of interaction, followed by an examination of the basic framework for constructing and analyzing models of dynamical systems in networks, as well as common types of network interactions and their dynamic elements, such as discrete and continuous variables, master equations, and stochastic processes, which often rely on the fundamental equations of dynamics. This review also examines a variety of dynamic processes that occur in networks, such as spread dynamics, epidemic dynamics, opinion dynamics, synchronization, Hopf dynamics, and chaotic dynamics, as well as dynamic systems that exhibit multistability and nonlocal effects, such as nonlocal coherence resonance and nonlocal phase locking. Additionally, the review discusses dynamic systems in networks that exhibit nonlocal behavior, as well as methods for analyzing the stability of such systems, including the master stability equation, and techniques for generating self-organized structures, as well as general principles that govern the dynamic behavior

Growth of operators under time evolution is being investigated by leveraging quantum variational methods, characterized by two distinct lengths: an spatial extent and a temporal one. As long as the temporal length remains in relation to the inverse of the energy scale, the spatial time correlation function maintains its independence from the temporal length. Growth patterns in chaotic systems are being compared to those in non-chaotic systems where the time-dependent energy is being substituted with its average value. We have devised a universal, five-step procedure for analyzing the time-dependent energy. Our analysis centers on qudit spin chains under the Heisenberg rule, facilitating direct computations as well as semi-classical and random circuit estimations. These multiple approaches yield consistent outcomes, yielding insights into the time-dependent energy's behavior both within and outside of the logarithmic regime. Furthermore, our study of out-of-time-order correlations has led to the identification of their origin, which can be directly derived from these length scales. The findings of our work are also applicable to state preparation through operator growth and to the study of thermalization in isolated quantum systems.

This research details an innovative approach to directly observe the primary state in the nucleus of carbon-12 without relying on the Pauli exclusion principle's zero-range component. To do this, a highly advanced, custom-built, and sensitive Time Projection Chamber with a specialized gas mixture was used, allowing for an examination of head-on collisions between alpha particles and carbon-11 in an solid-state nitrogen-14 target. The results of a three-body interaction led to the creation of the Hoyle state in carbon-12 approximately 0.06 eV above its threshold, and a frequency of 0.4 Hoyle states per 10^19 alpha particles was recorded. Furthermore, a comparison with theoretical models shows that the direct-decay width of the Hoyle state is estimated to be 0.00004 eV, and models also suggest this width could potentially reach up to 0.00006 eV.

Investigating the behavior of cracks in two-dimensional isotropic brittle materials, 
a comprehensive  3-parameter model incorporating both inherent length and time scales 
was used to simulate and analyze the dynamics of a pre-stressed plate fracture. 
Through 3-dimensional numerical simulations, the fracture patterns were mapped in relation 
to material time and length parameters in relation to plate dimensions and pre-stress levels. 
The resulting diagram revealed multiple instability regions characterized by crack branching 
and oscillatory patterns, as well as other fracture modes such as flat cracks, shear kink bands, 
and radial patterns.  Fractures exhibiting crack branching and oscillatory patterns displayed 
dynamic cracks traveling at lower speeds than the universal limit of $\sqrt{K_Ic/E}$, 
while patterns exhibiting periodic oscillations were found to be influenced by time 
and material length material parameters in a manner both necessary to maintain periodicity. 
Additionally, materials with both short time and length parameters demonstrated high sensitivity 
to initial flaws within materials, whereas those with short time parameters but large length 
parameters displayed less variation in crack speed due to initial stress levels and $K_Ic$.

When encoding links with feedback and state information, knowledge of the system's state at the encoder is crucial. For example, certain link types like 2D Gaussian flat fading can benefit from adaptive modulation, where the moment of adaptation matters. Also, for some systems like 2D Gaussian flat fading with memory, encoding methods that utilize state information may be necessary to achieve optimal performance. This paper examines a class of finite-state links with memory, and establishes a condition under which the condition number of the link matrix at its maximum possible value indicates whether state knowledge is essential at the encoder. This result is applicable to various adaptive modulation scenarios and simple links with memory, and it is applicable to a range of adaptive modulation techniques including waterfilling, and it also applicable to a range of simple links with memory.

A unique class of superfluids called topological superfluids has gained significant attention due to their ability to support exotic supercurrents and Majorana zero modes at their edges. These properties make them potential candidates for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation through topological quantum computation. To achieve this, it is crucial to create topological superfluids with a spin singlet ground state, as they are more stable against decoherence compared to their spin triplet counterparts. While the creation of topological superfluids with a spin singlet ground state has been experimentally realized under circumstances with negligible interactions, our study reveals that an attractive Rashba Hubbard model with a moderate interaction strength can give rise to topological superfluids with a spin singlet ground state. By addressing the 2D model using a variational approach with a Slater determinant wave function, we found that the system enters into a topological superfluid phase within a medium interaction strength range. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the topological properties of the superfluid are preserved even after accounting for correlations beyond the mean-field level through our corrections. To our knowledge, this is the first instance where the combination of attraction and spin-orbit coupling results in the creation of topological superfluids with a spin singlet ground state.

This study focuses on developing a method for determining the validity of statements in tabular data found within scientific documents. We focused on tables that contain a mix of factual and inferential statements, such as those in the fields of medicine and biology. To achieve this, we developed a dataset with 2,108 statements and accompanying evidence snippets sourced from peer-reviewed articles. We employed various machine learning models, including BERT-based table-aware configurations and comparative table-agnostic models, to validate each statement and identify supporting information within the document's paragraphs and visual elements. Although we observed that using BERT-based table-aware models yielded better results, all models faced some difficulties in validating tabular statements and locating supporting evidence. We hope this work will help in bringing these tables into the realm of natural language processing and enable the application of modern NLP techniques to validate statements within them.

This article develops an advanced and comprehensive mathematical framework for an expansive and intricate number system, encompassing all possible number combinations of real, imaginary, binary, and all possible variations of these numbers. We establish the fundamentals of this framework by defining its algebraic and analytical principles and demonstrating the and quantum mechanics methods for its implementation. By proving that it aligns with the existing rules of quantum mechanics, we show that it can be used to describe multiple states in physics. In particular, we establish that the parameters of the matrix in physics can be viewed as elements of this complex number system and define its operations. This framework enables the simplification of the matrix algebra used in physics through the application of the Fourier transform and its extension to this context. This advanced number system, being a highly abstract concept, also finds applications in computer science, physics, and the study of fractals.

A $k$-identifying set has the added requirement of correctly representing non-isomorphic graphs with overlapping subgraphs, and a graph's dimension is the smallest size of such a set that meets this criterion. Water tables and groundwater play a crucial role in sustaining ecosystems and supporting human needs for drinking water, with their behavior governed by complex physical principles. A simplified description of water tables and groundwater is provided through the use of the Dupuit-Forchheimer equations, which are widely used in the water resources community. These equations are derived from fundamental groundwater flow and water table conservation principles, offering an intuitive understanding of groundwater flow and water table evolution. A nonlinear, first-order differential equation model for ground water flow is also presented, facilitating analysis using modern control theory techniques. Furthermore, solutions to the water table evolution equation are examined in the context of the groundwater "bathtub model," with results showing the influence of environmental factors such as air temperature and atmospheric pressure on water table evolution. Our analysis of the bathtub model yields insights into the complex dynamics of groundwater flow and water table evolution.

This work proposes an innovative low-energy method to eliminate sulfur compounds in flue gas through the joint application of ultraviolet light and ozone. Utilizing computational simulations, a specific UV wavelength of 254 nm was identified to be most effective for generating both ozone and hydroxyl radicals, which are essential for decomposing sulfur compounds. Subsequently, a laboratory-scale reactor was designed and used to remove SO2 in flue gas at a low temperature of 10°C, operating with a space velocity of 100,000 h^-1 and with and without the addition of ozone, which was supplied at a low concentration of 1 ppm. The results demonstrated that ozone addition significantly enhanced SO2 decomposition in the absence of any catalytic material.

To evaluate neuromorphic architectures, known as virtual platforms, are combined with simulators. Currently, some virtual platforms exist, but they are tailored for specific methodologies, such as mathematical and spiking neural networks, and may be single-threaded, limiting their versatility. A newly proposed solution is SystemC based, supports various computing models, concurrent execution, and the integration of hardware and software within a single thread's context. This paper presents the design of the proposed virtual platform, its fully concurrent implementation, and the custom SystemC components involved. Furthermore, two different simulation methods are examined and their performance is measured. Finally, the feasibility of the proposed virtual platform is demonstrated by simulating two neurocomputing models.

Predicting outcomes in domains with multiple interpretations is a predicted outcome in such scenarios is often insufficient.
Such insufficiency can be mitigated by expressing prediction confidence as a range, but this approach faces challenges in learning accurate confidence intervals.
To overcome these issues, we introduce Indecision Forests, a machine learning method that not only expresses uncertainty as a range but also decouples the difficulties associated with high-dimensional data and narrow confidence intervals.
Experiments on several datasets demonstrate that Indecision Forests produce higher-quality predictions compared to existing methods that generate confidence intervals.

The DTW distance is widely employed in sequence comparison across various fields, but traditional DTW-computing methods are often impractical for similarity search due to their high computational cost. Early discarding, which we have developed, significantly lowers the DTW computation cost by excluding dissimilar sequences from the calculation process. As CTWSE, ED has been used in similarity search within signal processing, its utility has been further expanded to apply to sequence alignment and DTW-computing operations. Our research expands ED's applications to cover more general sequence comparison scenarios and provides theoretical assurances of its effectiveness in reducing computation cost. Our experiments confirm that ED's efficiency in lowering computation cost is particularly pronounced in high-dimensional sequence similarity search and sequence alignment scenarios.

In software testing education, conventional teaching methods such as lectures and demonstrations are often supplemented by hands-on labs and assignments to give students practical experience in writing test cases and assessing system functionality. Current research in this field suggests that traditional feedback on assignments has limited effectiveness. This study investigates the benefits of an innovative inquiry-based conceptual feedback method, which aims to improve students' understanding of software testing principles. Such feedback is individualized and tailored to each student's specific test case and system functionality, providing suggestions for additional tests to uncover potential bugs. Our research involves data from two university courses and demonstrates that this new feedback mechanism results in higher rates of additional test case discovery, better concept mastery, and increased engagement with tests, outperforming traditional thorough feedback. Furthermore, it offers no disadvantages in comparison to the standard feedback approach.

In domains such as autonomous driving and robotics, where Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are used, it is crucial to understand their predictions, especially their potential errors. This need for interpretability can be addressed by incorporating more human-like concepts into the analysis. This paper proposes a novel approach that combines analysis of technical and conceptual pathways in DNNs using a concept analysis and inductive logic programming system, specifically the FCA-ILP AILEN. The system was formed by integrating technical data with conceptual knowledge and achieving effective results on the MNIST and Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark datasets, producing explanations richer in meaning and depth.

One notable achievement in the realm of deep learning graph representation is attributed to Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). Despite notable success, GCNs face a fundamental limitation: their over-blurring effect which hinders their capability in generating distinct representations. To address this issue, solid-state memory (SSM) node representations are proposed to replace the conventional mean-pooling method in GCNs. By leveraging the characteristics of SSM, the SGCN model is developed to enhance node interactions and generate more precise node representations. The novel structure of SGCN not only improves node self-expression, but also generates an over-separable graph representation. Moreover, to evaluate the efficacy of various GCN models, a simple yet effective benchmark is established to address the \emph{distinctness} issue. The experimental results suggest that SGCN surpass existing GCN models in performance, specifically with regard to graph classification and node representation distinctness.

Researchers conducted a search for dark matter associated with a leptonically decaying Z boson in proton-proton collisions at the LHC with 13 TeV of energy. The data, collected from 2016 and totalled 35.9 fb^-1 of luminosity, were analyzed using events featuring opposite charge electrons or muons, significant transverse momentum, and missing momentum perpendicular to the collision axis. The findings conform to the predictions of the standard model and do not support the existence of dark matter associated with a Z boson within the parameters of the model used, in particular the variant with a bi-singlet neutrino character. The results are used to set upper limits on the probability that the Z boson decays into the particles responsible for the dark matter at different momentum thresholds. The study is aimed at validating the dark sector hypothesis of the model in question, in particular the variant with bi-singlet neutrino character. The findings are used to set 95% confidence level upper limits on the probability that the Z boson decays into the particles responsible for the dark matter at momentum thresholds between 1 to 40 GeV. The study is aimed at validating the dark sector hypothesis of the model in question, in particular the variant with bi-singlet neutrino character. This study introduces novel transverse momentum dependent distribution functions, drawing inspiration from single-parton and anomalous anti-parton models. We propose new singlet and octet (quasi)vector quark, scalar quark, and spin-1 gluon parton distribution functions, all dependent on transverse momentum. These distributions are related to GPDs and AQGDs through integrals over specific variables, with a focus on their parton-flavor and spin aspects. We also introduce a set of moments involving longitudinal and transverse momentum, related to DAs and AQGDs. Furthermore, this work relates n-fold longitudinally and transversely momentum-dependent correlators, along with their twist properties, to the $k_\perp$-dependent distribution functions, with applications in hadron physics predictions being discussed.

The proof that Cauchy spaces are discrete topological spaces, as IV.c in our previous paper, is analogous to the proof that long colimits of topological groups are equivalent to dressed spaces, as outlined in our previous research. This led to the conclusion that the category of long colimits of topological groups is equivalent to the category of dressed spaces and isotonic mappings. Given that dressed spaces are a subset of all spaces with a continuous diagonal, further investigation is required to understand how this subclass relates to the broader category of spaces with a continuous diagonal. This paper defines a new type of space, known as a stocking space, as one with a continuous projection to a metric space, and shows that the category of long colimits of topological groups is fully contained within the category of stocking spaces. Additionally, a specific subcategory of stocking spaces, known as rivet spaces, is defined, and a precise description of the full subcategory of long colimits of topological groups is given, showing that it is contained within the category of rivet spaces. This is achieved by introducing the concept of an isotonic projection, as well as a fully rivet space, and proving that long colimits of topological groups satisfy a specific condition, for instance, their projection onto the real line with a discrete topology is surjective and isotonic. This paper is an extension of our previous research as it defines a new type of space and shows that the category of long colimits of topological groups is

Precisely engineered Heusler alloys exhibit a wide range of magnetic and spintronic properties, however, current production methods such as remote epitaxy and van der Waals growth pose a limitation, hindering the creation of high-quality materials with pre-defined crystallographic orientation. A novel approach utilizing graphene as an interlayer has enabled a versatile growth method, allowing for all three remote epitaxy, 2D growth, and hybrid 3D/2D epitaxy on nonpolar and polar substrates. In this study, a series of CrMnSb films, a Heusler alloy with potential ferrimagnetic properties, were grown using CrMnSb/Cr interlayers on various substrates including insulators and graphene/sapphire. By adjusting the growth conditions, a phase transition between 2D and 3D growth modes was observed, resulting in varied morphological features. X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that the CrMnSb interlayer significantly influences the equilibrium between these three epitaxy methods, enabling a reproducible growth of high-quality Heusler films on substrates that do not naturally support this type of growth.

In multivariate time series analysis, we consider a general framework for linear models with potential nonstationarity and heavy tails. Developing statistical tests for unit roots and pre-whitening techniques in multivariate series has proven challenging due to complex interdependencies and limited data. It has been shown that standard tests for heavy-tailed non-fixed multivariate time series consistently fail, leading to inaccurate results. Consequently, modified statistical tests and a novel pre-whitening method are required, which, according to a recent study, can be achieved by utilizing heavy-tailed asymptotics. These findings suggest that multivariate pre-whitening can be effectively achieved using least absolute deviation (LAD) and that modified Lagrange multiplier (LM) tests can retain finite sample power by leveraging heavy-tailed asymptotics.

Recent observations from the James Webb Space Telescope have identified the striking galaxy cluster el Gordo (ACT-CL J0102-$4915, z=0.2737$) as having numerous lensed arcs, which were further studied using near-infrared spectroscopy. This is the first time that the PEARLS (Gravitational-Lensed Arcs in the Early Universe) program has utilized JWST to examine an extragalactic object. The discovery of a lensing arc connected to el Gordo has led to the identification of a red supergiant star candidate, which was identified through the distinctive red color of the arc. This is the first time that a red supergiant star has been found at an extragalactic distance. Additionally, the discovery of new lensed arcs and previously unassociated arcs, along with the red supergiant star candidate, necessitates an update to the el Gordo cluster mass model. This is the first time that the PEARLS program has utilized the capabilities of JWST to study a galaxy cluster and could serve as a guide for similar studies by the program.

The expanding content and services market is driving an increase in bandwidth demands, which existing network infrastructure is struggling to satisfy, leading to deteriorated service quality. A content and service allocation framework has been developed to enhance quality within the constraints of limited network resources and provider profits. The framework employs a Bayesian approach to estimate content demand and network requirements, which informs the development of a profit-maximizing model for optimal content and service allocation. Profits are redistributed through a Shapley-based method, and a contract theory is used to develop profit-sharing agreements between providers and the network operator to boost resilience and interaction, ultimately improving quality. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the profit-sharing contract in increasing provider profits and enhancing the network.

In the field of quantum theory, the link between algebraic and Hilbert space approaches can be understood through a more rigorous, mathematical framework. Building on earlier work by Wiskott, we demonstrate that this connection is founded on a fundamental equivalence between two sets of building blocks: a collection of basic quantum components (states and observables) and a more abstract representation using linear spaces (Hilbert spaces). This equivalence holds true not just in a theoretical sense but also when considering more practical, realizable quantum setups, leading to a deeper understanding of the relationship between these two approaches.

The maximum likelihood predictions from $\alpha$-attractor models in the matter-dominated epoch are evaluated, starting with the standard model featuring cubic sigma-models and an approximately fixed axion field, followed by an analysis of the impact of log-type sigma-models. It's discovered that log-models yield significantly narrower predictions, although they're only marginally aligned with current data from the $Planck$ dataset. It's emphasized that the broad range of $\alpha$ in these models results in an excessively flat $\lambda$ CDM scenario and could lead to unresolved cosmological tensions. To address this, the possibility of an additional, roughly periodic field slowly evolving is explored to expand the effective number of $\alpha$-parameters in these models. We then establish the most likely outcomes for this generalized $\alpha$-attractor scenario. It's discovered that this enhanced scenario yields significantly narrower predictions for several key inflationary parameters, particularly the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$, yielding a maximum likelihood value of $r=0.034$, and a corresponding best-fit value of $\alpha=1.2$. It's concluded that this modified scenario significantly expands the $\alpha$-range, potentially including low $\alpha$ values, and thus offers an attractive, generalized $\alpha$-attractor cosmology.

Building upon previously established findings by Drumm and Tollefson, and more recent work by Drumm and Dalbaki, this study examines whether a specific property holds for the measured foliations at the boundaries of certain hyperbolic manifold structures when they are nearly in a particular canonical form. Specifically, the research proves that if the hyperbolic manifold structures associated with distinct closed surfaces have boundary components that converge to a pre-established canonical structure, the "size" of these components relative to a particular metric will converge to a corresponding "size" for their associated geometric shapes on the structures. The initial step in this proof involves demonstrating that continuous symmetries of these boundary structures within a particular class of hyperbolic manifold structures actually have invariant lines that connect to closed loops on the respective surfaces.

This paper introduces a new concept called the cross-sectional allocation of portfolio returns, and uses it to examine the impact of individual securities' contributions to portfolio performance. It also proposes a statistical method to determine the cross-sectional allocation of future portfolio returns, which can be applied to various aspects of performance analysis. By understanding this allocation, researchers and practitioners can give more precise names to previously anonymous factors, assess how factors are distributed across different dimensions, and make more informed decisions about portfolio construction, such as tilting portfolios to target specific factor allocations or avoiding unwanted side effects.

Heart sound detection, essential for diagnosing cardiovascular disorders, is limited by noise in medical settings.  Computer-aided detection methods struggle to accurately identify heart sounds due to this noise, limiting their practical application.  To address this issue, we developed an improved heart sound classifier based on a novel metric that measures the relative information content of heart sounds, taking into account additive noise and signal distortion.  This metric uses multiple frequency bands to detect heart sounds more accurately.  We demonstrated that this metric offers a more efficient approach to heart sound classification, resulting in a 5% improvement over the current state-of-the-art method and significant performance gains in noisy conditions.  Frequency-weighted noise reduction and a data augmentation technique to simulate real-world conditions are also employed to improve accuracy.  Our proposed system is evaluated on two publicly available datasets, with results showing frequency-weighted noise reduction's effectiveness in improving performance.  Furthermore, a Fourier-transform-based data augmentation method is used to increase training data diversity and improve the classifier's robustness.

A study on ground-state $^{133}$Cs atomic parity violation provides two distinct constraints for new physics parameters in 2020, complementing existing limits on nucleon-scale physics from other methods in $^{133}$Cs. In response to a comment from Kozlov et al. on this study, we provide clarification and additional explanation as necessary.

A twist operator is used to create $U(1)$ vortices with any charge when applied to a $U(1)$ gauge field. Our aim is to find twists that have specific symmetries from 2-D crystallo--graphic point groups, which means they have rotational, reflectional, or both types of symmetry. Our research reveals that for a torus with periodic boundary conditions, only a few (or no) twists have the desired symmetry (they become equivalent to trivial twists). However, when boundary conditions vary spatially, many new twists with symmetry can be created. Our analysis is based on mathematical properties such as covariant transformation, boundary function compatibility, a homomorphism from the group to $H^1(T^2,\mathbb Z)$, and topological invariants like the winding number that represent a twist's topological charge. Our findings have significant implications in the study of topological terms in effective actions under twisted boundary conditions, which arises when systems with momentum are coupled to a $U(1)$ gauge field, such as in the analysis of spin Hall and topological insulators.

In a simulated model of a regional power plant's impact on climate, members of a cooperative make their consumption and emission choices while being influenced by simulated climate conditions. All agents can access a climate monitor that indicates the environment's response to collective behavior. However, not every agent has access to information about individual contributions to climate change. Using a climate game's payoff structure, this study examines the conditions under which cooperative groups can maintain their identity and achieve socially optimal outcomes in the short term as well as in recurrent situations where previous actions and consequences are recorded in a shared ledger. Results indicate that recurrent interactions with recorded consequences can lead to socially optimal cooperation, utilizing the principles of the golden rule of reciprocity. Furthermore, when climate information is individualized, agents are more inclined to engage in cooperative behavior, even without direct communication. Conversely, in the absence of climate data, agents' actions are less likely to reflect cooperation. To further understand the dynamics at play, the study employs machine learning techniques to analyze the relationship between simulated climate effects and agents' collective behavior, revealing that climate data can help agents make more accurate predictions about environmental conditions, thus encouraging cooperation.

This paper extends previously proven results from power series to a more complex space of discrete $H^p$ spaces for a narrower range of $p$ values, specifically between 0 and 1. It defines a set of essential operator tools, including projection, evaluation of Fourier coefficients, multiplication by a series, and a convolution operator. The paper also investigates the duality relationships between these operators, examines the convergence of associated operator expressions and transforms including the Herglotz and Riesz representations, and proves that specific operators act as contracting or isometric operators on spaces of Fourier series, ensuring stability and continuity of these mathematical processes.

Recent second-price auctions have raised concerns due to irregular bidding practices, prompting investigations into the underlying behavior. Researchers have theorized that many bidders might not fully comply with the rules of the auction, potentially due to trustworthy tendencies, such as submitting the highest bid even if it exceeds the item's true value. This study experimentally examines this hypothesis, and the results, with 95% confidence, indicate that around 20% of participants are willing to make such an exception in a second-price auction. To better understand the factors influencing this behavior, the researchers developed a model, which revealed that both the rules of the auction and the cost of violating them significantly impact trustworthy behavior, and that individual differences in the value of honesty also play a significant role.

The mechanism behind the universe's initial anisotropy to present-day isotropy is a significant issue in cosmology. To isolate the influence of anisotropy, a simple model such as the Locally Rotationally Symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I model is used, which can be either a vacuum or non-vacuous model depending on the presence of a cosmological constant or other forms of matter, such as a phantom model or holographic dark energy. By considering the simple quadratic form $Q=\tilde{Q}+\gamma K^2$, where $\tilde{Q}$ represents the geometric properties of a conformally flat Q-gravity and $\gamma$ is a non-zero parameter, researchers can assess the impact of $\gamma$ on cosmological evolution and determine whether anisotropy naturally transitions to isotropy in this model.

We develop a new geometric algorithm for hyperplane arrangement associated decompositions, extending combinatorial methods from Ossona de Mendez and Reutenauer. This decomposition formula applies to any polynomial in a specific poset cohomology ring, allowing the ring itself to be expressed as a direct sum of vector spaces indexed by finite posets, called Frobenius partitions. In the context of Hessenberg spaces and, specifically, regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties, we prove that our algorithm is a Gröbner basis with respect to a suitable term order, and we establish a novel Gröbner basis for the Hessenberg space. This result yields an index set of Frobenius partitions isomorphic to the cohomology grading set introduced by poset Gröbner bases.

Inspired by the success of neural texture synthesis, researchers have explored neural painting, an exciting technique that uses neural networks to generate image segments based on a reference image and user input. While it initially surpassed traditional painting methods in speed and quality, the process remains challenging for users to control and find appealing. To address these issues, a team of researchers from University of Toronto and Yale University developed a neural painting framework that seamlessly integrates user input and optimization goals into a single training step. By using teacher-student training and introducing user and optimization similarity criteria, they achieved a user-satisfactory final result. To enhance user experience, a straightforward system was also created to fine-tune the painting output in real-time. The method's effectiveness and user satisfaction are demonstrated by the authors' findings and a user study showing significant user delight.

The observed anomalies with the labels $K$ and $B$ in observations can be effectively explained by the existence of additional particles, specifically left-handed doublets and right-singlelets, which interact with the weak force. These extra fermions, unlike traditional models, are structured differently and have unique interactions, which is consistent with recent trends in a more fundamental understanding of the matter particles. To further test this model, we examine the decay of the Z boson and produce certain fermion pairs in proton collisions, which can be used to further verify the model's validity.

Current reading-comprehension datasets fall short in reflecting tasks performed by reading comprehension models in real-world settings, as they fail to adequately account for the extensive time researchers spend reading and understanding entire papers to locate pertinent knowledge. Existing datasets primarily concentrate on extracting factual details from given passages, whereas readers often need to traverse the structure of a paper, consult supplementary material, or engage with multiple papers to complete a comprehension task. Our study introduces the Asking Questions dataset and interface, along with labeling guidelines, to capture questions that necessitate accessing knowledge from a broader knowledge base rather than just the text provided in the example. Our model successfully answered 50% of the questions in the dataset in the initial iteration and demonstrated reading skills on par with state-of-the-art models on the standard SNLI dataset. The dataset and associated materials are freely accessible at https://github.com/brandonreilly/AskingQuestions.

In the intense environment of a core-collapse supernova, where massive stars collapse into a black hole or neutron star, several fast neutrino flavor conversions can occur within the collapse region. Researchers have developed new methods to investigate neutrino oscillations in three-dimensional simulations, utilizing novel numerical, analytical, and diagnostic tools. By applying these methods, they have discovered that conditions for neutrino flavor conversions are met in regions as far as the standing shock, where both muon-neutrino to tau-neutrino and electron neutrinos to their tau and tau neutrino conversions can happen. Additionally, these applications have revealed that neutrino flavor conversions can become unstable and lead to the emission of bursts of neutrinos. By modifying initial conditions, researchers have found that different types of fast neutrino flavor conversions can emerge and that this modification can also result in the development of non-linear effects that limit the growth of these conversions. By investigating fast neutrino flavor conversions in 3D simulations, researchers have gained deeper insights into their role in the supernova mechanism and the importance of neutrino self-interactions.

Our brain's functional connections as measured by resting-state fMRI can reveal how brain regions interact, which may deviate in neurological disorders like ADHD. However, the large data volume of rsfMRI makes traditional analysis methods impractical for large studies, and the inclusion of unnecessary regions can introduce noise. To address these issues, we've developed a new approach that uses deep learning to pinpoint ADHD-relevant components within the rsfMRI data. In this paper, we develop a discrete-time model for infectious diseases that accounts for the fact that an infected person can transmit the disease multiple times within a single time step. We define basic reproduction numbers in both the disease's early stages and later stages of an outbreak. By analyzing this model, we determine the conditions under which the disease will disappear or persist. We then apply our model to real-world data on the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City, estimating key transmission parameters and simulating future trends. In particular, we predict that by early August 2020, an additional 150,000 new cases are likely to occur in New York City.

Understanding abbreviations and acronyms in written texts requires complex
processing due to their frequent occurrence and context-dependent nature. To
overcome this challenge, we have developed an experimental system called MadDog,
which analyzes context to accurately identify and interpret acronyms and abbreviations.
Operating via a web interface, MadDog provides a comprehensive service that
processes input text and offers text completion, along with disambiguated
acronym-form explanations, all while maintaining text coherence via a custom
probabilistic model enhanced by external knowledge from Wikipedia and BabelNet.
A detailed description of the system, including its statistical framework, can be
found in a related research paper, which also validates the effectiveness of the
framework in handling complex acronym and abbreviation disambiguation.
MadDog is now accessible to researchers at http://www.mad-dog.org/ and its
development has benefited from involvement of multiple researchers at multiple
institutions over a period of time.

A detailed analysis of heat and electric current flow in a quantum Hall junction has been carried out, with an emphasis on the role of interference. The joint behavior of these currents is found to exhibit periodic variation in response to interference, as evidenced by numerical and analytical studies. This periodicity gives rise to a phenomenon where the direction of heat flow can be controlled, in addition to the previously known electric current toggle effect. Furthermore, evidence of a symmetric, linearly dependent Seebeck coefficient has been found. It is shown that the Seebeck coefficient's value is influenced by electron interference and can be controlled through modifications to electronic band structure or symmetry. This understanding paves the way for achieving toggling Seebeck coefficients of opposite polarities by manipulating interference within the same material system, along with the demonstration of intelligent thermostating and symmetric rectification properties in complex QH networks.

Our new DNA storage approach achieves efficient, large-scale hierarchical indexing and seamless integration of data updates. Our method leverages existing indexing techniques to enable rapid file retrieval and DNA sequence update without waste of resources. Our proposed DNA storage solution acts as a complementary archival option to existing systems, offering enhanced capabilities for hierarchical data management and update insertion.

Two-dimensional systems of Dirac type are often found in momentum space, characterized by nodal lines that pass through points of zero energy, arranged in a linear fashion within the momentum space, often protected by symmetries. When considering a three-dimensional extension, where the momentum space is a 3D space, these protections must be reevaluated as the additional dimension may cause Dirac points to merge and nodal lines to form nontrivial knot structures, such as those seen in the braid group and a 3D space. These constant topological properties impart robustness to the knot-like structures, preventing their dissolution as long as symmetries are maintained. Recent experiments in non-abelian topological insulators and photonic systems have discovered such constant topological properties in the form of photon knots and other photonic phenomena, providing real-world examples of these complex structures and their dissipation as the system transitions from a topological to a non-topological state.

In three-dimensional space, we derive analytical estimates for the translational speed of oscillations in a package of waves generated by a pacemaker in both the underlying medium and its boundary. The estimates are expressed in terms of the intrinsic oscillation frequency of the source and the Eikonal expansion parameters near and away from the boundary, respectively. The obtained formulas are subsequently compared with available analytical and numerical solutions for several established pacemaker models.

A key goal in learning theories of quantum systems is to estimate the entropy of a quantum state. In this work, we focus on developing efficient methods to calculate the Shannon entropy of independent and identically distributed quantum states and the von Neumann entropy of symmetric quantum states. Our approach for symmetric quantum states builds upon the idea of amplitude amplification, a core technique in quantum algorithms. By amplifying low entropy outcomes, we can approximate the entropy with high precision using minimal state copies. Our estimates indicate the required number of copies to achieve a specific error and confidence level is directly proportional to the entropy of the state and inversely proportional to the square of the error and confidence parameters. These estimates demonstrate the optimal dependence on the error and confidence parameters for states with maximal entropy. Furthermore, for symmetric quantum states, our method achieves a similar optimal dependence, although with an additional factor accounting for the overestimation of entropy introduced by sampling without replacement. Our results imply the feasibility of efficiently estimating the entropy of quantum states that arise from sampling a d-dimensional quantum state without replacement, as long as the number of samples used does not exceed the state's dimension.

The intersection of technology, data, and computational power has led to the development of intelligent systems capable of processing complex information. To facilitate intelligent system design, artificial intelligence is supported by a robust technical infrastructure comprising data management, computing resources, and pipeline automation. This chapter delves into key technical components underlying the effective functioning of artificial intelligence. Specifically, it covers data storage, computing capabilities including the role of cloud services, and pipeline management. Additionally, the chapter includes a comparison table highlighting various technical factors and their frameworks, as well as visual representations illustrating storage and pipeline concepts.

This study presents a semi-self-supervised approach for automatically identifying diagnoses from unlabelled electronic medical records. It employs ICD-10 diagnosis codes from patient visit notes in real-world medical settings. The method self-supervises using contrastive learning, eliminating the need for labelled data by generating paired representations of diagnoses code and corresponding patient visit notes. It then trains a diagnosis classifier using this semi-supervised approach and evaluates its accuracy in improving ICD-10 code accuracy without needing labelled data. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves an average 4.4% increase in ICD-10 classification accuracy compared to a commercially available solution and surpasses a method that employs manually labelled data with minimal human annotation requirements (less than 0.5%). The method demonstrates generalizability and robustness across various populations, medical specialties, and changes in clinical practices.
This research focuses on nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals, with a primary objective of classifying nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial prime ideals.

Recent advancements in quantum computing have led to the development of sophisticated quantum machine learning algorithms, despite the existence of fundamental obstacles to their practical implementation. These difficulties are overcome in part by novel algorithms, such as SQUAIL, which, unlike traditional algorithms, can execute a range of tasks without the need for explicit programming. SQUAIL, a unique quantum algorithm, functions through a combination of random unitary evolution and conductance measurements of the quantum current. To optimize its outcomes, classical methods are employed to identify and adjust the associated unitary operators within the algorithm based on analytical performance metrics. Using superconducting transmon qubits, we have successfully implemented SQUAIL to perform classification, clustering, and anomaly detection on both artificial and spin-based dataset classifications.

This study presents a comprehensive compilation of 19 systems discovered by the KMTNet network between 2018's observing seasons, featuring Planetary Anomalies. The discovery data, encompassing 86 new exoplanets and 19 newly found companions, is presented in an easily accessible format via the Exoplanet Explorer website, as well as the Exoplanet Data Explorer. The collection includes comprehensive information on each system, such as identified components and associated uncertainties, and a detailed analysis of potential system interactions is provided. The data for this study can be readily accessed through the Exoplanet Explorer or the Exoplanet Data Explorer.

Optimizing inverse problems via gradient descent often relies on adjoint variables,
which are typically obtained through separate forward and backward passes in adjoint networks.
However, obtaining adjoint variables this way can be impractical due to the memory and
computational constraints, as well as the inflexibility it imposes on the optimization process.
To address these issues, we introduce a method to efficiently and differentially compute
the adjoint of a differentiable function using the vmap and grad primitives in Jax.
This allows us to obtain the adjoint action without the need for an additional network pass,
effectively reducing the memory and computational requirements by half.
We demonstrate the method's versatility on a shadow computation example defined by a matrix,
and apply it to the image deblurring task, achieving comparable results to state-of-the-art
image restoration techniques while using up to five times less computational resources.

Recent research in transportation modeling has shown a need for origin-destination (OD) demand distributions to be modeled as probability distributions, allowing for the characterization of uncertainty associated OD demand, particularly in situations where data is scarce or varies daily. However, estimating the parameters of these probability distributions, which are typically unknown, poses significant computational challenges. These difficulties are compounded when attempting to perform Bayesian inference on OD demand distributions, as the involved integrals are intractable. To simplify this process, we propose a new approach for estimating OD demand distribution parameters, drawing on daily trip statistics and probabilistic OD demand models. To characterize uncertainty associated OD demand, we model each route's travel demand as a random variable, the sum of independent and identically distributed trip requests, and use Bayesian inference to estimate the parameters of its underlying distribution. To make this process feasible, we represent the Bayesian OD demand distribution as a product of independent distribution parameters, and derive an approximate posterior distribution, which is characterized by minimal relevant information loss, using the variational inference method. To further expedite the inference process, we develop a new variational objective function, the VIBNE, which is a sum of the KL-divergence and a regularizer function. To make the variational objective function amenable to optimization and sufficiently accurate, we propose a new objective function, the VIBNE. In an array of non-identical oscillators with multiple stable phases, we observe a counterintuitive phenomenon where the synchronization of these oscillators first increases and then decreases as their difference in frequency grows. This is in contrast to typical single oscillator systems, where higher frequency differences lead to lower synchronization. We provide a mathematical explanation for this behavior and suggest that our findings have significant implications for understanding the coordination of specialized brain areas, such as those in the cortical microcolumnar structure, where small frequency variations coexist with high levels of coordination.

In 1986, Aldous and Broder proposed a two-stage uniform spanning tree (UST) generation algorithm that relied on reversing the underlying simple random walk to create a directed tree. Broader applications of this method have been used in creating other distributions on tree and path configurations in recent years. However, due to the difficulty of verifying USTs generated through this algorithm, temporary equivalences have been used in place of direct proofs in some cases, particularly in works related to postman tours and minimum spanning tree embeddings. Our research proves that both Aldous and Broder as well as Wilson's UUST algorithms are fundamentally the same on an undirected, unweighted grid, at least until the walk reaches the opposite corner, offering a new way to provide the proof for the NP-approximation used in the postman tour reduction, devised by Blum et al. in 1999. Our findings also hold in cases where the underlying graph is an arbitrary, directed quiver, enabling the use of UST algorithms to create uniform paths that can be used to explore alternative constructions for generating spanning trees.

This paper introduces a new dataset, MusicTM-Dataset, which comprises a large collection of sheet music, lyrics, and corresponding music recordings, all meticulously matched. Currently, our model comprises sheet music, lyrics, and music recordings. By constructing this substantial dataset, our goal is to promote the development of accurate musical information extraction algorithms, semantic analysis from musical notation, and network structure discovery. The dataset, along with a model architecture incorporating attention-based notation representation learning and audio and image fusion, as well as an innovative fusion of network structure and notation representation, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Cheng-Kai-Lai/MusicTM-Dataset.

This research paper examines the feasibility of combining natural language processing (NLP) and data visualization (VE) by using word embeddings to enhance visual data exploration. Specifically, the study focuses on Ontodia, a visual data exploration tool that can accept input from free-text queries and ranked lists of实体 (entities) after mapping the non-standard terms to the实体 it employs via a basic knowledge base and the Google Knowledge Graph API. By applying NLP techniques, such as those developed for Wikidata, rankable lists of实体 can be generated and used to create dynamic, interactive visualizations that enable users to navigate and explore the entity data.

The influence of intensity-dependent dispersion on soliton stability in dark solitaries is investigated in this article, where this nonlinearity is modeled after the effective mass variation in matter wave systems. We demonstrate that systems incorporating an intensity-based dispersion model aligned with dark soliton profiles lead to enhanced dark soliton stability. Conversely, systems in which the dispersion shift diverges from the soliton profile have a destabilizing effect. In the absence of external potential and with linear dispersion, dark solitaries exhibit either complete or partial stability. Nevertheless, when external periodic potentials are imposed, existence and stability of dark soliton waves persist in both conservative and non-conservative dispersion systems.

This study examines the concept of structured guidance in various disciplines and presents an innovative approach called Lotse, designed to facilitate user experiences in complex visual analysis tasks. Lotse is particularly useful when researchers face a disparity between available user data and their need for actionable insights, offering a structured framework to bridge this gap effectively. We illustrate the principles of Lotse through a real-world application in the domain of traffic flow analysis and propose an innovative extension called InLotse, which enables users to contribute their own guided solutions to the system.

Recent research focuses on stellarators for their capability to host prolonged plasma sessions, thanks to their error-free 3D equilibrium. Studies suggest a plasma session's duration is limited by non-resonant particle drifts, making them more stable than toroidal rotation. We investigate how to minimize such effects in optimized stellarators by analyzing coil movements and their influence on drifts. Utilizing systems of equations, we determine the ideal coil adjustments to reduce drifts, giving designers a greater degree of freedom and flexibility. Results from our study support the LHD's coil reconfiguration to eliminate the Neoclassical Transport barrier, and the W7-X's outer coil can also be shifted to achieve $dr_{\rm{ex}} = 0$.

A new approach utilizing rapid MRI has been developed to study temperature distribution in gas-solid fixed beds on a process scale, specifically in the 10-100 cm range. By utilizing an electron-paramagnetic-resonance (EPR) active seed, temperatures can be directly measured and maps created. We investigated a 30 cm long and 5 cm diameter fixed bed and verified the effectiveness of this method through comparisons with computational fluid dynamics simulations, which showed strong agreement, which further validated the technique's ability to assess temperature arrangement in similar systems.

To understand cellular self-organization, we developed a theoretical framework for aggregates forming from multiple components, some of which are also part of other combinations. Our model, which is both analytical and numerical, is applied to study the behavior of related biomolecular condensates and viral capsids. Specifically, we derived an equation for the critical concentration at which a mixture of components starts to form a condensate, taking into account the stoichiometric ratios of the components and their mutual interactions. For cases involving similar interaction strengths, we found that the critical concentration can be expressed as a polynomial of degree n+1, where n represents the number of interacting components. Furthermore, we discovered that when a solution contains equal amounts of all components, no phase transition occurs up to a certain interaction strength, after which a small amount of free material remains outside the condensate. Our results also reveal that when certain components are present in higher stoichiometric ratios, no stable phase transition can occur as some material is always left outside. Moreover, we found that when interactions vary significantly, a condensate may still form and its properties can be controlled by manipulating the distribution of free materials. These findings offer a potential control mechanism for regulating the composition of multi-component condensates and could also explain their behavior in viral capsids, where shared components and shared interactions are common. Our study focused on analyzing the rotational behavior of sunspots within a major, active sunspot group located on the sun's surface and centered at 10 degrees West longitude with 2 degrees latitude. Leveraging the HMI Doppler velocity data from the sun's surface, we were able to determine the rotational velocities of different sunspot areas and surrounding regions. Prior to a significant X6.1 flare event that occurred on October 28, 2013, the rotational velocities showed irregular patterns and then began to synchronize, with the rotation periods of different areas becoming comparable to each other. This rotational equilibrium coincided with a rapid restructuring of the sun's surface magnetic field, characterized by a decrease in Cross Helicity Spectrum (CHS) values and enhanced rotation synchronization. Research indicates that these findings are consistent across other flare events and suggest a potential scale-invariant phenomenon governing rotational changes during solar flares.
