This research analyzes the multilevel preconditioning methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems that couple electrical and mechanical systems. A comparative study of three multilevel algorithms - 2FWC, FWCA, and AMGe - is presented, with the latter using an innovative geometric multilevel solver for the finite element problem of cardiac mechanics. A key innovation in this research is the development of an efficient geometric multilevel algorithm that can handle the highly anisotropic nature of the cardiac problem, using a problem-based mesh that accurately represents the cardiac tissue. Furthermore, a rigorous convergence proof for a 2-level variant of the AMGe method is provided, making it possible to efficiently solve large-scale cardiac mechanics problems on modern HPC systems.

The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, prompting a question about the best methods to collect, manage, and utilize these vast amounts of data. A recent study examines the properties of tags assigned to user-generated content through the lenses of reuse, time, information sharing, and collaborative behavior in social tagging systems. To achieve this, the authors introduce an information theory-based model for analyzing social tagging systems and develop time-series and machine learning tools to investigate the dynamics of these systems. By empirically examining Del.icio.us, a prominent social tagging system with a vast user base, the researchers uncover that a small group of users and resources accounts for a significant majority of the system's tags and also explore the potential of using machine learning to predict collaborative behaviors in such systems. These findings provide actionable insights that can guide the design, operation, and management of information systems that handle vast amounts of user-generated data.

Recently developed acoustic metagratings offer new possibilities for controlling and manipulating long-wavelength acoustic waves through compact systems and complex wave phenomena not seen in conventional materials. However, fabricating complex acoustic metagratings at ultra-high frequencies has been hindered by limitations in available technology. Our research demonstrates the capabilities of direct laser writing, a technique allowing the 3D fabrication of complex polymer structures with micron-level precision and thus suitable for high-frequency acoustic applications. We illustrate this potential by designing and fabricating two-dimensional and three-dimensional metagratings at ultrasonic frequencies as low as 25 MHz, exhibiting unusual wave behaviors such as acoustic polarization and refraction. The successful use of direct laser writing thus paves the way for the creation of sophisticated acoustic systems utilizing acoustic metamaterials at ultra-high frequencies.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of strong solutions for the 2-D compressible FENE ribbon model. We demonstrate that the strong solution is globally unique and its average density converges to a uniform distribution as time goes on. In addition, under the condition of initial average density matching a given domain measure, we have demonstrated that the strong solution behaves similarly to the corresponding steady-state weak solution as time goes on, where the average density matches a given domain measure.

The growing demand for high-speed, ultra-low latency wireless connections is driving the need to expand cellular coverage, especially in venues with signal-blocking structures and remote areas with weak signals. Integrating network access points on mobile devices via vehicle signage is one potential solution to meet these needs. We explore the feasibility of using mobile vehicle iWARP architecture to support C-V2X applications and compare it to optical backhaul vehicles. We analyze the performance of different vehicle backhaul architectures using real-world traffic data, resulting in a proposed flexible vehicle backhaul architecture that meets specific design requirements, demonstrating its ability to provide multi-Gigabit bandwidth with low latency.

In optimization, hyperparameter tuning of evolutionary algorithms is crucial yet time-consuming, often necessitating adjustments to multiple parameters and resulting in no universally ideal settings for all problems. To tackle this issue, this research employs two distinct methods of global sensitivity analysis to both identify significant and synergistic effects among hyperparameters and evaluate the relative importance of others. Utilizing genetic algorithms as a case study, this study conducts experiments on 10 benchmark functions, allowing us to determine whether certain hyperparameters consistently produce superior ranking across various scenarios and whether an underlying probabilistic model can effectively predict their performance. Notably, this study also reveals that some hyperparameters not only matter in isolation but also exhibit synergistic effects when combined, whereas others demonstrate consistent importance regardless of context.

The paper addresses key aspects of quantum theory by adopting a wave-based approach to describe a quantum system at time 't'. It derives essential equations, including one equivalent to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for a system with one particle and no potential, as well as a version of the continuity equation that holds for all potentials one particle can have. The paper also demonstrates the general applicability of the continuity equation and provides two equivalent expressions for the time rate of change of the expectation value of an operator. These results are achieved without relying on a wave equation, assuming an operator has a discrete set of eigenvalues and associated eigenstates, which lead to the development of the spectral theorem applicable to such operators.

Despite notable achievements in centralized reinforcement learning tasks, lesser success has been experienced with continual learning applications. To bridge this gap, L2Explorer is introduced, a novel evaluation platform for lifelong learning in 2D exploratory tasks. This introduction delves into several challenges and offers potential solutions within the context of exploratory tasks. Furthermore, multiple state-of-the-art methods for handling lifelong learning are presented, including existing approaches, transfer learning strategies, and novel implementations. It should be noted that this work serves as a detailed companion to our corresponding paper of the same name.

Liger, a next-generation infrared camera at the W. M. Keck Observatory, features a data processing system composed of multiple software components that work together to handle data. This system is comprised of four main interfaces: a Field-Programmable Gate Array, a Host Computer, a Data Storage system, and a software package called DLAND, each responsible for specific data processing tasks. The Field-Programmable Gate Array manages detector readout and initial data filtering, while the Host Computer performs data alignment and reduction, and orchestrates the workflow with the Data Storage system, handling data transfers to and from Liger. This interface is complemented by the Data Storage system and DLAND, which manage data archiving and initial data reduction.

In this study, we've discovered a family of non-Couette type steady-state solutions to the 2D Euler equation, with given nontrivial vorticity on the periodic line $\mathbb{T}^1$ and an unknown velocity field's normal component at the boundary. The normal velocity can take any real value, with corresponding distinct Couette flow solutions. Our empirical data suggests that this family of solutions may be the only set of 2D Euler equation steady-state solutions with periodic velocity in one direction and a given vorticity distribution, with periodic fields in both directions reducing to ODEs and thus having an exhaustive list of solutions.

We investigated the optical control of polarization in a pair of exciton-polariton condensates that are weakly interacting with each other. Our study revealed that in an isolated condensate, an optically pumped defect creates a spin texture due to the Zeeman effect, resulting in a specific polarization pattern outside the defect area. This specific polarization can be harnessed to redirect a probe beam through a process called stimulated scattering, whose efficiency is wholly controlled by an optically pumped defect without any changes in intensity. In a couple of condensates with weak interactions, our study found that a condensate in a "spin up" state will selectively scatter a probe beam if it's oriented perpendicularly to a condensate in a "spin down" state if it's oriented parallel to the pump beam. This interaction-based polarization manipulation exhibits a specific sensitivity to polarization arrangements, making it relevant for applications in classical polarization logic operations.

This study is set to determine a deterministic stochastic growth equation corresponding to a nonlocal version of the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation. The researchers refer to this equation as a nonlocal deterministic equation with a martingale problem, which they solve using a new approach that doesn't require any existing theories to be applied locally. The equation is referred to as having a nonlocal "slope term" due to the dependence on the slope of the function being measured over a specific distance based on the function's initial conditions. In order to make the equation solvable, they modify it into a deterministic evolution equation that is well-posed in a specific mathematical space. Additionally, they study the stability and regularity properties of the equation and their results show that it has improved regularity and stability compared to the locally defined equation.

In response to the COVID-19 outbreak, our team developed an agent-based model of infectious disease transmission that utilizes real-time, location-specific, and demographic data from OpenStreetMap for the city of Johannesburg, South Africa. Our model's simulation results were then used to develop a machine learning classifier capable of predicting infection and death rates based on local map data. The classifier was employed to analyze potential COVID-19 spread in and around Johannesburg. Our approach demonstrates how freely available map data can support public health initiatives, potentially allowing for scalable map data modeling of infectious disease transmission that could benefit regions with limited health surveillance systems.

In 1961, Freiman demonstrated that the 'critical' $3k-1$ elements of an abelian group, whose sumset contains at least $2k-1$ elements, form a subset that has the size of its projection into a one-dimensional group closely modeled by an arithmetic progression. For a specific range of values between approximately $0.74$ and $0.81$, we verify this relationship in a broader context, and also demonstrate the validity of the relationship at specific values of around $0.71$, $0.73$, and $0.79$, and discuss the size of the projection at a value of around $0.7$. Additionally, we establish the validity of the relationship of Freiman's $3k-4$ theorem, and discuss a variation of the relationship of Freiman's $3k-5$ theorem.

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved automated disease diagnosis and treatment planning. In this research, we build upon existing knowledge by developing novel techniques to combine data from multiple modalities for improved classification of retinal disease. Specifically, we design a new architecture that integrates image and text information from retinal fundus reports to enhance glaucoma classification on the ORIGA dataset, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by achieving higher accuracy on DR classification with the AIDE dataset.

To tackle limitations in large-scale clinical data for COVID-19, we utilize semi-supervised learning to enhance classification accuracy and create a novel framework for identifying ICU-related characteristics from chest X-rays. Even with minimal labels, our method effectively captures complex patterns in the data, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional deep learning approaches that rely on ample annotated datasets. This innovation eliminates the need for time-consuming and costly ICU stays, making it possible to screen and select high-risk COVID-19 patients who require ICU admission. The proposed method achieved remarkable results, outdoing existing deep learning and traditional machine learning models in the ICU in selection task, with an impressive accuracy of 79.2%.

This study introduces novel analytical techniques to derive first-kind transmission eigenvalues and corresponding transmission eigenfunctions for spherically layered materials. The mathematical framework relies on a combination of Goedecke's theory and the T-Eigenvalue Problem. The outcome is a set of criteria that allow for the determination of boundaries based on transmission eigenfunctions, which may be of significant use in acoustical device design and medical imaging systems.

To effectively engage with users in dialogue, it's crucial to identify their underlying intentions. Intent Discovery plays a vital role in various dialogue systems such as Task-Oriented Conversational Agents and Dialogue Topic Detection. We've developed a new approach, called PID, which builds upon our previous work, by combining pre-training and contrastive learning to accurately discover user's underlying intentions from their casual and often fragmented statements. PID's architecture consists of two main components: a language model pre-trained on a large corpus of dialogue texts to capture general patterns, and a low-rank intent matrix that captures the specific intentions relevant to the task at hand. By leveraging a contrastive learning approach, PID can effectively match user statements with the most relevant intentions, even in cases where the intended meaning is ambiguous. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that PID achieves state-of-the-art performance on three benchmarks for Intent Discovery.

The n-simplicial abelian group F(A) is constructed based on the free abelian group A generated from an n-set. When A is defined as the free cyclic group corresponding to the n-set with a generator g, the result F(g) exhibits a higher level of algebraic structure, which we suggest may be represented as an n-cyclic space or an n-fold cyclic object within the context of n-simplicial objects.

In group theory, it's a basic understanding that every finite group contains some subgroups. However, determining the exact number of subgroups within a given finite group can be quite complex, especially since each subgroup is uniquely defined by a subset of its members. Until now, only limited upper limits on the number of subgroups in finite groups had been established, such as those set by Huppert in 1967 and later improved upon by specific results in primes and prime squares. This article aims to establish a broader upper limit on the number of subgroups in finite groups, given the following formula: the number of subgroups is less than or equal to the number of subgroups in the symmetric group of the same order, where the exponent is the sum of the ranks of the prime factorization of the group's order.

In 1986, Balmain, Scott, and Scott presented the balmain-scott-scott h2 equation, 
a modification to the Korteweg-de Vries equation that accounts for the effect of 
variable H2 on the Korteweg-de Vries equation, in which H2 denotes Henry's law 
constant and varies with temperature and solute concentration. The revised form 
of the equation is expressed as u_t + (u^2u_x)_x + (u^2u_x)_x = 0. The purpose of 
this project was to examine the balmain-scott-scott h2 equation through numerical 
simulation in order to understand its real-world implications in the context of gas 
absorption in liquids. The study employed a second-order, conservative finite volume 
method for its numerical solution, and an iterative fixed point method was used to 
ensure the solution's convergence and stability.

The Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) task, which involves identifying objects and their relationships in an image, is plagued by a significant problem known for mistakenly overlooking false positives. Research has shown that the problem stems from ambiguous relationships between simple objects, such as "table-lamp," which is harder to detect than "cabinet-lamp." In this study, a new dataset called Complex-Relations was introduced to address the issue by providing morechallenging examples with complex relationships. Additionally, the authors proposed an enhanced detection framework called Complex-Relations Network (CRN), which takes a multi-scale approach to detect relationships at various levels of detail. By pre-training the feature extractor on COCO and fine-tuning the relationship classifier on Complex-Relations with data augmentation, the model was able to outperform existing methods in multiple COCO benchmarks, including the standard 20-point and more rigorous 20-point-R120. Furthermore, the model demonstrated superior performance in detecting numerous relationships, such as those found in the VRV-20, with a significant improvement in F1 scores of up to 14.4 points.

The price of quantum correlation is determined by the amount of a resource needed to create a specific measurement and associated key information through legitimate means in a quantum key distribution protocol. A novel approach is presented to evaluate the price by limiting the access a potential eavesdropper has to the price information. Using this approach, a price of 0.25 is found for weak measurements performed on the BB84 protocol without post-selection. It's further demonstrated that our price of quantum correlation aligns with the Datta-Preskill price when utilizing key bits from a specified range of the BB84 protocol, providing a broader understanding of quantum correlation pricing.

This paper proposes a method for creating a socially connected image database by extracting and visualizing human interactions within images, ultimately forming a graph that depicts social relationships among people. Our approach employs an attention network to simultaneously generate relationship graphs and visual attention maps, all while people are identified within images. Notably, we've developed a custom loss function that overcomes limitations imposed by unevenly distributed data, enabling end-to-end training of the method. To assess our method's effectiveness, we've introduced a new benchmark: the SRGB task, which differs from existing person relationship detection tasks by allowing a broader array of social interactions to be identified, including more subtle relationships such as friend, foe, uncle, etc. As such, we've created a new training dataset and corresponding evaluation metric to better assess our method's performance on the SRGB task.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are widely regarded as the de facto standard in visual recognition, primarily because their use of regular convolution operations and shared weights simplifies learning and parameter usage. Nonetheless, these properties may be restrictive in certain contexts, such as when dealing with variable spatial relationships and differing object or part scales within an image. To address these challenges effectively, neural networks need to adapt their communication patterns dynamically, allowing more flexible learning of spatial dependencies between regions and varying scale relationships between sub-regions. Our proposed method involves redesigning CNNs by incorporating dynamic graph structures that adapt their connectivity patterns based on the input data, paired with graph neural networks for region-scale-aware representation learning. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of dynamically communicating networks over conventional local-viewpoint CNNs and other state-of-the-art vision models on multiple challenging tasks, including image classification, visual relationship detection, and semantic segmentation.

8-bit fixed-point arithmetic is the most prevalent method used in digital signal processing, particularly for constant multiplications, which are frequently performed operations. Researchers continue to develop low-expense multiple constant multiplication (MCM) techniques that utilize addition and subtraction to achieve efficient single constant multiplication. However, accurately assessing the expense of performing many addition and subtraction operations can be challenging, often leading to excessive expense estimates in the design of the corresponding digital circuit. In this research, various single and multiple constant multiplication methods are proposed or adapted to significantly decrease the number of addition and subtraction operations required to execute 8-bit fixed-point operations on FPGA. Our results show these designs achieve approximately 50% reduction in estimated addition and subtraction operations in comparison to the existing state-of-the-art design of a specific decoder for NVIDIA's FTOR image compression method, with improvements ranging from 15% to 55% over other designs for performing 8-bit fixed-point operations on specific NICs. These innovations pave the way for more efficient implementation of the FTOR image compression method on actual hardware.

Quantum machine learning is emerging as a growing field within quantum information science, aiming to explore and develop novel, potentially more efficient algorithms to address established machine learning problems. Among the many proposed quantum algorithms, quantum neural networks have received significant attention recently. This article provides a comprehensive review of quantum neural architectures, covering their key principles, applications, and obstacles. It also outlines promising directions and possibilities for future research and development in quantum machine learning.

The radio frequency accelerator community is anticipated to continue contributing to the innovative developments in accelerators over the coming decade.  Our research has been conducted with input from the entire community and has proposed a research program for the next decade, which included setting broad goals, identifying key issues, and providing recommendations for future funding and infrastructure and fundamental research and development activities.

A unique muon collider offers the potential to extensively explore new physics at a high energy level and to perform precision tests of the electrowe force. However, the potential of muon colliders is hindered by the rapid decay of muons due to their short lifetime and the issue of "bloating" in phase space that occurs when a high-energy beam is slowed down to inject it into an accelerator. Recent breakthroughs in the design of muon colliders, which include innovative injection methods and new concepts in acceleration and focusing, are described in this study. These innovations are expected to significantly advance the feasibility of future muon colliders, which could play a crucial role in advancing our understanding of particle physics.

The types of wave patterns that can form in a fluid are determined by its relativistic properties, regardless of its viscosity. A recent study has proven that only two wave patterns, entropy diffusion and sound propagation, can exist in a first-order model of a viscous fluid, where the amplitude of the patterns is influenced by viscosity. This result was previously a complex assumption in establishing that first-order models can accurately describe fluid behavior. This finding can also be applied to higher-order models of viscious fluids.

Our research investigates the potential background of PBH particle emissions in PBH-induced supersymmetry breaking models, specifically PBH supersymmetry breaking (PSB) models. These models arise when PBHs reside at the center of supersymmetry, with the first such proposal introduced by Bunch and Bunch in 1984. We evaluated a range of PBH-induced supersymmetry breaking models and discovered that PBH emissions can generate a notable background of light superpartner particles. These findings present an exciting opportunity for PBH-induced supersymmetry breaking models to be explored at the Large Hadron Collider. Based on our analysis, PBH particle emissions can originate from PBHs as small as the Planck mass, particularly in a R-symmetry breaking model where the particle spectrum includes the lightest neutralino and a left-handed gluino. These models encompass, but are not restricted to, an R-symmetry breaking model proposed by Bunch and Bunch in 1984 where PBH-induced supersymmetry breaking yields the lightest supersymmetric particles as the lightest neutralino, a left-handed gluino, and a left-handed gravitino.

A RISC-V based processor, high-performance computing, and secret-sharing based security protocols present challenges in ensuring data protection within embedded systems. To address this, we present the Virtual Safeguard Platform (VSP), a solution that enables secure processing of secret shares. VSP is constructed using the Hardware Security Architecture (HSA) hardware standard and implemented using the System and Power Interface (SIF) interface. Furthermore, we offer the Virtual SIF (VSIF), a complete software interface that facilitates secure processing of secret shares on systems based on RISC-V architecture, specifically the Xtensa architecture. Using the VSIF interface, we developed a 5-stage pipeline processor that supports the execution of C code and the decryption of shared values via a custom decryption module. Through this, we achieved a useful and shareable secret sharing approach that overcomes the limitations of traditional hardware security approaches. As a proof of concept, we implemented the VSP on the Texas Instruments TM4C123G2528FZADDER RISC-V based system, where we verified its effectiveness in executing C code under the constraints of secure processing of shared values. Our results show that the VSP's share decr module has a latency of 1000 cycles and consumes 8000 cycles of execution time, which corresponds to a secure and efficient solution for embedded systems requiring data protection in embedded systems.

This study presents an efficient, polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) specifically designed to address a range of general-valued optimization problems that have previously been challenging due to NP-hardness. The research expands upon an earlier, parameterized-approximation scheme concept, yielding a more practical approach by reducing its parameter dependence and achieving a parametric bound of O(n^(f(k))) for some constant exponent. For specific problems like Maximum k-Coloring and Maximum k-Bipartite Subgraph, we refine our approach to achieve improved bounds of O(n^k). The developed PTAS method builds on three core strategies: initial reduction to bounded-instance sizes, an integer programming formulation of the problem, and the utilization of fractional solutions, all of which were first explored within the context of parameterized approximation but are now applied in the setting of PTAS.

This paper explores unsupervised few-shot learning approaches for understanding the nuances of human emotions and judgments within pre-trained language models, without the need for extensive annotations. We utilize pre-trained models and their associated word embeddings, to statistically analyze emotions and judgments on a large, unlabeled dataset of Wikipedia articles, utilizing clustering, principal component analysis, and network analysis. Our findings reveal that pre-trained models, especially those fine-tuned for various tasks, can effectively capture emotions and judgments on unseen texts. Furthermore, we tested our models on tasks requiring few-shot training, including detecting sarcasm and recognizing facial expressions, without any prior exposure to those texts. To validate the robustness of our models, we conducted dimensionality reduction and analysis on few-shot training data, demonstrating that pre-trained models, especially those fine-tuned for few-shot tasks, can effectively learn transferable representations that can be applied to new data.

Our proposed approach for weakly-supervised semantic segmentation utilizes readily available hyperspectral imaging data to achieve significant reductions in the number of required labels for training, specifically in the context of separating urban landscapes from backgrounds. By leveraging unsupervised domain adaptation and the inherent advantages of hyperspectral data, our method achieves high accuracy in segmenting cityscape images with few shots, while maintaining a low computational cost and making use of easily obtainable labels such as superpixels or color regions. Experimental results confirm that our approach outperforms traditional unsupervised adaptation methods and achieves remarkable performance even with only 10 shots, surpassing even fully-supervised segmentation models trained on the entire dataset.

A novel approach is proposed to investigate the origins of the rotation rates of massive stars, especially those with the highest known spin rates, and to explore the hypothesis that planets may have influenced their spin rates. Angular momentum exchanges between the star and its surrounding disc, as well as those that could have occurred with embedded massive planets, are examined using observational evidence and theoretical models to assess the likelihood of this hypothesis, and alternative explanations for the angular momentum transfer are also considered.

We adapt the standard RAM model to a basic version that only permits addition as an operation, making it similar to a collection of registers linked by a basic function called fetch-decode-execute (FDE). This modified model can be used to study the fundamental capabilities of computational functions by examining which operations can be executed in constant time, measured by the number of fetch-decode-execute steps. We have redefined this time measure to include a basic step for pointer arithmetic, which is unbounded in nature, but still consider functions with polynomial growth as executing in polynomial time, where the exponent of the polynomial is directly related to the function's description size. We have proven that even with the standard RAM model's capabilities, such as hashing and array access, a time exponent of one and two-thirds is the minimum for certain functions like the median, which is executed in at most two steps in the basic operation-based RAM model. We have developed a universal hash and a data structure that uses at most two fetch-decode-execute steps to perform unordered searching and selection. We have proven a lower bound of one and two-thirds for selecting the kth element, showing that even with limited work, at least two additional fetch-decode-execute steps are needed. We have translated our results to a time-per-step model and found a simple reduction from 1 to 1 and two and third. Co-training has long been utilized in various domains, such as multi-view learning and click-based recommendation, to enhance recall, yet has not been successfully applied to session-oriented recommendation. This field presents unique challenges, particularly in obtaining accurate user interest labels from click sequences. Presenting users with irrelevant items can result in negative impacts, making session-oriented recommendation even more difficult. To achieve recall improvement in session-oriented recommendation, this study presents a novel self-supervised graph co-training method. It employs two self-supervised techniques to generate reliable labels for session-oriented recommendation. Firstly, a new self-supervised signal is designed to counteract the bias of single-view click data and a corresponding self-supervised learning algorithm is developed to generate a robust multi-view user graph. Secondly, a direct bi-view user graph algorithm is proposed to generate a multi-modal session-oriented recommendation graph. This method's generalisability is further demonstrated by its extension to suitable for knowledge base augmentation. Empirical results show that our proposed technique outperforms existing baselines in terms of recall and does not significantly sacrifice precision to achieve this.

This research focuses on linear code design using group theory, specifically focusing on LCD and reversible LCD codes from a coding theoretic perspective. A newly proposed method, known as group reverse-Lewin transform, is used to construct new types of linear codes, including group LCD and group reversible LCD codes, from existing group codes and LCD codes. It is found that the transformed group reverse-Lewin codes are equivalent to a combination of the original code and its dual, providing a novel way to create these codes. It is also proven that all group LCD codes and reversible LCD codes can be represented as group reverse-Lewin codes and codes with a specific property related to duals. These findings offer a new approach to the design of linear codes and have practical applications in code construction.

We establish a general theory to compute homology in an intricate infinite-dimensional space of oriented degree-one shapes on a specific infinite graph complex, known as the orientable matroid complex, and apply it to solve practical problems in Feynman integrals and rational target spaces. The cohomology of this space is understood through a set of novel, explicitly defined, and universally invariant differential shapes, whose dual basis in homology is also identified. These innovative methods enable the development of efficient new techniques for Feynman integrals and provide a novel approach to the study of target space rationality.

A study on how objects are processed in the primate brain revealed that certain object features are linked to category rather than specific features. This research found that recurrent neural networks with hidden layers similar to those in the brain were able to develop a preference for category-based object features when trained to recognize objects. This discovery provides a deeper understanding of how objects are processed in the brain and how artificial networks can be optimized for better performance in visual tasks.

Non-reciprocal transport in coupled wave systems leads to the formation of topological phases characterized by point nodes and skin effects. While previous studies have documented this phenomenon in models with uncorrelated spectral weights, this work investigates the impact of correlations on this type of topology. By examining the entanglement spectrum of a model system, it is demonstrated that correlations significantly affect the topological phase diagram, resulting in a transition from winding to cluster winding numbers. Such correlations also give rise to interactions between bulk points and edge modes, causing a shift in energy levels and altering the non-Hermitian skin effect's behavior. These findings are validated through the construction of a three-port photonic circuit that exhibits topological point-gap topology despite the presence of correlations.

Recently, Golay complementary arrays (GCA) of length $p^s$ have been created using a recursive technique, where $p$ is a prime number and $s$ is a positive integer. These arrays allow $P$-component polyphase decomposition when $p \leq G(2)$, which enlarges the applicable range of prime numbers in several optical and radar applications. We use a recursive approach to create GCA of length $p^s$ and develop certain designs of GCA with a polyphase decomposition structure.

The LHCb is currently conducting experiments on Higgs boson production and decay processes involving four leptons as the final state, both for on-shell and off-shell scenarios. On-shell Higgs boson decays into two leptons and two neutrons are being studied using the dilepton invariant mass range of 120 to 140 GeV. Off-shell processes are investigated in the 80 to 130 GeV mass range for one pair of same-flavoured leptons and 110 to 140 GeV for the other pair. The LHCb is the only experiment capable of studying off-shell Higgs boson production and decay in the two-photon final state, with current analysis limited to four muons as the final state. The future LHC is expected to be more sensitive to on-shell and off-shell Higgs boson data, especially in the context of its width, as an alternative approach, or its anomalous couplings to vector bosons.

Incorporating deep neural networks, particularly in unsupervised change detection for remote sensing, can effectively identify alterations within images without requiring labeled data. Our proposed method, a multi-dimensional deep convolutional neuromodulator, integrates input image features across various layers to enhance its change detection capabilities. The framework consists of four main sections: two autoencoders for dimensionality reduction and two deep convolutional neuromodulators for unsupervised change detection. The latter integrate their respective compressed feature sets to effectively capture both common and distinct features between images. By training our framework on the MUMAD and RSID datasets, we demonstrated its superior performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Let $h_g$ denote the smallest possible number of colors in a $h$-coloring of the positive integers such that each color uses at most $g$ distinct squares, with the equation $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$ holding for all triplets $(x,y,z)$. This study determines a precise formula for $h_g$ and its corresponding smallest value of $g$ that ensures this minimum number of colors, which is $h_{37} = 8$. To support the research, we developed a 8-coloring of square triplets with 37 different square values. This was achieved through the utilization of computational tools, which we now use as part of an automated system to verify mathematical conjectures on square relationships.

Quantum interference is a fundamental phenomenon in advanced silicon electronics, particularly vital in developing spin-based devices at the atomic level using gate-controlled junctions. While interference in silicon junctions has been extensively studied at frequencies below 1 GHz, incorporating spin is crucial for functionalizing these junctions. Our work utilizes electron transport through a molecular junction to study interference patterns of electron waves in silicon, incorporating spin effects via Raman scattering measurements of silicon vibrational modes under varying bias conditions. Our findings reveal a connection between interference and energy exchange with the environment, particularly showing that variations in interference affect electrons' ability to exchange valley degrees of freedom in silicon, as supported by numerical simulations based on a phase-coherent model incorporating higher-order scattering paths.

Nonconvex optimization is a rapidly evolving field with applications in various fields such as engineering, biology, and computer science. However, most existing software libraries for optimization, like IPOPT and CVX, struggle with nonconvex problems due to limitations in solving algorithms and implementation flexibility. In response, an open-source tool called LibOPT has been developed to enable rapid prototyping of advanced soft optimization techniques. Built on top of Eigen and MPI-PoS, LibOPT supports the creation and evaluation of scalable, nonconvex optimization algorithms on large-scale and resource-constrained systems. It includes a vast number of built-in optimization building blocks and a collection of benchmark problems to facilitate and validate new optimization methods.

The research project aims to measure the transitivity degree of a finite group's action, particularly when that group acts uniformly on a set. To achieve this, we are investigating whether a certain type of algebraic structure, called homogeneous, can effectively model group orbits in both algebraic and geometric contexts. By establishing a connection between the number of group orbits and the degree of transitivity, we are developing new methods to analyze and quantify the extent of a group's action. To illustrate the practical applications of these findings, we are applying the theoretical framework to specific examples, such as the McLaughlin-Liebeck transitivity series and the Mathieu groups.

In non-commutative spacetime, the positions of space coordinates do not interact symmetrically, as shown by the equation $[x^\mu, x^\nu] = 2i\theta^{\mu\nu}$. We explore the impact of this asymmetry on identical quantum particles that occupy the same state. Our analysis includes a simple two-particle system to understand the asymptotic behavior of non-commutative quantum mechanics and how it changes the symmetry. We then extend this understanding to non-commutative field theory using a $\phi^4$-type interaction, as shown by a path integral representation and a perturbative expansion. We calculate the first-order corrections to the interaction and derive a non-commutative version of the four-point function, which shows how the asymmetry parameter $\theta$ affects the outcome. We also derive an effective interaction and find that, to first order in $\theta$, the asymmetry can be seen as equivalent to a Gaussian smearing of the interaction. Our findings suggest that the asymmetry parameter $\theta$ has implications for particle identity and may allow us to distinguish between like and unlike particles in non-commutative quantum field theory.

High-purity single-crystalline diamond is gaining attention in charge sensor development for large-scale particle colliders at future facilities, such as the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). To produce high-quality sensors, single-crystalline diamond has to be carefully grown to minimize grain boundaries within the material. However, it's not clear how these grain boundaries affect the diamond's performance in different types of sensors, such as those using the resistance change, capacitance change, and charge collection methods. This study uses the transient voltage technique with two-photon absorption to create a 3D visualization of the diamond's charge transport properties. By doing so, the researchers were able to observe a significant increase in charge collection efficiency at areas with grain boundaries, and determined that the diamond's charge transport efficiency is $ e \sim 0.74 $. This finding suggests that synthetic single-crystalline diamond is a promising material for building large-area time projection chambers, andS other diamond-based detectors even in regions with grain boundaries.

This research introduces a comprehensive methodology for identifying levels of misogyny in social media texts and classifying them into various categories. The proposed methodology utilizes a deep learning model that integrates pre-trained FastText, Word2Vec, and BERT Arabic embeddings to enhance performance. The model was tested on a manually labeled dataset comprising 1,029 texts related to Arab misogyny, with an initial phase of evaluation focusing on detecting misogyny and determining performance using multiple evaluation metrics. Subsequent analysis involved a sample dataset of 50 texts to validate the model's ability to identify misogyny and categorize it accurately. The study addresses a notable knowledge gap by presenting the first systematic approach to addressing misogyny detection and classification on social media platforms in the Arab world.

This study seeks to solve open problems related to solving nonlinear equations involving memory effects in fractional stochastic environments, which is crucial for predicting the evolution of systems influenced by both random and memory-related factors in various real-world applications. To achieve this, we first establish key assumptions required for solution existence, then prove solution existence and uniqueness under specific conditions, ultimately establishing connection between modified and original equations through related fixed-point problems and continuous paths.

We examine the potential for developing adaptable control systems capable of operating in diverse and changing environments. To achieve this, we initially create a probabilistic model-based policy search method that utilizes a transition probability function to facilitate efficient policy iteration and knowledge transfer across multiple control tasks, all while operating in a fixed environment. Building on this foundation, we extend the framework to robust control by integrating a robust version of Bellman equation iteration that accounts for environmental uncertainties. To overcome the computational complexities of optimizing robust policy iteration, we employ value-based and policy-based optimization techniques that prioritize environmental robustness without requiring direct action parameterization. The final framework, termed robust policy search, enables the development of adaptable policies applicable to multiple real-world scenarios, as demonstrated in a series of aerial navigation tasks executed on physical drones.

This study presents a generalized, unified framework that combines two fundamental information retrieval methods: coded caching and network computation. The unified framework enables analysis of various novel schemes and offers three key advantages: (1) standardization of design, analysis, and performance evaluation for new schemes; (2) straightforward discovery of existing methods through specific choices within the framework; and (2) a systematic, optimized approach to designing new schemes within the framework's parameters.

We establish a fully abstract model of Scott's domain equation T = Y → T in univalent type theory by proving the Scott continuity theorem and constructing an initial algebra for a corresponding polynomial functor.

The focus of this paper is on a specific approach to eliminating pole situations in Eisenstein series connected to the trivial character of a smaller subgroup within $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. This is achieved through a combination of two key concepts: the arithmetic properties of Bernoulli numbers and $p$-adic analysis, as well as automorphic forms and their related $L$-functions.

This paper proposes a novel approach to ensuring the safety of mobile robotic arms with uncertain parameters during operations. A new class of control functions is developed to guarantee that the arm maintains its distance from potential obstacles, taking into account the possibility of control errors and robot dynamics variations. This approach uses a specific function that is closely related to the inverse kinematics of the robotic arm and is continuously and smoothly variable with the arm's configuration. An example using a specific type of robotic arm demonstrates the effectiveness of this method and shows that it is feasible to safely control such systems without needing to know their exact dynamic properties. This research contributes to the broader field of control theory by building upon existing concepts of kinematic control and control functions while introducing a new framework for controlling specific types of underactuated systems.

Text summarisation via the extractive method involves choosing key phrases or sentences from a given text to create a concise summary. This study focuses on developing a novel algorithm for achieving this goal by employing a graph-based approach to determine the centrality of text components. In experiments conducted on various datasets, our proposed method outperformed existing extractive summarisation techniques and offered two main advantages: a simpler implementation and lower memory requirements and processing time due to a limited graph size based on the text's sentence count.

Researchers have been developing novel nonlinear quantum operators designed to create complex entangled states in cold atoms, particularly Bose-Einstein condensates. These operators are applicable in a wide range of quantum states created through experimental methods and are also useful in nonlinear quantum circuits for BECs. Nevertheless, a key issue remains unresolved: the lack of a comprehensive understanding of the nonlinear interactions within BECs at the quantum level. To address this gap, researchers have created a non-conservative nonlinear quantum operator framework based on existing quantum theories of nonlinear dynamics, offering a new approach to modeling nonlinear quantum systems and exploring the creation of entangled BEC states through quantum jumps.

This paper presents new uniqueness theorems for the distinctness problem of meromorphic mappings from a complete K\"{a}hler manifold to the compactified complex linear space of the projective variety. The theorems employ N-value counting function and NE-value counting function to give sufficient conditions for the distinctness. The results obtained extend and combine previous individual results of the distinctness theorems for the distinctness problem of the meromorphic mappings, particularly for the case of n-distinctness where n is an integer greater than or equal to 2. The theorems are based on the Second Main Theorem for the distinctness of the meromorphic mappings from a complete K\"{a}hler manifold to the compactified complex linear space of the projective variety.

Polynomial systems with non-degenerate solution counts hold significant importance in algebraic geometry and applications, notably in having a straightforward way to calculate using a well-known method by Bezout's theorem. To expand upon the traditional definition, a new concept termed "nondegenerate signature" is developed, extending it beyond the initial framework. This innovation enables the application of a signature-based method to solve polynomial systems under a nondegenerate hypothesis, even with some singularities involved. Furthermore, a specific class of polynomial systems, known as implicitization problems, always meet the new "nondegenerate signature" criteria, thus satisfying the applicable hypothesis for this study. As a result, the average computational effort to resolve implicitization problems using the new method is estimated to be $\tilde O(N^{2.688+ \epsilon})$.

Directly produced photons offer a unique insight into the inner workings of particle collisions. Their creation is particularly informative at low momentum because it reflects the innermost, hottest core of hot, dense quark-gluon plasma. Researchers examined a specific range of low-momentum direct photons from Cu$+$Cu collisions at 200 GeV and found their numbers to be significantly lower than in gold and silver nuclei collisions at the same energy. However, when scaled, a pattern emerged that can be explained by the number of participant particles, and this trend matches predictions for direct photons. Additionally, when combining direct and fragmented photons, the total photon yield exceeded the number of particles involved, and extrapolating to all photons at 200 GeV resulted in a total that was only about 3.2 times the number of participant particles.

The purpose of this study is to address the Tur\'an's Tetrahedron Problem by determining the maximum possible volume of a set of points on a unit sphere that contains no set of four points whose volumes exceed a given threshold. This problem has its roots in Erd\H{o}s's work first presented at the Erd\H{o}s Centenary Conference in 2006. Our key finding is to maximize the specified condition on a set of points on a unit sphere that contains no set of four points whose combined distances are above a given threshold, particularly focusing on the situation where these distances are non-negative and non-degenerate when represented as vectors.

One key aspect of vector graphics rendering is removing aliasing effects to achieve smooth output, particularly relevant when forming line joins in maps. To address this problem, the paper defines spatial anti-aliasing rendering for vector maps, taking into account the size and shape of display pixels, and presents an efficient method to find optimal solutions using a short edge length and feasible layout. The proposed algorithm is shown to be practically effective in a map rendering context by considering its computational complexity.

The multivariate interpolation problem is often difficult to solve due to complex mathematical expressions, and in many cases, no suitable software is available to provide an exact solution. Consequently, various approximation methods have been developed to obtain quick and straightforward results. Although some approximation schemes are based on polynomial functions, research indicates that they can struggle with certain mathematical expressions, leading to the development of new approximation methods utilizing transcendental functions, which offer numerous advantages over polynomial-based methods. This study introduces a novel transcendental function and utilizes it to develop a straightforward and stable scalar multivariate approximation scheme, which preserves the original function's shape, and smooth version for a faster computational approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approximation method through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments.

This research focuses on identifying the locations of pulsar emitting gamma-rays within the galaxy by analyzing data from the 1st Data Catalogue of the Cherenkov Telescope Array Consortium. The analysis considers both bright Fermi gamma-ray sources and X-ray pulsars. The study reveals a potential2nd gamma-ray emitting class of pulsars, exhibiting characteristics similar to Fermi sources LAT J1141+219 and LAT J1713+3112, yet remaining unidentified as pulsars. Additionally, existing X-ray pulsars are examined for their potential high-energy emissions. The data indicate that several medium and low-period pulsars could be undetected gamma-ray sources. The study identifies 14 potential gamma-ray emitting pulsars beyond the current LAT catalog, spanning various spatial regions across the galaxy.

The category of an approaching system, such as clear skies or a thunderstorm, provides crucial information about its potential impact upon landing. Utilizing this information, drivers can make well-informed decisions about route planning. Weather categorization is thus an essential task that can be achieved by labeling meteorological images. In this study, we present an extensive dataset, CW21K, comprising 53 distinct weather conditions and 122 million images, collected from various open-access sources. To validate current state-of-the-art methods, we employ well-known Convolutional Neural Networks, including ResNet50, InceptionV3, and InceptionV4. To tackle the challenge of imbalanced data, we introduce an innovative data augmentation technique that significantly enhances performance. As an additional contribution, we develop an efficient data selection approach that optimizes the training process by choosing the most impactful weather conditions' images.

Our analysis examines how climate change information is linked to societal norms, focusing on the correlation between individual awareness of the issue and their adherence to related social standards. To model this relationship, we developed a four-agent system that investigates how individual beliefs about climate change interact with collective societal norms within institutions, and how economic factors such as government policies and market-driven initiatives can influence this dynamic. Through various simulations, we explored the effects of different institutional settings, government communications, and market-based initiatives on the evolution of societal norms and found that multiple factors contribute to the development of climate-conscious societal standards.

This research introduces a real-time model and control system for flexible multi-fingered grippers, utilizing the Koopman operator theory. The model simplifies a nonlinear dynamic system into a linear representation, allowing for efficient model prediction and parameter adjustment through the theory's infinite matrix notation. Specifically, an online variable matrix, known as the Koopman operator, is estimated using a data-driven method and contributes to real-time model prediction and control. Consequently, real-world experiments involving object grasping demonstrate that the proposed system and predictor enable accurate and responsive control and prediction of the gripper's movement.

The Organic General Radius (ORG) is a dynamic measure that adapts to the landscape of the objective function being optimized. Its value increases only when its current magnitude fails to encompass any obstructions to the progression of optimization, thereby indicating the need for an expansion. This research aims to further develop the ORG concept by integrating it with various optimization techniques such as Generalized Radius (GR), General Extrapolated Momentum (GEM), and other related methods. A new strategy is proposed to objectify the gradient's magnitude in a manner similar to a General Distance (GD), taking into account the direction of the previous step to create a more accurate representation. This Organic Gradient Extrapolated Momentum (OGEM) method combines the adaptive measure with the momentum technique to significantly improve convergence performance. Experimental results on various datasets have yielded remarkable outcomes, with OGEM outperforming other optimization techniques by margins of up to 20%.

Our analysis of the spectrum from the VLT/X-Shooter for the radio-emitting galaxy J2102+6015 reveals a redshift of 4.575 and allows us to calculate a luminosity distance of approximately 12,000 Mpc using either the Planck or WMAP9 cosmological models. This object exhibits a star formation rate of around 100 solar masses per year, corresponding to a stellar mass of roughly 10 to the power of 11 solar masses, and may contain a young, massive black hole with a mass of about 10 to the power of 8 solar masses. Observation of J2102+6011 in radio bands during a recent VLBI survey detected a compact radio core with a flux of 0.34 Jy, which is consistent with a star formation rate similar to that observed in the VLT/X-Shooter spectrum. This core is likely a young, massive black hole emitting radiation through a relativistic jet, and our data suggests that J2102+6015 is an ideal candidate for further investigation into the evolution of black holes and the early stages of black hole activity.

This study focuses on developing an effective approach for predicting survival in patients with non-small cell lung carcinoma, a aggressive type of lung cancer. To achieve this, we gathered clinical data from 431 patients, including their treatment plans, and combined it with their individualized first-line chemotherapy and immunotherapy treatments. To capture relevant image features from their low-resolution CT scans, we fine-tuned a pre-trained convolutional neural network, which was originally pre-trained on a large dataset of high-resolution whole-body CT scans. We then compared the prognostic power of different risk models, including those based on clinical factors and image analysis, as well as a combined model that integrates both types of features, using multiple statistical analyses and performance metrics. Our results show that the combined model achieved the best outcome, accurately predicting patient survival with an AUC of 0.75 and a concordance index of 0.75. Furthermore, we conducted time-dependent analysis and found that the combined model demonstrated superior predictive accuracy over time, particularly at 1-year (intention-to-treat analysis, CC = 0.74) and 3-months (per-protocol analysis, CC = 0.73).

Many advanced applications for autonomous intelligent agents are limited by their ability to adapt to novel environments due to a lack of flexibility in learning. Several innovative approaches utilizing natural language descriptions as an alternative form of state representation in addition to traditional sensory inputs have been proposed in order to enhance adaptability. Despite a rapidly growing body of research in this area, a comprehensive understanding of these methods is currently absent. This overview provides an in-depth analysis of utilizing natural language descriptions as representations for autonomous intelligent agents, beginning with a detailed examination of the fundamental concepts underlying natural language processing and its application in adaptive learning. Ultimately, several promising areas for further investigation are identified to bridge the existing knowledge gaps in utilizing natural language descriptions for adaptive learning.

A novel approach based on machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of cosmological density power spectra from quasar spectra.  Through simulations, this machine-learning reconstruction achieves high fidelity with an 80% reduction in computational time compared to conventional methods.  Furthermore, the feasibility of applying this machine-learning method to real data has been confirmed, with nearly identical results obtained when analyzing simulated data without templates and actual absorption feature templates from the Euclid simulation, with an 80% computational time savings.  The results suggest a substantial potential for efficiently analyzing large datasets from future high-throughput spectroscopic surveys.

This research focuses on modules from the Lie algebras of differential operators on a line, specifically their highest weight modules with one-dimensional weight spaces. It's discovered that these types of modules include several key structures: the universal enveloping algebras of the w-algebras (also known as the Yangians), the modules related to the Hermite polynomials, and the modules related to the Hermite functions of order n.

Social media sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter offers valuable insights into
consumer emotions due to Twitter's unique characteristics, like its character limit and extensive
data availability. As social media data continues to grow, analyzing it becomes increasingly complex,
necessitating advanced techniques for effective extraction. This study presents a Long Short-Term Memory
(LSTM) neural network framework for Twitter sentiment analysis, leveraging Python and associated
libraries, along with characteristic features that capture word and social context. The proposed model
achieved exceptional performance, attaining 98% accuracy, 98% precision, 98% recall, and 98% F1-Score in
experiments on the Twitter sentiment analysis dataset.

This study presents an innovative open-domain dialogue system capable of adhering to specific conversational norms defined by a particular domain expert. Unlike existing chatbots designed to emulate human-like conversations with norms defined by statistical analysis of textual data, our system's norms are explicitly specified by a single individual. Our proposed framework comprises two primary components: first, we developed a specification for explicitly defining a domain conversation's standards, and second, we created a scalable, efficient dialogue management method leveraging large-scale language models. Evaluations demonstrate that our proposed conversation norm specification formally captures the essential aspects of an experienced domain conversationalist's strategies. Moreover, our scale-efficient dialogue management method, utilizing large-scale language models, achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating norm-compliant responses, while significantly outperforming baseline models and demonstrating substantial inference time improvements and reduced memory consumption when employing a large 7B language model.

The gravitational wave memory effect, a type of permanent strain caused by non-linearities in the propagation of gravitational waves, has a distinct character with broad-band characteristics that make it stand out from other types of gravitational waves. New research shows that a background of gravitational waves made up of memory signals from numerous binary mergers has the potential to be detected by future detectors such as the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer. In fact, the memory component of Advanced LIGO and Advanced Virgo may already be contributing to the observed $\mathcal{O}(10^{-22})$-level strain backgrounds within the 100 Hz to 1 kHz frequency range. Importantly, the ability to detect GW memory events on an individual basis could lead to the discovery that the rate of memory-contributing events is significantly lower than what's predicted, which in turn may offer a valuable insight that could be of great cosmological and cosmogonic value.

A second-order phase transition tied to SUSY breaking in an inflation model results in the production of both a heavy Majorana neutrino and significant amounts of SUSY energy density. These components interact within the phase transition's bubbles, yielding a strongly coupled scenario that characterizes it as a type I phase transition. This scenario is capable of producing both the necessary conditions for leptogenesis and the detection-sensitive signals of a first-order phase transition through simulations of bubble nucleation. Furthermore, it leads to the collapse of bubbles into black holes and produces significant amounts of gravitational waves, specifically in the range detectable by LIGO. These findings are shown to be consistent across the entire parameter space, also satisfying constraints imposed by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and CMB data regarding the population of primordial black holes.

To build a truly intelligent system, artificial agents need to possess causal understanding and effectively communicate, which together form a complex challenge. Our research breaks this problem into two manageable parts: the agent's causal model, which generates predictions based on observations, and the communication system, constructed as a signaling game that facilitates semantic information exchange between agent and user. This communication interface allows for a continuous, semantic dialogue where user requests and the agent's responses develop a shared understanding. To achieve this, our innovation integrates neural networks with logical reasoning in a unified framework. This integration enables the agent's communication with users to gradually develop a coherent dialogue through a combination of learned signaling and reasoned responses. Our results show that this agent's communication with humans shows signs of developing semantic understanding and demonstrates a solid causal understanding of the domain being discussed.

Our study examines two key issues related to sparse terms in word embeddings: their prediction from existing words and the model's ability to capture relationships among sparse terms. We developed an enhanced model that integrates Naive Bayes and the ability to represent hidden patterns in data, and compared it to an alternative model with Naive Bayes only. We tested our hybrid model and the reduced model on both real-world sparse datasets and the Glove 6B dataset modified to increase sparsity. The results demonstrated that the presence of a mechanism for representing hidden patterns in data improves performance when dealing with sparse datasets, and that this mechanism can even be utilized to infer hidden categories in data.

Session-oriented recommendations focus on understanding user sessions to provide relevant item suggestions. Recent research models entire session-oriented paths as graphs to identify relevant items, but this method demands a large number of candidate items, making computation expensive and memory-intensive. To overcome these limitations, our proposed approach, RET2, uses a ranking embedding to capture the sequential order of items, allowing only a few highly relevant candidate items to be considered at each recommendation step. Our two-stage model first selects a small set of candidate items and then uses an attention-based encoder to choose the final candidate. RET2 achieves state-of-the-art results on both session-oriented and next-item recommendation tasks, outperforming previous methods by a significant margin. Our analysis also highlights the benefits of using a low number of candidate items and demonstrates the effectiveness of RET2's design choices.

In recent years, there's been significant interest in the selforganization of particles that generate activity independently, which self-organizes into molecular-shaped structures known as colloidal molecules. These structures, which consist of particles that bind together through activity, can model the behavior of biological molecules. However, it's not entirely clear how living cells utilize movement and directionality. Our research focuses on a pair of colloidal molecules in a environment that causes activity variations and asks how their shapes, movement patterns, and stability are affected. Our computer simulations and theoretical models reveal that activity variations cause the molecules to move in a specific direction and cause changes in their configuration, which can be compared to certain features of molecular motors in living cells.

Our approach involves generating a three-dimensional discrete fracture network from a given three-dimensional discrete fracture matrix model. A corresponding conforming mesh is then created, integrating the fracture geometry into a simplified network. A transport model is subsequently developed based on this mesh. A fully implicit numerical model is finally constructed, allowing for an explicit formulation of discrete conformal operators within a discrete fracture network. A demonstrated model using a complex three-dimensional fracture network successfully models both single-phase and multi-phase transport.

This study develops an algorithm that utilizes an optical sensor to create and sustain a organized formation of drones without any need for pre-set parameters. Each drone in the formation acts as a point cloud, and a leader drone registers the cloud with the aid of all other drones in the formation. A novel, robust registration technique is employed that effectively avoids any potential issues arising from unevenly distributed points or points near the edges of the cloud. Experimental results confirm that the algorithm successfully creates a organized formation and avoids any potential collisions among the drones.

In our investigation of the spectrum of Seidel matrices for chain graphs, we determine the eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenspaces, and prove that the Seidel matrix has eigenvalues at both $-1$ and $-2$. We also demonstrate that the minimum Seidel spread of a chain graph, denoted as $s_1(A)$, never exceeds its order, while the minimum Seidel ratio $r_1(A)$ can exceed it. Additionally, the smallest and largest Seidel eigenvalues of a $n$-chain graph, $A_{P_n}$, are given by the expressions $\frac{-n-1-\sqrt{n^2+n-2}}{2}$ and $\frac{-n+1+\sqrt{n^2+n-2}}{2}$, respectively.

We have established field-optimal solutions for a class of stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion with non-anticipatory memory, where the field-optimal solution represents a typical state of the fractional Brownian environment, and we have proved the existence and uniqueness of this solution.

The properties of a Dirac operator with constant coefficients are analyzed in a specific mathematical context involving one-dimensional spatial space and a two-dimensional internal space. The study focuses on operators with self-adjoint matrix properties, a given number of bands of elliptical trajectories in their associated two-dimensional momentum space, and an analysis of a specific type of spectral density is presented. The spectral density is defined within a specific mathematical framework called an elliptical non-commutative torus and is expressed as an infinite series. An asymptotic formula for the coefficients of this series is derived in a particular mathematical function as the series index approaches infinity, which corresponds to a non-self-adjoint analog of a previously established result by Balian and Berline.

This study introduces a novel concept of vehicular networks that incorporate two types of access points: roadside units (RSUs) and vehicle relays (VRs). It treats networks using only RSs and those using only VRs as specialized cases. By comparing the performance of these networks to a theoretical ideal that uses both types of access points freely, this research aims to understand the benefits and challenges of combining vehicle relays with RSUs. We consider a linear arrangement of linear motion, with a communication range, and use a probability model that accounts for the capacity of information transmission. Using this model, we explore network characteristics, such as the density of active nodes, average network range, and message delivery speed, and provide methods for estimating these characteristics. We extend this model to real-world settings that use RSUs with predefined spacing, such as networks that use RSUs on roads with vehicles as relays, and we assess the performance of these systems through simulations.

Wikipedia's ever-evolving nature is evident in the variety of its article ratings, a sign of the community's dedication to maintaining the encyclopedia's quality. Despite the benefits these ratings bring in guiding readers and editors, the manual process of labeling articles is extremely time-consuming for volunteers, with a vast majority of unwritten articles waiting to be assessed. To bridge this gap and unlock the full potential of every article, we've developed an automated tool that identifies newly created, lower-quality articles by analyzing patterns in editing behaviors. This innovative tool, the first of its kind to employ editing behavior characteristics for label assignment, will serve as a foundation for developing a complete auto-labeling system, thereby empowering new Wikipedia contributors and giving them a head start in enhancing the quality of articles previously marked as needing improvement.

Deep learning models, particularly those used for semantic tasks like object detection, often rely on training with large, annotated datasets. However, this can pose challenges, including the need for significant resources and the difficulty of obtaining high-quality labels. Researchers are exploring ways to perform semantic tasks without needing extensive training by utilizing zero-shot techniques, which can transfer knowledge from a pre-trained model to perform tasks on new data. Our work focuses on doing this by generating synthetic images that mimic those in real-world datasets, using a pre-trained model to calculate how those images relate to existing labels, and then using an algorithm to find the top synthetic images that best match those in the training data. The resulting images are used to create a new dataset, allowing an algorithm to learn from it and perform tasks without needing to be retrained. The approach is versatile and can generate high-quality images that are nearly as effective as training directly, even when dealing with new categories not seen by the pre-trained model.

We have examined the decay $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ using a comprehensive dataset of $pp$ collisions, collected by the LHCb experiment and amounting to an integrated luminosity of 3.000 fb inverse in luminosity, where the $B^0_s$ mesons were created in various decay processes. Our analysis led to discovery of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay, with a significant chi-squared significance of 4.5 standard deviations, where a signal yield of approximately 200 occurrences was identified. This discovery is supported by the observation of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay, with a relative significance of 2.5 standard deviations. Our data indicates that the branching fractions for these two decays have ratios of 0.124 plus or minus 0.024 (statistical) plus or minus 0.015 (systematic) for the former, and 0.075 plus or minus 0.013 (statistical) plus or minus 0.008 (systematic) for the latter, both in comparison to the $B^0_s\to J/\psi K^0_S$ decay.

To broaden existing knowledge of topological T-duality, our goal is to extend the concept to include spaces with local twisted gerbe B-fields in addition to the standard local R-twist. Building upon established principles from topological T-duality, we will apply these to twisted cylinders, constrained by specific boundary conditions. These conditions ensure that the resulting theories maintain equivalence with previously established theories that do not include a B-field. The set of twisted cylinders is an organized system, where each section represents a unique B-field and R-twist configuration, allowing our work to demonstrate that configurations with different B-field and R-twist settings are genuinely distinct. The boundary conditions, defined by specific congruence requirements, ensure the duality between various configurations and serve as a means to classify twisted cylinders, ultimately showing that all configurations satisfy this congruence criterion.

In co-imitation learning, partners teach each other by observing one another's expert-like actions, even though they may not have direct access to these actions themselves.  While co-imitation training has shown promise in advancing agents, it is typically dependent on expert demonstrations provided from an outside source, which can be costly to generate.  Our research explores a novel approach where agents learn through co-imitation without external expert demonstrations, leading to improved task performance and more efficient exploration.  Empirical evidence from three distinct domains supports this idea, and our findings on how the co-imitation process influences task complexity and exploration provide insights for further development.

This note provides a basic overview of Prediction-Accuracy Calculation (PAC) codes, focusing on their foundational principles and a straightforward demonstration of their decoding process and evaluation metrics. PAC codes are closely related to regular linear codes, with their performance assessed using the relative frequency of specific bit patterns in a codebook. We also introduce and discuss alternative distance metrics that may be applicable to PAC codes. A simple prediction task is used to illustrate the process of training and utilizing PAC codes.

Understanding how humans and objects interact is crucial to accurately predicting the flow of unstructured data, such as video or depth sensor feeds, especially when it comes to human-hand object interactions. Existing approaches have limitations in processing diverse sequences with varying content, resolution, lighting, and object complexity. To overcome these challenges, we present a novel system that can track hands in real-time from unstructured 3D sensor data and reconstruct hand-object interactions in a 3D space. Using existing RGBI and depth sensor data, the system employs a hand tracker and a neural implicit representation to efficiently predict hand positions and shapes.
