Furthermore, it leverages this information and learned associations between human hand and object interactions to forecast hand object interactions in a 3D space. The system can predict future frames up to 12 seconds ahead with high accuracy, and can also be used to fill in missing data in occluded or noisy sensor data. Extensive experiments on a diverse set of in-the-wild data demonstrate the system's effectiveness and robustness. The system's source code and a demo are available at https://github.com/robovision/HandObjPrediction.

This study classifies C-groups with a specific structure, being non-crystallographic, having a rank of 4 and an interleaving number of 2. A total of 12 distinct C-groups fitting this description were identified, with their Coxeter diagrams drawn out visually. Furthermore, the study determined the geometric configurations of their associated regular polytopes.

A novel approach endorses the utilization of a depth-enabled end-effector in a mobile robot for diverse depth learning applications and pose estimation, specifically using a SICK Vision AI-X camera attached to a UR5 robot. Since external calibration is impractical due to the attachment of end-effector and camera, an internal calibration method leveraging a SICK laser scanner and a software package named indigo is proposed. Moreover, a neural network based on a modified ResNet architecture is designed to facilitate markerless adjustment and end-effector pose estimation in a markerless environment. Finally, our method is validated by attaching the equipment to a UR5 robot and utilizing various software tools and data sources to achieve promising experimental outcomes.

Research on policy changes often faces obstacles due to concurrent administrative modifications, which can mask the effects of the interventions being studied. Such complications pose significant challenges for analysts attempting to identify policy impacts. This research addresses these difficulties by developing an estimator that enables the detection of policy effects even when multiple administrative changes occur. A policy effect is considered detectable if it alters a detectable characteristic of detectable K-nearest neighbors among controls. The proposed estimator treats subsequent administrative modifications as control variables and utilizes an exhaustive search over all feasible combinations to identify the impact of the intervention under study. This estimator comes with strong assurances, demonstrating that as detectable K-nearest neighbors among controls grow, any combination leading to an average difference in the detectable feature will result in consistent estimation. Furthermore, under randomization, this estimator also enjoys strong asymptotic normality properties. Empirical evidence suggests that by expanding the set of feasible combinations considered, this new estimator significantly enhances statistical power and provides reliable effect size estimates along with valid confidence intervals. This estimator is particularly applicable when administrators implement numerous policy changes and when ensuring strict internal validity proves difficult. However, when fewer concurrent administrative modifications are involved, alternative solutions may offer better efficiency and consider researchers' theoretical assumptions about effects.

In the context of Neutron Stars, we examine the annihilation of Dark Matter particles that occur when they emit neutrinos, specifically in the case where these particles have a certain level of "pseudoscalar"特性. This situation arises primarily due to the interaction between the pseudoscalar mediator and the strong nuclear force, allowing for annihilation processes that emit neutrinos. Given that the norm of the pseudoscalar mediator's coupling to photons is constrained by observational factors, our analysis shows that the resulting neutrino emissions from DM annihilation can be significantly amplified compared to scenarios involving only vector mediators, specifically in the range of hundreds to thousands of times more intense. This intense emission occurs primarily through an enhanced annihilation rate involving three particles, two of which are fermions and the third is a pseudoscalar mediator, and can happen at lower energies compared to two-body annihilation processes. This phenomenon is most pronounced when the pseudoscalar mediator's coupling to photons is normatively higher, and as a result, it has far-reaching implications for analyzing the feasibility of DM annihilation in pseudoscalar-mediated interactions within the context of Neutron Stars.

I introduce ShapePipe, a cutting-edge software pipeline designed for the precise measurement of galaxy shapes, specifically designed to analyze weak lensing effects. By taking preprocessed images as input, the pipeline delivers accurate shape measurements along with an in-depth analysis of their reliability, all within a user-friendly, high-performance framework. Furthermore, I apply ShapePipe to the UNIONS project's CFIS dataset, resulting in a comprehensive catalog of over 140,000 galaxy shapes and derived quantities, including those of interest for a dark energy study. The pipeline not only includes a thorough assessment of its own performance, but also provides an estimation of the uncertainties associated with its results, revealing that its non-cosmological shape measurement covariance covariance is readily available for research purposes.

We establish modified equidistribution theorems derived from a combination of H. Weyl's work and the trace map in algebraic number theory. By integrating these modifications with a result by M. Boshernitzan and P. Varjú, we extend the classic Kronecker-Weyl theorem and AP Dickson's theorem. Furthermore, we formulate additional generalization theorems that also yield expansion rules for $p$-adic integers and $p$-rational numbers, as well as outcomes related to the approximation of real numbers by rational numbers.

We show that for a specific class of two-dimensional local complete varieties, being k-Du Bois or having a rational singular point of type $A_k$ are equivalent to the singular point having a specific characteristic polynomial and tangent space characteristics. Similarly, breaking down simple Du Bois points into strata based on their Du Bois number yields similar results for rational points, where each result type corresponds to a specific tangent space characteristic. Additionally, this breakdown is also applicable to three-dimensional Du Bois and rational singular points. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the Du Bois and rational types of certain mixed-characteristic singular points and find them to be in equivalence. Lastly, we define and investigate a specific class of two-dimensional local complete varieties with specific properties related to their reductions modulo principal ideals.

We explored the possibility of observing Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transitions in a quantum heisenberg model on a three-dimensional lattice. Utilizing advanced computational methods known as tensor network algorithms, we investigated the thermodynamic properties of the model. Our study revealed that the model can display BKT critical behavior under a strong external field when two of its spin components commute. Furthermore, we found that this critical behavior can be identified through universal scaling relationships between different measures and is accompanied by the emergence of gapless excitations and power-law decay patterns. Our results demonstrate that the BKT critical manifold exists within the three-dimensional heisenberg parameter space, forming a three-dimensional surface that can be accessed through different combinations of exchange couplings and external field configurations.

This study proposes a theoretical framework where axions and sterile neutrinos coexist as dark matter within composite "shadow matter". In this model, a $Z_2$-symmetric sector is linked to the visible universe through a "portal" involving both $SU(2)_L$ $|W|$ bosons and Higgs bosons. As a result, massive sterile neutrinos and axion-like particles naturally emerge. We find that to satisfy dark matter requirements, we must have a very light mass for the sterile neutrino, approximately $10^{-23}$ eV, and an associated decay constant of around $10^{19}$ GeV for the axion. We show that the production of these particles is consistent with their observed relic abundance due to specific interactions with both the weak and scalar fields. We also investigate the potential detection of these lightly massive sterile neutrinos through their resonant coherent scattering off nuclei, which can be detected by future TRISTAN or ETRISTRONB labs. We derive the relationship between the mixing angle between visible and sterile neutrinos and the mass of the $W$-portal, which has potential implications for various studies, including the study of sterile neutrinos in neutrino physics and gravity mediators in axion models.

Developing efficient quantum computers faces a significant obstacle in overcoming limitations imposed by linearity in quantum mechanics, which requires unbounded growth in certain function arguments to surpass linear complexity. To bypass these limitations, researchers introduce non-classical resources known as magic states. A crucial inquiry in quantum computing is the minimal cost of decomposing polynomial evaluations into magic states. Unfortunately, existing research only provides exponential upper bounds for specific input sizes due to constraints in applying quantum amplitude amplification. In this study, we overcame this limitation, providing a sub-exponential, specifically $2^{O((\log n)^4)}$, bound for evaluating $|0^n\rangle + |1^n\rangle$ under similar conditions.

This research investigates the application of Complex ESSM on TTDE within the coordinate system $(t,r)$, where the curvature of spacetime is assumed to be the maximum feasible holographic density linked to the IR cutoff scale ($R$). Utilizing complex form of ESSM, we can derive two distinct state equations for TDLE, enabling a comparison with observational data to determine whether the data aligns with the standard ESSM or its complex counterpart. Further exploration of the derived state equations, considering both $R$'s standard and complex forms, allows us to examine the model's behavior in terms of acceleration and density, ultimately determining its stability and physical feasibility.

Identifying all transient phenomena in the galaxy is a highly desirable goal, though not entirely achievable in reality. The Lamontostart (LAMOST) Start-up team has observed four $K$2 plates from the Lamontostart Time Domain Survey (LTDS), yielding 1,022,709 unique sources and 4,426,649 astrometric measurements, with an average parallax accuracy of 0.51 mas. The data also revealed the redshift distribution of the observed sources, ranging from 0.02 to 6.4, with the majority originating from the galaxy. Furthermore, the data included measurements of 1,410 known variable stars, of which the majority were identified as stable stars, with the remaining categorized as eclipsing binary systems, pulsating variable stars, and other non-stable objects. The data also revealed the detection of 10 potential supernovae candidates. The LTDS's goal is to introduce a new, large all-sky, low-resolution spectroscopic redshift survey, with the potential to significantly expand upon existing surveys.

This paper presents an innovative approach to generating secure random numbers by leveraging the inherent instability of SRAM storage cells. Previous studies have utilized SRAM cell timing variations to create random numbers, but the proposed method in this paper exploits the lower supply voltage threshold of SRAM cells to produce entropy. To verify the effectiveness of this approach, the results from HSPICE simulations were validated against those from actual experiments performed on industrial-grade SRAM chips, revealing the presence of high-quality randomness. Furthermore, the results indicate that entropy is easily extractable from the SRAM storage cells and can be easily converted into random numbers using the von Neumann algorithm.

A meticulous design of a single-electron resistor switch (SER switch) has been achieved through the strategic placement of a polymer or PEM molecule in a quantum interference coil. An analysis of such a design's behavior reveals that the intercoil tunneling rate strongly depends on the chemical composition of these molecules, enabling reasonable tunneling rate adjustments by incorporating a polymer or a PEM molecule in the coil. An adequate supply of electrostatic energy provided to the coil by trapping a charge in its gate allows for the flow of current in the SER switch, thus demonstrating that it can operate in an efficient manner. An extensive simulation of the SER switch's current-voltage characteristics was conducted, showcasing that its behavior is robustly influenced by the molecular composition in the coil and can be effectively utilized in the development of high-density nonvolatile memory systems.

To compute complex loop corrections in quantum field theory, advanced numerical techniques are employed, particularly for caustic graphs involving multiple loops and multiple particles. A new approach is presented to evaluate the fundamental scalar caustic graph numerically, breaking down the graph into simpler pieces using a mathematical representation called Feynman parameter space. This representation transforms the graph into a set of connected regions bounded by flat and curved surfaces. By decomposing these graphs into simpler pieces, each piece can be represented as a numerical function that depends on its boundary parameters. These functions are estimated using a specialized algorithm based on caustic landward propagation, enabling precise computation even in challenging尖点 situations. This method is general and can be applied to any caustic graph, featuring up to three loops and multiple propagators.

We analyze quantum walks with a one-dimensional two-state quantum particle, focusing on symmetric one-particle density matrices to understand the system's behavior. To do this, we derive a second-order difference equation for the eigenfunctions of the evolution operator, which is based on a self-adjoint, bounded linear operator. This operator has a compact form, allowing us to apply spectral theorem to obtain the complete set of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, which in turn allows us to express the one-particle density matrix in terms of these components. To do this, we apply the Fourier transform with a bounded domain, which is necessary due to the non-compact nature of the one-dimensional quantum walk Hamiltonian. As a result, the one-particle density matrix can be expressed as a sum of projections onto the eigenfunctions, with the terms weighted by the corresponding eigenvalues, which are expressed as functions of the Fourier variable. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we consider two quantum models: one with a homogeneous Hamiltonian and another with an inhomogeneous Hamiltonian consisting of a potential barrier, which we use to calculate and plot the one-particle density and one-particle probability for the latter model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars, where the up, down, and strange quarks coexist with a single heavy octet baryon and one non-charge doublet baryon octet. The authors combine the MIT and NJL models with the Sigma-Omega-Rho theory to coexist with the other quarks, where the parameter is adjusted to match the mass of $510$ MeV. The resulting hybrid star mass-radius relations are then plotted for various ratios of strange to non-strange quarks within the star. The maximum mass of the hybrid star is found to be around $2.16 M_{\odot}$ in this model.

$q$-deformed optomechanical systems, comprising an deformed Jaynes-Cummings cavity with a two-level atom and a phonon mode, are analyzed in this paper. The system's non-Hermitian dynamics are investigated under two scenarios: normal incidence and oblique incidence of a probe beam. Exceeding the input-clarity threshold allows the system to enter an exceptional point, leading to significant amplification of the probe beam. This phenomenon, observed in both incidence scenarios, exhibits a remarkable dependence on the deforming factor. Additionally, under specific conditions, the phase-sensitive gain can surpass the standard quantum limit, thereby offering a potentially advantageous application in optomechanical systems-based sensing technologies.

This research examines R-parity broken scenarios within supersymmetric models, specifically those involving a rotator model with two parts, which are equivalent to hadronic and gamma partial waves in high energy collisions that break reflection symmetry. A detailed analysis of these adverse R-parity broken scenarios is conducted using the Two-Rotors Model and compared with calculations based on the Scissors Mode Scaler Hamiltonian to derive an expression for the broken R-parity contribution.

Our research focuses on ultrathin multilayered materials, specifically in the context of spin and orbital physics. In very thin oxide films, even when dimensionality is extremely low, electron correlations can be exceptionally strong. This incredible ability to generate complex states through a combination of spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom opens up a range of physical properties that can be tuned using various external stimuli such as electric fields, mechanical strain, and specialized preparation techniques. These unique properties make oxide materials ideal test beds for theoretical models and a foundation for novel technologies in the field of multiferroics and superconducting devices.

In a dissipative optical setup, a laser-cooled atomic ensemble is observed where each group of atoms occupies a separate lattice, displaying specific correlation patterns. Our research reveals that there is a distribution of statistical correlations among the atoms, with an average effect that is negligible but can be more significant at higher temperatures. Moreover, there is a reverse relationship between correlations and temperature, with higher temperatures leading to higher orders of correlation, with an effect that grows linearly with increasing temperature. To explain these findings, a theoretical model based on a stochastic master equation has been developed, taking into consideration the discrete nature of energy exchange and the effect of finite widths of lattice density states.

This study examines how cryptocurrency trading networks evolve over time, focusing on the connections between individual coins' price changes. We analyzed the effects of various factors, such as the choice of correlation metric, coefficient, and time interval, on the resulting network properties. To gain a deeper understanding, we introduced novel ways to visualize the cryptocurrency market, such as geographic plotting, plotting, and network visualization. Additionally, we used advanced analysis methods, such as community detection and graph theory, to uncover the underlying high-order connections in the market. Our research reveals several key findings, such as the existence of a distinct Ethereum-centric sub-group, a more independent Litecoin sub-group, and a common sub-group consisting of coins such as Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, and ETC, which are heavily influenced by Bitcoin's price movements. These results reveal a temporary two-phase structure in the market's community organization, with the phases switching based on market fluctuations. Our approach provides valuable new insights into the complex dynamics of individual coin prices and their interconnections within the cryptocurrency trading platform.

The smallest possible molecular clusters composed of either one or two H2O and H2SO4 molecules are extensively studied using two distinct methods to calculate cluster energies. The first approach uses harmonic approximation to calculate zero-point motion, while the second approach, a more accurate method, takes into zero-point motion path integral. The relative importance of these zero-point motion corrections, along with electronic structure corrections, is evaluated in the context of the small molecular cluster studies. The results of these studies, involving the H2O and H2SO4 molecules in their different possible configurations, indicate that the zero-point motion path integral is a significant factor, particularly in the context of the small molecular cluster of two H2SO4 molecules. The calculations also reveal the relative stability of different acid and water cluster configurations, indicating that structures with more hydrogen bonds are generally more stable.

We establish the definitions for an compactified perception pair and a compactified space of non-expanding operators, accompanied by their essential characteristics and sealed constructions. Furthermore, it's shown that if a group compactifies its invariant perception pair with a finite type, it's equivalent to compactifying the corresponding space of group-invariant non-expanding operators, with the result being the maximal possible outcome.

In one spatial dimension, we develop a kinetic approach to understand how the thermal Hall effect arises in interacting systems, and establish under what conditions the thermal Hall conductivity is non-zero. By applying the same 1D kinetic theory to satisfy certain symmetries in thermal transport, we derive an extended set of Einstein relations, which are then applied to both hydrodynamic and non-hydrodynamic regimes, enabling a systematic understanding of thermal transport in 1+2 dimensional systems, and confirming the underlying symmetry underlying the thermal Hall effect.

This study delves into the unexplored connection between a neural network's performance and the regularizers of its simplicity, a concept often considered a byproduct of its design or training process. We argue, however, that network complexity is directly influenced by its geometric properties and can be controlled through network architecture, regularizer magnitude, and the type of regularizer used. By using two-model and multi-class classifiers, we examined the impact of 14 geometric properties on classifier regularizer performance. The experiment revealed that a network's design can produce distinct regularizer effects on its classifier, and different geometric properties tend to promote specific regularizers. For instance, the cross-entropy loss in conjunction with the L2 and elastic weight decay (EW) regularizers encourages simpler, more compact decision boundaries. Conversely, the L1 and label-smoothing loss functions promote outliers and produce a specific type of regularizer effect that encourages robustness to noise. This comprehensive analysis provides new insights into the relationship between network geometry and its performance, and may aid neural network architects in designing more effective networks.

A study of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays is performed to measure the Wilson coefficients in an approach that does not rely on input from other processes. Wilson coefficient values are calculated based on experimentally measured ratios of forward and backward probabilities in $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays across four $q^2$ intervals. This analysis also uses input from lattice QC simulations to determine the Wilson coefficient $c_{7\mathrm{L}}^\mathrm{eff}(q^2)$ in the same $q^2$ ranges. As a result, a new effective Wilson coefficient, $c_{9\mathrm{eff}}^\mathrm{eff}(q^2)$, is calculated and found to be in disagreement with the standard model by approximately two standard deviations in three of the $q^2$ ranges and by one standard deviation in the remaining range.

Automated essay scoring is crucial due to the vast number of students and limited staff available for grading.  Paraphrasing has been proven to improve NLP task performance, and research has explored its application for improving essay scores.  Using sentence similarity techniques, it is possible to augment a small dataset of high-scoring essays with sentences from a larger dataset of essays, and then fine-tune a model for scoring.  This novel approach was applied to the 2014 and 2016 Inscrition exams, demonstrating its effectiveness in scoring essays more accurately than models trained on the original exam datasets alone.

As extreme weather events and financial losses escalate, studying tail dependence has become crucial.  In this paper, we introduce a framework for developing models of marginal dependence that captures how extreme events behave in specific areas while remaining flexible for applications in any number of dimensions.  The framework is based on a novel class of copulas that separately control dependence in the extreme positive and negative directions, allowing for $m$-way extension and easy application in practice.  The paper also relates these models to key concepts like spectrally stable measures and provides a method for parameter estimation in practice.  Through various simulations and a real-world data analysis, we demonstrate the models' effectiveness and practical applicability.

This research examines an economic model that explores how wealth is passed down through generations, focusing on how unequal opportunity affects social mobility. By examining the relationships between intergenerational wealth correlations, social mobility rates, and the distribution of opportunities, we discover significant connections between these factors. Our analysis reveals that dynamic models exhibit distinct characteristics compared to static models, particularly in the variability of social mobility rates and the shape of the Pareto index distribution, which is influenced by the inverse square of the Pareto index, ranging from 0 to 2.

The relationship between spin and statistics in non-relativistic physics is more fundamental than previously thought, stemming from a more basic principle rather than Galilean relativity. This principle is that particles with odd integer spins exhibit fermionic behavior, while those with even integer spins exhibit bosonic behavior. Conversely, particles with half-integer spins follow statistical rules independent of this principle.

Delegated RingCT (DRCT), an enhancement of RingCT, aims to address the performance limitations of RingCT while preserving its security properties.
Delegating verification to a trusted group allows ring signatures to efficiently verify transactions, thus mitigating the leakage of public keys to participants and minimizing their computational load.
This paper presents an exploration into leveraging this load distribution within the DRCT protocol to utilize a network's computational resources more effectively, leading to potential improvements in verifying transactions.
Specifically, we propose two methods to redirect verifiable path information and ring public key validation to network nodes, enabling them to verify a delegated RingCT transaction.
Our analysis, using a simulation, compares the performance benefits and practical feasibility of these methods to offer potential applications of participating in transaction verification.

This study explores the complexity of solving linear systems where matrix entries are quantum bit strings representing sparse vectors, with each vector element's magnitude inversely proportional to its norm, and matrices constrained within a specific sparsity and condition number limit, denoted as $(s,\kappa)$-structured linear systems. Similar systems are commonly encountered in numerical simulations of various quantum algorithms, with researchers seeking efficient numerical and quantum solutions. We introduce a model, termed space-toughness, analogous to time-toughness, to assess the memory requirements of solving these structured linear systems on a quantum computer. By adapting a time-toughness result, we establish space-toughness for these systems, with an exception for a scenario involving highly conditioned matrices, thus implying that the O($\tilde{t}\tilde{s}\kappa$) memory and $\tilde{t}\tilde{s}$ working memory are generally optimal. However, an inner-loop iteration of the quantum linear system algorithm can be solved using only $O(\tilde{t}\tilde{s})$ working memory.

For the search of VBB production, specific selection criteria are established and various signal and background processes are simulated using PYTHIA 8.1 and MADANALYSIS. Lepton isolation, significant missing transverse momentum, significant jet multiplicity, and high scalar sum of jet transverse momenta are among the key criteria used in this investigation. Both same-flavor and opposite-flavor dilepton scenarios are examined to evaluate VBB signals. All results are derived under the assumption of mass-degenerate VBB states, yielding exclusion limits at 95% confidence level for WWWW, ZWWW, ZZZW, ZWWW, ZWW W, Z Z W W, Z Z Z W, Z Z Z Z VBB combinations across a range of masses from 1.2 to 3.0 TeV. Additionally, the study compares the expected results to the LHC VBB search results obtained at 13 TeV in 2016.

Hebrew is one of the top five most utilized languages globally, yet it still lacks the comprehensive linguistic annotation of a gold-standard corpus, which hinders advancements in Natural Language Processing for this language. In 2018, the Hebrew treebanking project was released under a Creative Commons license, making it freely accessible for research purposes. This project underwent an complete overhaul, incorporating the latest Hebrew orthographic standards. In our study, we utilize this new annotation to fine-tune and evaluate various cross-domain and baseline parsing models. By employing this new, high-quality annotation, our latest model demonstrates significant improvements, outperforming previous and contemporary Hebrew parsers by a margin of 24-47 percentage points in the F1 score of our custom evaluation metric.

We create and analyze a new dimension measure, ε-isometric dimension, which is an dimension metric introduced by G. Cheeger and D. M. Gurevich and it closely relates to the original Assouad dimension. This dimension, which takes into account a specific type of function, has an advantage over other dimension metrics as it satisfies the property of hereditary inheritance for subsets that are almost incompressible. We demonstrate that Cheuegg's function can give an almost precise estimation of this dimension for a specific subset of the incompressible part of the Minieson space.

In the fast-paced world of data-driven problem solving, a single organization can no longer keep up with the rapidly growing volume of data and models. To bridge this gap, a new approach to modeling has been proposed, drawing inspiration from the principles of collboration in software development and scientific research. By breaking down the process of data-driven modeling into reusable components, such as data, features, models, and performance metrics, these building blocks can be shared and utilized by other teams working on similar tasks. Through a proposed experimental platform, this method of cooperation is tested and evaluated to demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency.

This study develops an optimal two given edge-weighting method for degree degree correlated low density parity check codes by first optimizing the edge weight distribution and then applying an optimal given edge weighting. Numerical results show that optimal given edge weighting outperforms other schemes, including constant edge weighting and deletion resistant LDPC codes. Furthermore, it is discovered that given edge weighting achieves the best performance at high deletion rates and low density compared to other weighting methods.

A predictive security filter has been created to monitor complex network control systems against malicious cyber attacks. Using an System Level Synthesis approach, the filter continuously generates secure trajectories for the system and determines the safest path forward based on current measurements and uncertain conditions. These trajectories enable the detection of malicious cyber attacks in real-time. A system level synthesis-based method is advantageous as it can create secure trajectories for systems with constraints that are subject to uncertainties, unlike traditional model predictive control methods that require precise information. Furthermore, the proposed filter can operate without detailed knowledge of the system's true state, making it suitable for use by system operators or commercial security tools. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the filter was applied to networked systems including a storage network and a power grid.

In our analysis of the security of quantum key distribution, we evaluate a method called active photon number allocation (PNA) that relies solely of the mean phase variance (AMPV) of individual decoy states. It's found that PNA is vulnerable to a specific type of attack called the cloning attack, which can compromise security even when PNA accurately allocates key bits and rejects incorrectly identified basis settings. As such, our findings strongly advocate for PNA to either forgo active photon number allocation or ensure the phase of each photon in a given pulse is completely randomized to maintain the security of quantum key distribution.

This study investigates the influence of pretraining corpora on a model's in-context learning capabilities, utilizing the 540-billion-parameter GLM-130B language model. It compares two pretraining corpora, specifically WebText and Chinese Web data, for both English and Chinese evaluations. With task prompts supplied out-of-sample, our results from eight distinct tasks demonstrate that pretraining on diverse, real-world corpora can considerably boost a language model's in-context learning performance across multiple metrics and significantly enhance data efficiency and task flexibility. Notably, our findings also demonstrate a strong correlation between a model's in-context learning performance and its zero-shot evaluation capabilities. Moreover, we extend our analysis to explore the impact of pretraining on the structure and distribution of a language model's latent representations.

To investigate the effect of turbulence, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction on the behavior of the intracluster medium (ICM), three models of ICM were developed: radiatively cooling with different cooling rates, heated by turbulent dissipation, and also with additional contributions from cooling of cold clouds and turbulent heating and thermal conduction. This was done to replicate the cluster Abell 2142 and understand the interaction between the hot ICM and its precipitation. It is shown that the relationship between the heat flux and temperature in the ICM is non-linear and affected by radiative cooling, turbulence, and thermal conduction. This is affected by the size of the turbulent eddies and a new relationship between heat flux and magnetic field strength and turbulent turnover time has been proposed. This is affected by radiative cooling of the cold ICM, and cold ICM precipitation is promoted by radiative cooling and restricted by thermal conduction, and it is shown that this can be affected by the structure of the turbulent cascade and the magnetic field strength and orientation.

The violation of the conservation laws of C and P is an intriguing topic in particle physics, the study of which in the context of the Standard Model and beyond the Standard Model is an exciting area of research. This article provides a comprehensive overview of the latest research findings in C and P violation within the beauty elegance framework.

This research investigates how the string interaction cross-sections of string states change at high energies within various string theory models. We demonstrate that in all bosonic, type II, and type HO string theories, the ultraviolet behavior of string state scattering is proportional to $(\sin s/\Lambda^2)^n$, where $\Lambda$ denotes the string scale and $n$ is either 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Our findings align with the Gross conjecture for bosonic and type II string theories, whereas in type HO string theory, the high-energy scattering behavior is found to contradict the Gross conjecture.

As 5G networks approach core network deployment, understanding their self-organization, sustainability, and scalability will be crucial to 5G success. To this end, a novel framework for modeling and analyzing 5G core networks has been developed, enabling designers and operators to evaluate the efficacy of new technologies, troubleshoot issues, and make informed decisions based on future growth and changes in cellular networks. At its foundation, this framework is a sustainable, highly adaptable model that uses a combination of existing and adaptable modeling techniques to represent 5G core networks. This paper outlines the theoretical underpinnings of the framework, its underlying modeling methodology, and its capacity for incorporating new modeling techniques. Following an examination of 5G core network architectures, the paper then explores the fundamental building blocks of the framework, including a database for storing operator and network data and a modeling engine that incorporates existing and future modeling techniques. Next, the paper delves into the framework's underlying methods for knowledge representation and reasoning, including the utilization of ontologies, logic, and the semantic web to create flexible and adaptable services. Finally, the paper demonstrates the efficacy of the framework by applying it to analyze a 5G core network, including its ability to identify issues, predict future growth and changes in cellular networks, and make sustainability-based decisions.

In the absence of available text-to-speech data, we propose an innovative approach leveraging internet-scavenged speech units to create a realistic voice profile from speech audio alone. First, the speech audio is segmented based on acoustic units of reference speakers, and the speech of an unknown target speaker is then modeled using speech units of reference speakers, with parameters fine-tained using unit-segmentation-based image patch-segmentation model. Evaluation of our proposed method reveals that it can create highly accurate voice models even without any prior knowledge of the target speaker's voice.

We approach the challenge of coupled trajectory optimization in complex environments by interweaving it with learning-based approximations of the crucial McCormick bounds. Our method utilizes trajectory snapshots to refine these bounds, ensuring a crucial balance between computational efficiency and planning accuracy. Through simulations of various navigation tasks involving dynamic obstacles, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel approach, revealing that our learned approximation offers superior quality compared to conventional methods and leads to a notable reduction in solution time using IPOPT.

Cup and coffee can be modeled as a system where the pivot point is the cup's center of mass and the effective bob is the cup's center of mass, with the coffee's mass acting as the bob. The movement of the hand holding the cup introduces a forced oscillation, leading to a challenge in achieving steady circular motion due to the need for the acceleration vector to remain aligned with the bob. The dynamics of this system are influenced by parameters such as the amplitude and frequency of oscillation, with a change in parameters leading to the emergence of complex, chaotic movements. Notably, an increase in the bob's amplitude is observed as oscillation frequency increases, and the system may exhibit signs of type-II intermittency, leading to complex, chaotic movements.

In a decentralized setting, where multiple agents are linked through a graph, they aim to find a consensus solution to an optimization problem through iterative communication. However, the existence of malicious agents can distort the optimization landscape, rendering it unsuitable for learning. To address this, we introduce a robust algorithm, DR-DSGD, that incorporates a Wasserberg penalty to mitigate the impact of contaminated data and uncertain topologies. When applied to stochastic optimization problems, DR-DSGD converges to a neighborhood of the optimal solution at a rate of O(1/K), given certain constraints on corruption and neighbor selection. We further examine its performance in finding a consensus solution to a sum of convex functions, and compare it with a variant of Nesterov's algorithm in an uncontaminated setting.

This work develops a general method for creating initial conditions for relativistic heavy-ion collisions by combining kinetic theory and hydrodynamics into an hydro-kinetic approach.  The model links the non-equilibrium energy density from kinetic theory with the equilibrium values used in hydrodynamics, allowing for the discovery of hydrodynamic attractors that can ease the transition between the two regimes.  By employing this hybrid approach, we can generate event-by-event initial energy distributions, which will be crucial for understanding the initial state of quark-gluon plasma and how it is formed in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

Observations from ALMA reveal that molecular jets powered by young protostars, moving at high speeds, have been found to drive much slower outflows, which are more abundant and move in all directions. These fast-moving jets interact with the surrounding dense clouds, causing the surrounding area to expand at a lower speed in every direction. This process is shown through 3D simulations of the early stages of star formation within a dense cloud environment. According to theoretical calculations and the existing ALMA data, this outward expansion could be responsible for launching and directing colliding wind binaries and other features in early star formation.

This study develops a performance-satisfaction equilibrated control approach for nonlinear systems subject to constraints. Beginning with an introduction to equilibrated control, the research derives and investigates performance and saturation functions along with their respective sets. An optimization problem is then formulated to equitably distribute the system's state from the performance set to the saturation set. A novel iterative algorithm is employed to solve this optimization problem and efficiently compute equilibrated control laws. The resulting laws are applied to a constrained nonlinear system for validation, with further exploration into its potential for enhancing nonlinear model predictive computation.

Orbital resonances caused by the radiation pressure from the Sun significantly impact small satellites, particularly those in resonant states where small disturbances lead to large variations in their altitude, affecting their mission lifetimes and orbit predictability. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the solar radiation pressure semi-secular resonances using both analytical and numerical approaches, beginning with an examination of the characteristics of the resonances, followed by a study of their analytical solutions and then a comparison with numerical algorithms for their acceleration computation, highlighting the advantages of the proposed method over existing algorithms in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

A model of light-matter interactions based on first-principle tight-binding models demonstrates light-confinement neutral security, which we establish with a detailed proof. The sample's security with respect to the speed of light in vacuum is shown to be equivalent to its security with respect to the speed of light within the material itself. The equivalence is shown by expressing the non-Hermitian dyadic Green's functions in a tight-binding model as a power series expansion of the free-space dyadic Green's functions in the speed of light. The accuracy of this power series is further validated through numerical tests across various material types, which demonstrates a high level of accuracy with very small relative errors with rapid convergence.

This research introduces a novel framework that leverages category-specific semantic information for three-dimensional object reconstruction and orientation determination. The approach utilizes sparse two-dimensional keypoints observed from an object and identifies corresponding three-dimensional landmark positions by referencing a model repository of shape models trained on specific object categories. The framework's innovation is twofold: a novel optimization technique that incorporates isotropic scale-invariant visual features for simultaneous object positioning, rotation, scaling, and pose alignment estimation; and a new object representation strategy that incorporates variation learning for enhanced reconstruction quality and alignment accuracy. The framework is evaluated on difficult category-level object perception tasks in cluttered environments and demonstrates superior performance over novel network-based methods for accurate 3D reconstruction and orientation determination.

This studyIntroduces a novel interval estimation technique for parameters of a Cauchy distribution, employing method of moments estimation. The primary objective is to derive exact confidence intervals for the Cauchy location parameter and exact confidence regions for the Cauchy parameter vector, based on P-values resulting from exact inference. The symmetry of P-values allows for the construction of exact confidence intervals and regions at any specified level. The method of moments estimation's asymptotic distribution, which aligns with a Cauchy distribution, facilitates the development of a Gaussian-based approximate interval estimation procedure, and this is also applied to the Cauchy parameter vector. The comparison between these three methods, including the maximum likelihood estimator, demonstrates that the method of moments estimation yields confidence intervals with comparable precision to the maximum likelihood estimation, but with significantly reduced computational complexity. The existence of closed-form solutions for all three estimators provides an advantage, and this method can be readily implemented using standard software without specialized tools. The quality of coverage for the intervals is assessed through simulations.

Conducting research involving multiple patient groups, such as those receiving different drug doses, can be time-consuming and require more participants than necessary when underlying biological similarities are exploited through statistical analysis. This study develops a statistical framework for determining an optimal number of subjects in Bayesian designs, where multiple groups' mutual relationships are considered, by estimating posterior distribution of subject size and selecting the median size size. Two potential decision criteria are proposed for choosing which group sizes to actual recruitment. Under non-informative prior assumption, the proposed method shows significant improvement over traditional non-recursive methods in terms of total subject numbers, while considering simultaneous maintenance of pre-specified significance levels to ensure safety and efficacy.

High-performance motion systems are susceptible to disturbances and uncertain dynamics, which pose significant challenges for sequential loop tightening under the precompensator approach, a strategy that uses a feedforward controller to enhance performance in the inner loop while a feedback controller ensures robustness across outer loops with slower response times and distinct shaping objectives. A precompensator, typically a stable inverse of a performance matrix, may introduce robustness issues due to system and dynamics uncertainties. This research presents a method that incorporates an performance and robustness shaping feedback controller, allowing for tighter loops in some frequency ranges and more conservative feedback in others, which can improve robustness without reducing loop bandwidth. This controller, derived from a specific feedback structure and parameter choices, can be efficiently computed using convex methods. The approach is demonstrated on a 3-axis stage under the influence of disturbances and uncertain dynamics, yielding an improved robustness margin compared to traditional sequential loop tightening.

Our research centers around the crucial real-world alignment task of aligning partial point cloud views with other partial views, excluding traditional full-cloud alignment methods and regression-based approaches susceptible to mismatches. To overcome these limitations, we develop an efficient, versatile, and robust deep learning framework called PRNet for alignment of arbitrary partial point cloud views. To enhance the network's robustness against occlusions and imperfect correspondences, we design a reversible, two-way correspondence module that generates a reliable matching signal through self-supervised learning, free from the need for external supervision. To ensure alignment precision and robustness, we integrate a view-invariant point-wise normal-consistent module, and introduce a new loss function combining cyclic correspondence, point-wise normal consistency, and a multi-scale point set regression that aligns key geometric features while penalizing regression loss with the geometric alignment error. Experimental results validate the enhanced occlusion and noise resistance of our framework, outperforming the state-of-the-art on standard benchmark datasets.

A group G is classified as R-infinite if any two co-register elements of its completed form are conjugatable within G. In this paper, we demonstrate that the quotient of the Baumslag-Solitar group BS(2,3) by its lower central series' R-infinite nature is confirmed, which implies the verification of the R-infinite nature for the Baumslag-Solitar group BS(N,2) for all odd values of N greater than or equal to 3. Additionally, our findings enable the validation that a wide variety of nilpotent groups possess R-infinite nature.

If the Standard Model is inherently unstable, as indicated by meta-stability, high-energy collisions at a future collider would have a non-zero probability of triggering a transition to a low-energy vacuum state. This process is highly unpredictable, making it challenging to anticipate which collider, if any, could potentially initiate this transition. A recent research study examined the operational ranges of several future colliders, including the Future Circular Collider at a circular tunnel and the Linear Collider, to determine their likelihood of producing large-scale vacuum decay events. Contrary to previous research, this study found that a 23- to 33 TeV circular tunnel collider has the highest probability of producing at least one vacuum decay event per 10 years of operation. However, if the unknown Higgs-boson self-interaction is positive, as the data slightly suggests, the Linear Collider has the highest chance of producing at least one vacuum decay event.

A new method is developed to accurately forecast complex molecular processes, such as the movement of electrons and shift of atoms, from time-resolved experimental data like X-ray diffraction patterns. This approach uses molecular dynamics simulations to compare and adapt to simulated and real-world data, measuring their similarity through mutual information and optimizing orbital representations to minimize differences. The method was tested on molecular systems with known structural changes and shown to be adaptable to variations in real-world data, such as changes in mutual information scaling and fluctuations in signal amplitude. The method was applied to simulate the movement of atoms and electron distributions, providing accurate predictions of structural changes for the photolyzed Azobenzene molecule and other key structural features of the photolyzed Cytochrome C Oxidase molecule.

The primary goal of this research is to calculate and compare the spatial distributions of the D*, D, and Ds* mesons. This study calculates the Bethe-Salpeter amplitudes for these mesons, which in turn allow for an examination of their internal wave functions and form factors. By analyzing the wave functions at zero momentum transfer and leveraging a light-front approach, we are able to extract and compare the distribution profiles of the D*, D, and Ds* mesons.

We on purpose tackle two inquiries regarding the Fourier transform of Schwartz functions within specific Beurling-Gelfand-Shilov spaces. The first inquiry concerns the characterization of functions whose Fourier transform resides in the same space, while the second concerns the assurance of a non-empty space of functions whose Fourier transform does not reside in the same space. Our analysis yields the necessary and sufficient conditions for addressing these inquiries, which in turn have applications to Toeplitz operators on associated weighted $L^2$ spaces.

This study proposes an approach to train an instance segmentation model on data from an unlabelled modality, leveraging pre-trained models for other modalities, termed cyclic division generative adversarial network (C-DGAN). C-DGAN maintains a generator that takes an image from a pre-trained modality and an instance segmentation model, generating output that matches the modality of the original image, making it identical to having an instance segmentation model on that modality. By utilizing this novel module in the pre-trained modality that precedes a pre-trained model, the system maintains the original pre-trained model' optimal performance while training on the modality for which an instance segmentation model has been optimized, effectively transferring the learned features to the modality for which label information is unavailable. The method's performance was evaluated through training on an unlabelled modality within the Cityscapes dataset, employing pre-trained models based on Mask R-CNN and Deformable Mask R-CNN based on the COCO dataset. The results show that C-DGAN can train effective instance segmentation models on urban driving scenes, outperforming previous methods that have been based on the model training on the COCO dataset.

To enhance the accuracy of action prediction through increased temporal distance, our method utilizes an information-rich feature that utilizes an adaptive, recurrent model to bridge the gap in predicted features.  The model's effectiveness is demonstrated by its ability to outperform multiple comparison benchmarks in predicting actions with a moderate error rate of 12.1 percent for Kinetics-400 and 10.7 percent for TF-AWSome-10M.

A remarkable UV continuum emission was observed during AD Leo's Great Flare on April 12, 1985, by the HEOSAT satellite at wavelengths 140-165 nm and 155-175 nm. Observations revealed enhanced emission in the blue region of the UV spectrum compared to its red, contrasting with typical stellar flares. Extending typical models of flares into near-UV wavelengths, we found that UV continuum simulation required higher electron densities, temperatures, and filling factors to match observations. Specifically, a dual-component model, consisting of cool (80-100% fill factor, 20% fill factor) and hot (2% fill factor) plasma, was used to fit observed spectra. While fitting 160-175 nm, a cool plasma model with high electron density ($N_e \sim 10^{12} cm^{-3}$) and temperature ($T \sim 15-20 kK$) was used. Conversely, a hot plasma model with low filling factor ($f \sim 0.02$) and temperature ($T \sim 30-50 kK$) was used to fit 140-155 nm data. Such UV continuum simulation required higher fill factors and filling factors in star flares compared to typical solar flares.

We are exploring the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons defined on four-dimensional manifolds that feature nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry. The research provides a deformation sequence for these moments, along with a deformation complex and the first and second deformation obstructions, effectively establishing the complete deformation theory for such moments. Additionally, we examine the application of this deformation theory in the context of nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ geometry reductions of four-dimensional self-dual Yang-Mills fields.

This paper investigates the conditions under which a composition operator with symbol $\varphi$ and a symbol $\psi$ of a $C_{\psi}^{2}$-normal operator on $H^2$ yields a $C_{\varphi}^{2}$-normal operator.

Given a large prime p and a positive integer n not divisible by p, we define a (p-core, p'-sequence) of length n as a strictly increasing sequence of p-core numbers a_1, a_2, ..., a_n, where each number is congruent to the previous one modulo p. We also consider a graph where vertex numbers are non-core numbers and an edge connects two vertices if the connected numbers are congruent to each other modulo p. Our results show that the number of such sequences is equivalent to the number of non-core numbers, which equals the number of walk of length n in the graph, that is, (Tr(A^n)+Tr(A^(-n)))/(2), where A is the non-singular adjacency matrix of the graph.

Our proposed method, Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC), treats point cloud model smoothing as a shape matching task to preserve details in detailed areas and remove noise in less detailed areas. By leveraging an established metric-driven framework for network-driven shape matching, we develop an iterative framework that gradually aligns point clouds with a template mesh. The process creates correspondence points that in turn inform an adaptive regularization term, removing over-regularization in high-detail areas while removing over-regularization in flat areas. Experimental results demonstrate that tpc achieves state-of-the-art smoothening outcomes with minimal user input, producing high-quality results even with low template density and limited user input.

We investigate methods to enhance the reliability of FMCW radar networks using medium access control protocols. Our research focuses on two alternative access methods: Slotted ALOHA and ALOLA-DBF (Direction of Beamforming), as well as a variation of CSMA that incorporates beamforming. Our analysis assumes that nodes can determine the location of interfering signals and use this information to adjust their transmission power towards each other. Our findings show that the proposed beamforming-based protocol significantly outperforms Slotted ALOHA in terms of achieved throughput. Our model is adaptable to real-world implementations by taking into account practical constraints, such as finite slope and transmission power limitations in FMCW radar systems.

This study explores how the energy distribution of a photon pair influences their behavior in a Hong-Ou-Mandel experiment when interacting with a non-linear medium that facilitates absorbed energy. Specifically, we examine a scenario where a photon pair enters a Hong-Ou-Mandel setup from opposite directions, with one photon passing through a thin non-linear material and triggering a process of entangled photon absorption. As a result, even with a fully coherent photon pair source, we observe reduced two-photon correlations at the output, accompanied by a selective consumption of specific energy distributions and a shift towards higher photon numbers. Interestingly, if the photon pair interacts with two identical beamsplitters, we observe restored two-photon correlations, with selective consumption of higher photon number distributions, all occurring at a rate proportional to the square of the first. These effects are highly sensitive to the spectral properties of the photon pair, particularly when an energy sharing imbalance or momentum mode overlap occurs, ultimately determining the absorbed photon number.

This paper calculates the elliptic cohomology for compact Lie groups, given T is a maximal torus of it. We utilize a more inclusive T* -equivariant elliptic cohomology theory for our approach. An earlier study of C*-equivariant cohomology by Anderson and Nahm has been a guiding factor here. We develop the concept of logical C*-theory and demonstrate its relationship with C*-equivariant cohomology, leading to a determination of the T*-logical elliptic cohomology. This, in turn, enables us to find the elliptic cohomology of CP(V) by the application of T*-logical elliptic cohomology operations.

Temporal knowledge graphs evolve over time, exhibiting distinct temporal patterns in their representation.
Existing models typically depend on pre-defined representation learning techniques which limit their flexibility and efficiency.
These methods also necessitate a substantial number of parameters, posing challenges in cases of sparse data with limited entities and relations.
To overcome these limitations our proposed framework involves three key components.
Firstly, representations of facts are decomposed into structural and temporal aspects, with the low-rank structural representation enhancing representation efficiency.
Secondly, predictive representations are learned through a model-agnostic approach, allowing the framework to operate independently of specific representation learning methods.
Thirdly, facts are matched by aggregating facts with high temporal and structural similarities to factual and factually similar groups, facilitating effective learning through consideration of these grouped facts' representations.
