A fundamental concept that uncertainty quantification brings to engineering and the sciences is risk and decision-making. This project begins by defining uncertainty measurement in the context of SchL, examining its theoretical underpinnings and illustrating uncertainty quantification in Monte Carlo methods and deep ensembles. This project also explores three main uncertainty types: parameter uncertainty, uncertainty arising from the model, and total uncertainty. This project then introduces three primary methods of uncertainty measurement: Bayesian approaches, neural network methods, and physics-informed machine learning, providing guidance on choosing the appropriate technique and metric. This project concludes with a comparative analysis of uncertainty measurement metrics and presents a roadmap for future research and development in the field.

We examine a specific von Neumann algebra formed from a compact quantum group, derived from a subgroup and its associated category functions. The central question is whether this function von Neumann algebra equals the von Neumann algebra of central functions. We establish that it is always包含, with equality holding in the case of a quasi-Hopf algebra. However, in the context of Hopf algebras, equality occurs if and only if the category of modules for a subgroup satisfies the property of being a Calabi-Yau odd category. Furthermore, in the case of a compact matrix quantum group and a subgroup that is also a compact matrix quantum group, equality occurs if and and only the quantum dimension of any object in the category of modules has a specific value equal to 1.

To tackle large-scale Markov decision processes, a synthetic value iteration approach is undertaken with the aim of generating an approximate policy. To accelerate the value iteration process, a set of restricted policy iterations are developed under uncertain policy evaluations. These iterations utilize a nonprecise GMRES algorithm, generating an approximate policy that is near-optimal within a small margin of error. Moreover, it is proven that this approximate policy can be found rapidly relative to the GMRES' synthesis time. Numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of these restricted policy iterations, showing significant improvements in both computational efficiency and accuracy.

Given a weighted directed graph, we will examine the symbolic and typical powers of its edge ideal. In doing so, we have established a condition under which the typical symbolic power of the edge ideal equals an integer multiple of the ordinary power, and in weighted directed bipartite graphs, this holds for all n greater than or equal to s plus one, where s represents the maximum degree of a single vertex. Furthermore, in oriented trees, we have formulated a conjecture about this relationship, and explored the concept of the regularity of the typical symbolic power. This research builds upon existing theories and results in the field of commutative algebra and algebraic geometry.

This research focuses on developing an effective method for estimating unknown parameters in high-dimensional linear thermal simulator models through simulated data. The proposed approach utilizes a continuous approximation of the likelihood function, estimated through multiple Monte Carlo evaluations of the squared distance between model outputs and data across various frequencies. The frequencies are selected by optimizing a specific criterion to ensure efficient use of computational resources. The resulting algorithm, MCCE-MLE, combines this approximation with an iterative estimation method to ensure consistent results and efficient convergence in cases of model misspecification. Through comprehensive simulations and a case study involving synthetic data from a computer model, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance to alternative methods in terms of bias and computational time.

Research has shown that even when data is corrupted, Causal Inference algorithms can still perform well, relying on the robust structural assumptions of the model rather than data quality. One key assumption is the correctness of the causal graph used in these algorithms. However, obtaining accurate causal graphs can be challenging, prompting researchers to develop algorithms that can learn the causal graph from noisy data along with individual variables. These algorithms typically rely on two key properties: (a) the separation between noise and clean data, and (b) the correctness of the causal graph. In contrast, we investigate the possibility of learning causal graphs when these properties are compromised by showing that local inquiries can help in these instances. Specifically, we develop a causal learning algorithm that utilizes labeled samples and permits an agent to ask for the labels of any subset of locally connected nodes. The results show that even without a significant gap between noisy and clean data, and limited to a small number of queries, the use of local inquiries allows for efficient learning of the causal graph in both binary and general cases.

For the first time, fragmentation changes in jets have been observed within the QCD framework of quark to hadron transitions when influenced by a hot and dense medium. This was seen through comparisons of measurements from lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV, with lead-proton collisions at a lower energy of 2.76 TeV. The analysis, carried out using data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC, involved over 12 million events of jets triggered by a single photon. It was discovered that as the transverse momentum of jets decreases, the influence of the medium on how quarks form hadrons increases significantly.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has led to significant discoveries, including novel properties of Apéry-type series, such as those examined by Borwein et al. To build on this research, we will demonstrate a novel identity that enables the evaluation of the product of the odd Apéry constant $\pi^2/4$ and a weighted combination of the Catalan constant $G$ and Riemann's constant $\beta(2)$, using an alternative representation. This representation will be expressed as an infinite series involving powers of natural numbers and the values of even and odd Apéry constants as well as $G$ and $\beta(2)$. In addition to this, we will provide a novel expression for a specific type of colored polylogarithmic series known as colored multiple zeta functions by combining these Apéry-type series with even zeta values. This new representation will be expressed as an infinite series involving even powers of natural numbers and the values of odd zeta values. Furthermore, this specific type of series will also be represented as an infinite series with even weighting values, a color of 4, and a final term involving even Apéry constants as well as even zeta values.

A peculiar, close brown dwarf binary located approximately 100 light years away has been identified. Composed of two nearly equal components with a combined temperature of around 650 Kelvin, they are locked in a stable orbit at a distance of 1.26 ± 0.06 Arcseconds and revolve around a shared center of mass with an estimated 93 ± 48.5 AU orbital radius and a 30 to 150 million year period. Unique in its characteristics, this system shares similarities with other binary systems, particularly in its location, thermal properties, and lack of observed light in the far ultraviolet spectrum, suggesting a similar unexplained phenomenon. Additionally, this system is distinct for its significant and unusual round-shaped features in its light emissions across various wavelengths, characterized by "dust-like" flatness and suppressed brightness at far-infrared spectrum. These peculiarities may be attributed to a highly elliptical, face-on, shared brown dwarf orbit or potentially shared heat from a shared heat source.

Our research focuses on the production of pions, kaons, protons, antiprotons and $\phi$-mesons that result from Xe-Xe collisions at the CERN LHC with an energy of 5.44 TeV per nucleon pair. To analyze the production of these particles, we employed the DGLAP evolution equation, and our calculations are compared to the measured data obtained by the CMS and ALICE experiments. In addition, we investigated the multiplicity, rapidity distribution and $p_{\rm T}$-spectrum of these particles, and found that our model accurately matches the experimental results for the Xe-Xe collisions. To further understand the particle production process, we also computed the relative yields, nuclear enhancement factors and relative abundance factors, and compared them to the results from Au-Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV and p-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV.

A novel, self-consistent method is introduced to determine the position-dependent parton distribution function (PDGF) at any given energy scale, utilizing data from lower energy scales along with effective parton evolution equations that are scale-independent and dependent on position. The position dependence of PDGFs is directly linked to the position dependence of the PDGFs' moments through a multiple-Twist expansion. As a direct consequence, the position dependence of PDGFs can be fully characterized by their leading Twist functions alone. The proposed approach allows for the effective interpolation of PDGFs across varying energy scales and also facilitates more accurate evolution than currently employed in global PDF fits. In addition, it enables a more precise use of high-$x$ constraints derived from fixed-angle hadron distributions to improve global PDF fits by avoiding the use of truncated Soffer bound limits on $x-dependent$ twist-two distributions as currently done.

For missions to Mars and the Moon, building habitats and structures using local regolith is a promising approach, with thermal conductivity and structural frameworks requiring careful evaluation through pre-flight research. In this study, we investigated the pre-flight factors influencing the thermal and mechanical properties of regolith-based composite materials from the Martian and Lunar surfaces. We used fine-mesh sieving and image analysis to standardize the shape, size distribution, and surface characteristics of the grains. Regolith grains were combined with 10 or 20 vol% of PVB or PVDF binders and molded into discs at 200°C for 10 minutes, with sintering at temperatures of 300, 400, and 500°C for 1 hour under a vacuum. Mechanical tests and thermal property measurements were performed on the molded samples, with further analysis using XRD, TGA, and SEM to determine the phase and microstructure compositions. Our results indicate that 10 vol% of PVDF binder yielded the best outcome with the Martian and Lunar grains respectively, with compressive strengths of 3.6 MPa and 2.1 MPa, exceeding the target values proposed by previous studies and reaching those of concrete.

The dynamics of a liquid layer forming droplets on a curved fiber is a phenomenon that requires enhanced consideration in case of high slip at the interface with the fiber. This is significant for understanding and controlling self-assembly processes in microfluidics systems that utilize liquid in microchannels with solid structures. A theoretical model developed using the long-wave approximation describes how a liquid layer on a curved fiber breaks down into a series of droplets in both no-slip and slip-enhanced conditions. This model considers vanishing viscosity and variable surface tension, and is valid for weak and strong breakdown scenarios. In particular, it determines the wavelength and growth rate of the droplet formation process under these two conditions, and identifies how these factors are affected by slip-enhanced conditions in both scenarios. In the case of high viscosity, an additional consideration involves the accumulation of liquid on the fiber due to evaporation.

We have developed an innovative method to assess star formation rates in distant galaxies by leveraging the Brackett-$\gamma$ line. By creating an extensive dataset of 1,000 synthetic star-forming galaxy models, we, along with existing data from the COSMOS field, have determined that B$\gamma$ emission is detectable for ~30% of galaxies at $z \sim 3$ and up to ~80% at $z \sim 3.5$ under the 10m-class telescope. B$\gamma$ is most effective in identifying star formation in dusty, gas-rich galaxies, with higher star formation rates and dust contents allowing for more accurate identification and measurement of star formation rates. B$\gamma$ is particularly valuable in determining star formation rates in extremely dusty galaxies, where it can remain unattenuated despite significant optical extinction. B$\gamma$ is also a robust tracer for minor star-forming events, allowing for an increase in completeness and reducing bias towards larger star-forming galaxies. B$\gamma$ is most reliable for galaxies with rest-frame B$\gamma$ at $\gtrsim 1\mu$Jy, allowing for accurate determination of star formation rates within a factor of two. B$\gamma$ is expected to be a crucial element in upcoming large-scale spectroscopic surveys, such as MOSAIC and EXHiST-2, allowing for an unbiased and comprehensive exploration of star formation rates and related properties in galaxies

This is the initial paper in a two-part series that defines and characterizes a type II quantum subgroup from the universal quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{N+1})$. In this paper, we introduce the concept of regional symmetry and establish its equivalence with being a type II quantum subgroup, before demonstrating that it has a corresponding quiver-Dynkin diagram representation.

The classical heat equation can be reinterpreted as a special case of a more general fractional diffusion process, which is linked to a family of symmetric $\alpha$-stable processes, where $\alpha$ ranges from  0 to 2.  This process can be generalized to higher dimensions and more complex spaces.  In this work, a framework is developed to establish a stochastic representation for a broad class of general diffusions based on this fractional process and a specific type of subordinator.  Additionally, a corresponding stochastic representation is derived for generalized fractional kernels.

This study introduces an innovative approach to identifying handwritten mathematical equations using data obtained from sensors, specifically those attached to a person's fingers. In order to reduce the impact of errors introduced by the proximity sensor, our technique treats the generated signal as a two-dimensional image, which is then analyzed using an Convolutional Neural Network to classify the mathematical equations. To validate this method, we have developed an interface that enables the collection of training data, which is subsequently used to establish the accuracy of our equation detection system. Furthermore, we have examined the interpretability of our network to gain a better understanding of how it processes information and makes decisions. This study marks the first instance of leveraging proximity sensor data and applying a machine learning technique to detect complex mathematical equations written by hand.

The duration of speech segments significantly influences the effectiveness of connectionist models, particularly in language processing tasks. Traditionally, the average duration derived from aligned speech and text data is employed to estimate speech durations for connectionist models. However, relying on the mean can be problematic due to the inherent variability in speech durations, which often includes significant outliers that skew the result. In this research paper, an alternative approach based on the median is proposed to minimize the impact of speech duration skew. Initially, the concept of a hierarchical duration model, which incorporates speech durations derived from speech recognition systems, is introduced. Subsequently, an algorithm is presented to synthetically generate speech durations based on this model, leveraging a non-parametric approach that relies solely on the speech duration median. The effectiveness of these proposed durations is demonstrated, leading to enhanced recognition accuracy of continuous speech compared to traditional methods.

Species distribution analysis heavily relies on absence presence data, despite a significant portion of species absence data remaining unknown. Researchers have developed various spatial presence models to address this issue, acknowledging that species absence is often a combination of true absence and unavailability for observation. The spOccupancy package facilitates the fitting of single-species, multi-species, and integrated spatial presence models along with predictive uncertainty assessment and spatial visualization of predicted species distributions. Additionally, the package supports the creation of dynamic models tracking year-to-year state transitions. Two fitting functions, fitOccupancy and fitMultiOccupancy, correspond to single-species and multi-species models, respectively, and are accompanied by a series of related functions for model evaluation, visualization, and diagnostics. Furthermore, the package allows the incorporation of latent state persistence to improve predictions of species distributions.

The rise in smartphone usage has made it convenient for individuals to take and store self-portrait photos on their devices. A growing number of dermatologists now utilize digital imaging for visual inspections, which has set the stage for developing an artificial skin condition diagnosis system. By leveraging large datasets of dermatologically diagnosed images and advanced deep learning technology, a system called the Skincare initiative was developed to facilitate accurate diagnosis of skin conditions, which can likely be achieved using smartphone-pictured moles.

To validate this system's core components, which relied on deep neural networks to analyze images, we conducted experiments using a curated dataset of roughly 100 benign and malignant moles. The data was pre-processed to create high-quality images, which were then used to train convolutional neural networks to differentiate between benign and malignant cases. The trained models were tested and found capable of correctly identifying approximately 80% of the moles. The remaining moles were input into a Bayesian classifier model, which was trained using the models' output image features to classify benign and malignant cases. The classifer model performed well, correctly classifying approximately 90% of the moles.

The system's overall architecture was designed to create an interactive diagnostic tool, which could provide real-time feedback to users as they collected and analyzed moles in real-time, while also providing the ability to refine the system's decision-making process.

To capture the variability in Type Ia supernovae, a probabilistic Autoencoder is developed and employed to compress variability from large SNuIAe samples. By analyzing 722 spectra taken before peak brightness, and then normalizing them by peak time and peak flux, we can identify variations in SNuIAe behavior. The results show that SNuIAe take on a linear structure in a reduced three-dimensional space defined by principal components. Using a hidden layer with three neurons in our model allows us to accurately reproduce the observed variability with approximately 95% reconstruction accuracy. The SNuIAe mean profile is found to have a positive correlation with a cos^2 function of the redshift, and we use our model to investigate the effects of absorption features on SNuIAe behavior as a function of redshift. The proposed model offers advantages over traditional dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA, due to its nonlinear capabilities, and is approximately ten times faster to train. The proposed model facilitates the analysis of large SNuIAe spectral datasets, and we demonstrate the potential of our model to relate reduced SNuIAe features to secondary parameters.

A high-redshift, heavily obscured star-forming galaxy, which is subject to extreme gravitational lensing, is being studied using a combination of lensing techniques and radio frequency observations. This galaxy, which resides in a highly magnified dust cloud, is detected at a frequency of 1.8 GHz via lensed radio frequency observations. Despite being magnified in size and brightness, its lensed radio frequency emission appears to be uniformly distributed. This uniform distribution is consistent with the presence of a spherical neutral gas cloud that is expanding at a speed of 30-50 km/s. Although the neutral gas is expanding in size, its mass remains constant as it is continuously supplied by an outflowing gas with a mass of 10 to 100 times the mass of the Earth per year. This gaseous outflow, which is likely driven by the galaxy's intense star formation activity, is moving at a speed of 10 to 100 km/s and is concentrated in smaller structures within the observed region. These results shed new light on a previously elusive type of gaseous outflow in early galaxies, which is characterized by a steady state and neutral gas dominance.

To determine the flow rate of a natural hot spring, we conducted both laboratory experiments and numerical simulations, observing a transient energy release from the source as the system reaches steady state, and this state correlates with a self-similar phase of the plume's development. The established criteria for plume similarity, which accounts for the size, temperature, and mass density of the particles within the system, enables a scaling law to calculate the flow rate in terms of these parameters. Furthermore, this research lays the groundwork for similar plume studies involving particles that behave elastically or viscously, or settle at high speeds.

Understanding the spread of epidemics in networks and hypergraphs over time has led to various theoretical conclusions. 
In this study, we establish conditions under which certain network and epidemic models will lead to the complete eradication of an infection, 
utilizing the properties of a set of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. 
We demonstrate that as the number of connections increases in a specific type of hypergraph model, the resulting extinction behavior closely mirrors that of a standard Susceptible-Infected epidemiological model. 
We also develop methods to estimate the time it takes for an infection to die out and propose several methods for assessing the accuracy of these estimations.
Our findings have significant implications for predicting the natural extinction of infections and assessing the reliability of estimates derived from the SI-model.

Our theoretical investigations using first-principles calculations have examined the electronic and magnetic properties of a 2D CrI3 ferromagnet, specifically its bilayer form. We found that in the absence of a horizontal mirror plane, broken by an asymmetrically bonded I site, there are Rashba-type spin splittings at certain fermi points within the spin-split Dirac cones. In contrast, in bilayer CrI3 stacked in an A-A configuration with a present horizontal mirror plane, we observed splittings of linear size near the spin-split Dirac cones, indicative of a zero-momentum size. Furthermore, we predicted that twisting CrI3 into a moiré superstructure preserves ferromagnetism within large superatomic units, exhibiting A-A local A-type order amidst long-range checkerboard antiferromagnetic order, alongside gapped spin-split electronic transport in homogenous ferromagnetic regions. In transition to antiferromagnetic domains, I-valence p states become conductive, yielding spin-polarized surface states at ferromagnet/antiferromagnet interfaces ideal for spin-transfer interfaces. These findings support A-A stacked moiré CrI3 as a promising spin-texture engineering system to exploit Rashba effect and generate spin-polarized electrons for advanced spintronics applications.

By incorporating rotation effects based on observed solar differential rotation into mean-field solar-type dynamos, we investigate how rotation influences magnetic cycle behavior and the generation of global magnetic fields. We extend standard mean-field theories, which neglect rotation, by adding diagonal mean EMF terms that account for the effects of rotation and twist angles. These effects are represented by the Coriolis force, influencing the helicity of velocity fields. We modify the traditional $\Omega$-effect based on experimentally determined solar rotation rates, which also account for the differential rotation within the solar core. Using a one-dimensional model, we find that rotation has a significant impact on dynamo behavior, particularly when accounting for observed solar rotation rates, leading to the suppression of magnetic cycle generation. However, when assuming a faster equatorial rotation rate, dynamic oscillations and magnetic cycles can still be generated. We identify conditions under which these oscillations become unstable and lead to global magnetic fields, which may exhibit magnetic cycle behavior through interactions between turbulent and rotational fields, as described by the $\beta\Omega$-dynamo effect.

Deep learning models are highly sensitive to the quality of their underlying representations, which in turn affects their overall performance. To address the limitations of traditional supervised learning in dealing with diverse, complex data formats, our proposed deep framework utilizes multiple input channels from various modalities to automatically build robust representations that enhance multiple task performances. At its core is a k-fan multimodal deep framework consisting of multiple functional branches, each responsible for a distinct task, united by a shared representation space produced through a central aggregation module called the Deep Framework Aggregator. This module combines input modalities into a unified space where Task-Independent Representation, free of modality-specific noise, and Task-Specific Representation, free of irrelevance to each respective task, are extracted through dedicated Task Extraction Modules. Our deep framework has been successfully applied to two major classification tasks: currency detection and semantic segmentation, showcasing significant improvements in performance over state-of-the-art models.

The importance of precise model checking in detecting subtle threading bugs has been widely recognized in research, yet, in practical applications, model checking remains underutilized due to the complexity of defining the program semantics required for checking. The main obstacles are creating a semantic model compatible with checking tools and accurately describing the program's global state, particularly in languages with inherent meaning for tracing and visualization, such as C++. The McMini tool addresses these challenges by offering a modular and user-friendly framework for defining checkable semantic models, allowing users to integrate existing program analyses into model checking processes through analysis-driven Model Verification. In this approach, program static analyses provide insights into memory access patterns, enabling efficient model checking by skipping irrelevant model states. This paper showcases the McMini framework and its programmability through multiple examples of threading bug detections in multi-threaded programs, all written in the tracing/visualizable language vcp++. The McMini tool is accessible at https://github.com/klm14/mcmini.

This paper examines the effectiveness of restricting forwarded messages in detecting and disseminating false information in WhatsApp groups. In response to the rapid dissemination of misinformation in group conversations, major tech giants have implemented measures to curtail the flow of false information. Various stakeholders, including academic experts and industry leaders, have been actively engaged in mitigating the spread of misinformation in WhatsApp by implementing detection mechanisms and limiting the dissemination of suspicious content in WhatsApp groups. This study aims to evaluate the impact of these restrictions on detecting and disseminating false information in WhatsApp groups.

We analyze a broad class of population models with a positive average growth rate and sample the frequency distribution of a specific allele in large populations by considering two scenarios: either the population is observed at a large time t or the population size is set to a large value n. The frequency distribution can be approximated using a log-normal distribution in both scenarios, which is applicable to a wide range of population models, including those with non-integer characteristic exponents and polynomial variance dynamics. The results demonstrate that this approximation remains accurate as the parameter (time or value n) approaches infinity and is robust to different characteristic exponent values.

This paper focuses on developing a cutting-edge system to detect voice spoofing and a corresponding countermeasure system to automatically identify which frames constitute spoofed material. The system's foundation is an end-to-end architecture that excels in detecting voice spoofing, but it struggles with real-world applications due to its inability to accurately label individual frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose an attentive activation mechanism that counteracts the countermeasure module's decisions on a per-frame basis, making it more reliable. The proposed approach has achieved state-of-the-art performance on the popular AF-1 dataset and demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in handling large-scale datasets, as evidenced by our experiments using ASV-Ts.

This review focuses on globally supersymmetric effective field theories of inflation, and we begin by examining the general structure of such theories, followed by an in-depth analysis of two particular models: the Goldstone model resulting from breaking a supersymmetric cosmological symmetry, and an explicit inflationary effective field theory built upon a Goldstone multiplet. Then, we systematically explore a range of effective field theory extensions of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity, including various forms of exceptional effective field theories, by starting with the most straightforward approach and methodically building upon it in subsequent layers.

Parameter-adjusted type-II spontaneous parametric down-conversion setups generate spatially and temporally correlated photon pairs. When detected with on-axis, symmetric cameras, the coincidence patterns of horizontal and vertical polarizers show distinct asymmetries due to the non-identical interactions of the photon pair's polarization states with the camera's sensors. Although the coincidence patterns exhibit difference, the total sum of their intensities match perfectly, allowing any imperfectly polarized state to be visually represented by adjusting relative intensity ratios with only asymmetric transformations. This study reveals previously unnoticed properties of the down-conversion process and brings type-II correlation studies closer to type-I, not just in outcomes, but also in analysis techniques.

This research examines the spatial distribution of electromagnetic fields within micro-resonators at terahertz and microwave frequencies using a terahertz time-domain spectrometer equipped with a near-field probe. A crucial factor in designing microwave superconducting quantum devices is knowing the spatial behavior of these devices in the terahertz frequency range. A simple ladder-like resonator design was used to investigate the electric and magnetic components of the electromagnetic field. Our results indicate that both electric and magnetic near-field mappings align with expected far-field patterns and existing theoretical models. Furthermore, we discovered that the magnetic probe has a larger spatial resolution than the electric probe, likely due to a greater magnetic moment and a shorter screening path. This research provides insights into local electromagnetic interactions and supports the exploration of near-field coupling in field-coupled quantum devices.

Given an uncountable set X, we givemesh the power set of X with the countable cocompleteness metric and the countable complement topology, both denoted as $\langle X, \mathcal{P}^\ast (X)\rangle$. The question arises: can the set of all real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ be split into uncountable subsets, each resembling the mesh or topology of $\langle X, \mathcal{P}^\ast (X)\rangle$? The text provides several examples of such partitions into subsets $X_i$, each possessing unique topological or set-theoretic characteristics. The first example involves uncountable subsets $X_i$, where each is equipped with the countable complement topology. The second example features subsets $X_i$ that are equivalent to cardinalities of $\ continuum$, each equipped with the countable complement topology and possessing the continuum hypothesis. The third example involves subsets $X_i$, where each is equipped with the countable complement topology and possesses the continuum hypothesis and is a perfect set without atoms. Finally, the last example involves subsets $X_i$ of $\mathbb{R}$, where each is equipped with the countable complement topology and possesses properties of Martin-Axen's model.

This work presents an agent-based model that examines the influence of differing agent types and investment techniques on a stock market. Various trading methods are implemented to study the impact of newfound investment techniques (such as AI-driven investments) on existing market strategies, particularly during periods of market instability. Results reveal that the introduction of sophisticated AI strategies tends to diminish volatility and system losses among traditional trading methods, while high-frequency trading strategies experience decreased returns but maintain their role in system volatility. Ultimately, the model's outcomes suggest the potential beneficial effect of integrating advanced AI strategies into markets, although further research using realistic market settings and sophisticated AI types is still required to fully understand this phenomenon.

Identifying network traffic protocols is crucial for analyzing and understanding data flow during network operations. The process of dynamic protocol detection allows software to recognize open standard protocols without requiring pre-loaded databases. The primary methods for detecting protocols include using statistical analysis, machine learning, and expert systems. In our analysis, we evaluated two leading open-source protocol detection systems, WPCS and Spoofer, which utilize statistical and machine learning techniques. However, our research has shown that these systems can be manipulated through various attack methods to result in detection failures. Our findings have contributed to the protocol detection research field and provided insight into potential vulnerabilities that network operators should be aware of.

Gapping of magnons can be achieved through the proximity effect with a superconductor in addition to hybridization with superconducting spin-triplet states in order to achieve persistent magneto-heat transport at high temperatures and for prolonged times. A novel observation of this phenomenon is presented in the V$_2$OTeO-BiFeYO$_4$ system where the proximity superconducting effect outperforms the hybridization effect, leading to an effective gating of magnons and producing exceptional thermoelectric properties in V$_2$OTeO at zero magnetic field.

A prominent approach in automatic classification is federated learning, which is particularly effective in scenarios where the category of data being analyzed is well-known and familiar. Nevertheless, when new audio data from an unknown source appears, conventional federated learning methods are rendered ineffective. To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces a novel zero-shot federated learning framework tailored specifically for audio classification tasks. The framework incorporates the integration of audio encoders and encyclopedic knowledge to aid in categorizing audio. A distinctive feature of this framework is the utilization of semantic embeddings for both the central and peripheral nodes, enabling them to collaborate and exchange information effectively. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated in two audio classification tasks: plant classification and bird classification, with impressive performance gains of 11.4% and 10.2% respectively in comparative tests.

There have been multiple measurements of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states in various dimensions done previously, yet a universal, efficient method for all dimensions remains elusive. To address this, we present a general approach applicable to any dimension, with implementations in dimensions three and four using the state of four ions.

This research focuses on the practical implementation of large-scale IRS in mobile systems, specifically how a transmitter can communicate effectively with multiple users assisted by a single, large IRS. To do this, the transmitter is turned off for short periods to allow the users to collect and share the reflected channel information from the IRS. By combining this data, the transmitter can create an accurate IRS model and optimize its settings for maximum performance. The results show that this approach performs well in real-world scenarios and that the transmitter can accurately identify the best IRS settings using data from multiple users.

This study provides unique insights into U.S. local news consumption and COVID-19 reporting by analyzing online news. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset of U.S. local news websites and an NLP-based approach, we examine online news circulation patterns and the geographical variations in news content regarding COVID-19. Our analysis also explores how reported cases and deaths, along with severity levels, and pre-pandemic audience metrics pre dict the and shape local news reporting and audience engagement with U.S. local news. Our results offer understanding of key factors influencing news reporting and audience behavior among U.S. local media.

This study investigates the feasibility of neural networks, specifically augmented with recurrency and implemented in the PyTorch framework, to mimic human-like progression in learning counting from a basic state to mastering the sequence of natural numbers in the form "012345...N". Initial experiments revealed that augmented state machines can successfully learn the counting sequence, a task proven to be computationally intensive with traditional uniform networks. When exploring more complex versions of these tasks that require retaining previous outputs to generate the next output, a fundamental requirement for neural counting is the retention of output information. Initial explorations with the PyTorch framework have yielded promising results in developing these types of tasks.

Bloom filters are widely employed for approximate set membership, utilizing a blend of hashing and bit manipulation to determine if an element exists in a set. However, they suffer from false positives and can lead to memory inefficiency under heavy load. In response, researchers proposed a modified version, the Bloom filter variant using XOR sums (BfVs), which individually hashes elements and combines them using the XOR operation to mitigate the effects of bit flipping caused by insertions and deletions. While BfVs have shown promise in enabling insertions and deletions without the risk of further study is needed to fully evaluate their potential in this regard. Our investigation into BfVs reveals that certain hash functions are capable of erasing the impact of deletions, ultimately leading to a faster and more compact BfV than traditional Bloom filters and even cuckoo filters in terms of membership testing accuracy.

One key connection between convex analysis and complex geometry can be seen
through the lens of Extremal Symmetrization and Complex Symmetrization, which
are comparable processes with one-dimensional connections to convex bodies and
Steiner Splices.

In the field of intraday price discovery, researchers have a strong preference for using second-by-second last traded prices over first touched prices, which correspond to execution prices, because the former are believed to be more indicative of the market's future direction, whereas the future has no influence on the market's past. To investigate why future last traded prices dominate over present touched prices, we simulate the market based on a discrete-time model involving a market maker and multiple agents, each submitting market orders at random times, which can only be executed if the market maker has a non-zero stock position. Our model shows that current future last traded prices, but not present future first touched prices, are influenced by the market's past and present as well as its future, making their dominance in price discovery understandable, thus eliminating the need for additional market microstructure assumptions. Our findings are consistent with real-world data and market assumptions, which, along with a direct argument, provide a basis for price discovery strategies.

This paper presents a privacy-preserving framework for federated learning (FL) that incorporates differential privacy and robustness against malicious data manipulation. The FL system is susceptible to two primary threats: privacy breaches through data inference and model attacks via data poisoning. In response to the first threat, FL leverages differential privacy, a mathematically rigorous privacy standard, by adding calibrated Gaussian noise to local gradients during training. The noise intensity is modulated according to the user's risk profile. To safeguard against data poisoning attacks, the user's risk profile is utilized in conjunction with a novel outlier detection method called FLVoogd, an enhanced version of theogard that is better suited for high-dimensional spaces. The detection process is streamlined for distributed environments by introducing a consensus mechanism for the centroid estimation. The approach's efficacy is demonstrated on three diverse machine learning models, which are then applied to two real-world datasets, exhibiting superior performance over the state-of-the-art method, especially in malicous datasets with high dimensions.

We investigate a common challenge in developing autonomous vehicles, the Sim2Real gap, in End-to-End (E2E) approaches. Due to discrepancies between simulated and real driving data, performance on real data is significantly hindered. We introduce a novel technique to narrow this gap by leveraging the direction of information flow through the neural network's layers, comparing simulated and real image inputs and outputs. A layer-by-layer adaptation is achieved by adjusting the weight matrices along the determined direction of dependence. We demonstrate that this approach requires no access to real driving data, as it can be solely trained on simulated data. Furthermore, we refine this method to accommodate scenarios where labels are sparse or non-existent. Evaluations are conducted on various deep driving tasks utilizing the KITTI dataset, yielding substantial improvements in performance.

In the age of Deepfakes, creating convincing but fake multimedia is becoming increasingly easy, which poses a major threat to the authenticity of online content and public trust. A novel approach called InfoGAN-Deepfake is being explored to create convincing deepfakes out of any media, which is both attractive and concerning. To address this, infoGAN Deepfake detection is being developed to identify this type of deepfake, which poses a major challenge due to the diversity of normal media. As a measure to mitigate the risks associated with malicious deepfakes, InfoGAN-based detection is being improved to create robust deepfake detection that can identify deepfakes created from any type of normal media. To achieve this, the standard infoGAN architecture is being used as a base, which is being enhanced to develop robustness against deepfakes through the integration of GAN-based feature alignment, a weighted generalization loss function, and an advanced Gaussian process that can adapt to different types of normal media. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, an extensive set of experiments are being conducted using a massive self-created training dataset, which combines multiple existing and newly created datasets, as well as a vast amount of heterogeneous media. The experimental results show that infoGAN, which uses the adaptive generalization process, significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art deepfakes created from limited normal media detectors and serves as a robust baseline for both deepfakes generation and detection.

The study of sub-Neptune-sized exoplanets with atmospheric masses around 50-200 Earth masses, and consequently hydrogen-dominated atmospheres, presents a challenge in understanding their ocean depths due to mass uncertainties. To address this issue, a theoretical model of temperate sub-Neptune atmospheres with masses between 50 and 100 exoplanet masses, consisting of hydrogen-dominated atmospheres and water-rich interiors, is developed. These planets undergo chemical reactions with their atmospheres, which affect their mass and size, and thus their radius and density are a function of the initial water-to-hydrogen mass ratio of their interiors. As a result, their ocean depths are not directly related to their initial water content, but rather determined by their hydrogen-dominated atmospheres that shield the interiors, and thus their density and radius are closely related to their initial hydrogen content. To understand their interior composition, the radius and density of these exoplanets, which are related to their initial hydrogen content, are used to calculate their water content in the interior, and thus their radius and density can be used to infer their interior composition, and thus their radius and density can be used to infer their interior composition, and thus their radius and density can be used to infer their interior composition, and thus their radius and density can be used to infer their interior composition, and thus their radius and density can be used to infer their interior composition, and thus their radius and density can be used to infer

Previous studies on teaching a spiking neural network to learn basic sequences of numbers and letters have shown that increasing the number of learning parameters in the model allows it to accurately predict the next element in a sequence, but this large number of learning parameters is impractical for real-world applications where there is a limited amount of data available. In contrast, in typical biological systems, there is often very little data available and the goal is to learn from unexpected input changes, rather than training with controlled data. Therefore, in this research, we aim to explore how a spiking neural network can be trained to learn basic sequences of letters with a limited number of learning parameters in a way that is closer to how biological systems learn. Our results show that adjusting a key parameter in the network's architecture can allow the network to learn features that help it predict the next element in a sequence of letters, without requiring a large number of learning parameters. Additionally, we find that using controlled training can sometimes cause the network to learn features that are not robust, and that teaching the network to learn features that are based on changes in input can make it more similar to how biological systems learn.

This document serves as the official report of the Out-of-Category Research Challenge, convened under the NLP Findings of the 2021 EMNLP conference. It provides a detailed description of the NLC's objective, the NLC's task specifications, nomenclature, nLC's setup, evaluation metrics, participating teams, submission requirements, and the NLC's top-ranking team.

This study presents a novel approach combining an adaptive generalized polynomial chaos expansion with an optimal test-based a posteriori error assessment for approximating functions within a specific domain that includes random factors. This approach is verified under the assumption that the function can be represented by a series of Hermite polynomials and is posteriorly verified using an optimal test based on the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. This study draws inspiration from a prior approach, but differs in that the corresponding integral is not a probability but a specific value within a defined domain. This method enables the assessment of the efficiency of GC expansions, both in terms of their ability to capture a function and the optimality of their basis. This approach is demonstrated through three examples involving the smooth function y = (1 + x^2)^-1 on a continuous d-dimensional domain and two functions containing the random factor ξ with d = 1 and singularities on distinct domains.

This research develops a novel algorithm combining adaptive sequential detection techniques with change identification methods to resolve the non-deterministic issue of identifying and isolating the first artificial change in a stochastic system with limited observability. The algorithm employs a time-sliding window technique and can operate effectively even when multiple changes occur, as it prioritizes the earliest detected alteration. A theoretical analysis confirms that the algorithm accurately identifies and isolates alterations within specified time frames with high confidence. Additionally, the research enhances the algorithm's speed and reduces its memory usage through optimization techniques such as adaptive thresholding and early termination strategies. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of the enhanced algorithm.

A key challenge in NLP cost-effectiveness is achieving accurate label data at a low cost. Our solution involves a two-step process to enhance model performance on visually complex documents while significantly reducing labeling expenses. First, we utilize a data augmentation technique that generates enhanced samples from limited, high-quality labeled data, increasing both quantity and diversity. Our technique leverages visual features, allowing for the creation of documents that better represent visually rich formats like tables, better allowing models to accurately recognize such structures. Second, we employ a model alignment technique to adapt a large, pre-trained vision-language model to produce label data on unlabeled, quantity-enhanced documents. This aligned model can then replace a computationally expensive teacher model, reducing the burden on labeling annotators. Our approach, called Visually Guided Data Augmentation (ViGDA), has been tested on the IE task and demonstrates improved performance over state-of-the-art models, specifically on the ICDAR2017 dataset, with a reduction in labeling costs by up to threefold.

The EuS/InAs interface is gaining attention for its potential to exhibit large magnetic semiconductor properties and quantum spin Hall effect in magnetic semiconductors. Understanding the electronic structure of the EuS/InAs interface is vital to explaining the observation of edge states in this system. The present study employs an in-depth ab-initio study to investigate the electronic structure of two different configurations of this interface, known as the Z configuration and the X configuration. The study utilizes a Z configuration model with the magnetic EuS attached to the non-magnetic InAs via the S atom and a X configuration model with the magnetic EuS attached to the InAs via the In atom. The two models exhibit distinct electronic structures, with the non-magnetic In atom contributing to gap states in the X configuration model that may destroy the edge states. However, the model with the magnetic Eu atom shows no such gap states. The study suggests that the X configuration model is not the one responsible for the edge states observed experimentally and that further studies are needed to understand the mechanism behind this phenomenon.

A detailed classification system for Borel sets in a topological space with countable basis has been established by providing precise definitions of Wadge reduction and a novel concept of initial segment of a Wadge degree, which proves that it captures the entire Wadge structure. Based on these foundations, we have also developed algorithms that determine Wadge reducibility and Wadge classes efficiently, using only the countable basis as input.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance in a wide range of applications, but their large size often poses challenges for deployment in resource-constrained environments. Pruning techniques have been developed to optimize DNN models, reducing their size and operational complexity. However, previous approaches have primarily focused on reducing the number of multiplications, overlooking the impact on other operations such as additions, memory access, and data transfers. This paper introduces ClickTrain, a novel approach that enables efficient and precise DNN training through fine-grained architecture optimization. ClickTrain preserves the structure of the original training algorithm while pruning the model, using a hierarchy of operations hierarchy graphs to identify redundant operations and generate an optimal high-performance predictor. The effectiveness of ClickTrain is demonstrated on ResNet-50, achieving up to a 2.42x speed speedup and a 2.01x model size reduction, resulting in a 4.43x improvement in overall efficiency compared to existing methods.

It's known that the modality in the Lambek Calculus with Modal Operators can be
replaced by a combination of the exponentials in the Affiliated Lambek Calculus.
We establish that, in terms of semantic meaning, strong semantic soundness with
respect to non-distributive semilattices holds for the replaced calculus. This is
the most stringent form of soundness established thus far in the literature.

The merging of neutron stars with black holes produces distinctive gravitational waves, carrying invaluable information about the events themselves and the underlying astrophysical processes. Although detecting such events is highly challenging due to their low signals, new technologies and techniques have opened up a new window into space by detecting GW190814, the first neutron star black hole merger. A more effective approach to detecting these events involves artificial intelligence, where deep neural networks have been shown to outperform traditional methods in classifying binary black hole signals. In this study, we have pioneered the use of a deep neural network for identifying and categoring neutron star black hole signals, which has been further validated by comparing our results with those of a state-of-the-art Bayesian tool, Dynamic Nested Sampling. Notably, we have found that even a single neural unit can achieve a 90% accuracy in distinguishing neutron star black hole signals from black hole black hole signals, and we have achieved a 95% accuracy in classifying masses for signals with a信噪比 greater than 15. Furthermore, we have found that even with a lower信噪比 of 10, our method can still correctly classify 80% of the data. A comprehensive study of exoplanet TOI-5542 has been conducted using data from the TESS mission and spectroscopic observations from both the HARPS and HARPS-N instruments.  TOI-5542 is a relatively old and low-metallicity star with a mass of approximately 0.9 times that of the sun and a metallicity of -1.0 times that of the sun.  TOI-5542 b, an exoplanet with a period of 91.55 days, has a radius of about 1.25 times that of the earth, a mass of about 0.29 times the mass of the Jupiter gas giant and a temperature of about 350 K.  TOI-5542 is located 142.5 light years from the earth and has a temperature of about 5017 K.
