Three-body semileptonic tau decets, particularly those involving mildly hadronic final states, can provide precise tests of fundamental QCD and weak interactions.  To predict hadronic decay outcomes accurately, a comprehensive theoretical framework, including hadronic current matrix elements and form factors, is needed for multi-particle systems.  Given the complexity of these mathematical components for three-body systems, this work offers a thorough examination of all three-body hadronic currents and the associated form factors in mildly hadronic $\tau$ decays.  Additionally, a proposed method to calculate the three-body hadronic weak currents and the associated form factors in terms of single-particle form factors is presented within the context of QCD, including Hadron Model and SU(3) Flavor symmetry.  Furthermore, this work predicts the hadronic decay rates for specific multi-particle channels resulting from $\tau$ lepton decets, including hadronic currents and the associated form factors.  Hadron model calculations indicate that hadronic decay widths involving the proton, neutron, and various mesons are within experimentally accessible ranges.  These predictions can guide upcoming precision studies in multi-particle hadronic $\tau$ decets, including hadronic currents and the associated form factors.

Parametrizing the Tversky similarity for two sets, $A$ and $B$, yields a distance that is bounded by the smaller cardinality of the sets, unlike the Jaccard distance, which is normalized by the cardinality of their symmetric difference. In contrast, the normalized information distance is parameterized by two variables and is bounded by the ratio $k/\ell$, where $\ell$ represents the length of sequences and $k$ is a constant. We propose a parameterization of the Tversky distance, controlled by $\alpha$ and $\beta$, that encompasses the Jaccard distance as well as a newly identified metric. This new metric is based on a formula first introduced by Li and Vitanyi in their study of the universal probability approach to information theory.

To generate high-quality motion-deblurred images from severely blurred inputs, we must first generate plausible high-quality images to guide the de-blurring process. Direct motion de-blurring often results in poor quality due to the loss of structural details in the resulting image. To overcome this problem, we propose motion de-blurring by pseudo-blur synthesis (PBS), which generates high-quality low-resolution images by adapting a versatile model to utilize the motion de-blurring signal in the blurred image. PBS produces synthesized images with sharper details and greater clarity that effectively remove motion blur. A subsequent super-resolution step then yields final images at the original resolution. Our proposed method achieves superior results on a variety of publicly available DMB datasets, particularly severe motion de-blurring (SMDB) datasets. To further aid research in this area, we have developed a new, challenging DMB dataset, called SHRM, which features a large collection of severely blurred human and scene images with corresponding high-resolution images, annotations, and a novel set of algorithms. To utilize PBS effectively, we propose integrating it with a motion de-blurring network that predicts whether a given blurred image is realistic or not, thereby maximizing the use of this signal in the PBS process.

Neuromorphic hardware, programmed to mimic the brain, offers promising solutions for complex artificial intelligence and machine learning tasks, given the brain's innate efficiency with such problems. To fully tap into biological computing's potential, however, novel materials and new programming methods are required, especially if future systems are to be built at the atomic and molecular scale. Our research demonstrates a novel approach to algorithmic programming using a classic chemical reaction, commonly employed in DNA computing, to emulate the dynamic properties of a single neuron. By leveraging the fundamental concepts of chemistry, we've created a universal framework to run any algorithmic task within a single test tube, thus paving the way for the development of robust, fault-tolerant, and scalable atomic and molecular neuromorphic systems.

This article offers a refined, more inclusive version of the ultrapower theorem in the field of ordered set theory, directly addressing and proving a statement that was previously described as Open Problem 5.14 in the book "Order Theory, Ultrafilters, and Categories" published in 1977 by North-Holland Publishing.

We introduce 'Dataset Particular Profiling', a concept that encompasses task- and dataset-specific characteristics of neural network optimization under various gradient update rules. This Profiling involves profiling these characteristics by examining neural network optimization landscapes on various benchmark neural network problems. Notably, we identify four distinct neural network characteristics on the CIFAR-10 image classification task using SGD, Adam, and Nadam optimizers, and our analysis of the CIFAR-10 task reveals that 'easy-to-train' datasets are hyperinitialized near critical points of the neural network, whereas 'hard-to-train' datasets are hyperinitialized near a local minimum of the objective function. Furthermore, we validate that 'Dataset Particular Profiling' is valuable, and its insights can enhance neural network optimization performance. This profiling not only offers a unifying framework for reconciling conflicting findings but also provides a clear pathway for resolving such discrepancies. This paper serves as a pioneering example of 'Dataset Particular Profiling', and we anticipate that profiling will become a standard tool in neural network research and development.

A potential enhancement to Hadwiger's conjecture for a specific graph G is that its odd cycles are all edge-disjoint when properly colored with five colors. This idea, a potential reinforcement of the conjecture, is being studied to confirm if it holds as a valid theory. Furthermore, another potential reinforcement for the conjecture suggests a specific coloring for the graph's vertices where each set of odd-cycle-colored vertices uses at most four colors. This theory is also being considered as a potential reinforcement of the conjecture. Both of these ideas have significant implications in understanding and visualizing the proper vertex coloring of a specific graph. We have found that these two theories are closely related and consistent with each other.

This research introduces an innovative approach, a correntropy-based regularized least-squares criterion, for efficiently reconstructing smooth graph signals under various noise conditions. Building on this approach, we developed an adaptive graph signal reconstruction method that enhances performance, particularly in non-Gaussian noise scenarios. The proposed method utilizes adaptive non-linear correlation measures and kernel width adjustment to optimize signal reconstruction. The resulting algorithm, BGA-RLGSR, exhibits improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing graph signal reconstruction techniques. The efficiency of the proposed method is efficiently maintained through the development of an efficient iterative re-weighted minimization optimization algorithm that avoids complex kernel width maximization problems. The effectiveness of the BGA-RLGSR approach is demonstrated through successful graph signal reconstruction in various scenarios, showcasing its improved performance and adaptability.

An advanced atom interferometer based on spinor atoms has the potential to produce highly entangled states, but current generation methods are limited by technical noises, specifically magnetic field noises and state detection fidelities below the optimal level of $\sqrt{N}$-limited sensitivity. Our study develops new techniques to create quantum interferometry using entangled spinor states through spin-exchange interactions, utilizing an isotopically pure $^{87}$Rb and detecting the interferometric phase with high-precision thermometry based on the Rabi width, enabling optimal extraction of the phase from noisy measurements and achieving $\sqrt{N}$-limited sensitivity even when the fidelity is lower than expected and the noise is present. These techniques can be universally applied to other spinor atoms as well as Rb and Cs with similar properties.

This research offers accurate estimates for the initial eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic problem with a nonlinear boundary condition. The specific type of estimates depends on the form of the boundary and a parameter, with two distinct cases identified. In the first case, when the boundary can be approximated by a plane at a certain scale, estimates are provided that are symmetric around the minimum first eigenvalue for a related linear problem with a constant boundary condition. In the second case, when a non-zero mean curvature is considered, estimates are provided with a specific dependence on boundary curvature and the boundary's geometric properties. The research builds upon a previously developed change of variable technique and utilizes results from other studies to derive these estimates.

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) serve a comparable purpose to traditional Convolutional Neural Networks, yet they operate on graph-based data instead of grid-based information. This introduces distinct challenges in designing and interpreting filters within GCNNs in relation to the underlying graph structure. This study introduces an intuitive understanding of GCNNs as a matched filtering process, facilitating design and analysis of the network's higher layers. Furthermore, this study provides guidelines for the selection of lower layer filters within GCNNs and explores how this choice impacts the matched filtering process at subsequent layers. The findings illustrate that appropriately selecting filters in GCNNs can lead to improvements in performance, structure, and training speed.

Parsing sentences with limited sentence labels has long been a major challenge in NLP.
Self-training techniques that enhance models using manually labeled data and generated labels have emerged as a promising solution for improving unsupervised parsers.
Most self-training methods rely on simple models or past decision-making processes to filter out inaccurate model decisions, but these techniques often fail to consider the context of sentences or the relationship between model decisions, leading to poor self-training performance in low-resource settings.
This paper presents a novel self-training method called Deep Contextualized Self-learning (DCS), which employs advanced neural models to identify and correct context-dependent model errors in sentences.
A self-learning process that adjusts sentence-level and word-level model biases based on the interaction between model decisions and human data is implemented in DCS.
Experimental results on Konkor 2020 and English datasets show DCS significantly outperforms existing self-training techniques in low-resource dependencies parsing, particularly on English datasets, achieving an average lead of 2.14 F1 points in Konkor 2020 and 1.92 F1 points on English datasets.

The $B\to D\ell\nu_\ell$ weak transition form factors have been studied over a broad momentum transfer range ($q^2$) using the self-consistent light-front quark model. The resulting form factors were compared to other theoretical models and experiments, with the aim of identifying the transition's pole mass and discussing how it influences the form factors. The findings suggest that our model's calculated pole mass is in good agreement with that determined from the BESIII experiment, while showing some discrepancy with form factors analyzed by LHCb and Belle experiments. Moreover, our theory's predictions for certain $Form Factor/ M_B+M_D$ ratios may be able to help clarify some of the LHCB's anomalies.

The AdS/Conformal Field Theory correspondence has led to a significant understanding of the relationship between gravitational theories of the form $N=2$ super Yang-Mills theory, described by quiver diagrams, and AdS branes. These brues are often characterized by Non-Riemannian properties and Non-Holonomic constraints, which are associated with the development of Non-Hamiltonian systems. The dynamics of these systems are governed by both Non-Symplectic and Non-Symmetrizable properties, which are explored in the Branes and Non-Reversible Symmetries paper. A detailed connection is established between the structures of quiver diagrams and Non-Symmetrizable forms, which describe the dynamics of adS brues. Our research shows that the type of diagram, either loop or tree, has a substantial impact on the existence of Non-Symmetrizable forms in diagrams of loop type whereas the existence of generalized forms in tree type diagrams results in the generalized Semi-Negative Curvature property in AdS. The existence of this property leads to the dissipation of energy in the $N=2$ super Yang-Mills theory, which is a significant finding as it demonstrates that energy can only be dissipated and not conserved.

The choiceless Polynomial time (PTime) class of problems is defined by its reliance on a finite set and a finite number of relations over that set, allowing a uniform evaluation of problems across different sets and sizes. Its relationship with PTime on fixed structures has been the subject of ongoing study, with recent research establishing a connection to symmetric circuits, which are circuits incapable of differentiating between equivalent elements. The current paper establishes a link between PTime and symmetric circuits for a specific class of digraphs introduced by Cai, Fu\"urer, and Immerman, and shows the feasibility of evaluating path and reachability using such circuits within this particular class.

Insulating behavior has been observed in pyrochlore iridates A2Ir2O7 (where x = 0), attributed to the formation of Mott-Hubbard bands. To assess the insulator-to-metal transition (IMT) upon substituting Eu with Bi, we analyzed the x = 0.1 sample using HAXPES, with a photon energy of 705 eV that can bypass surface effects. The HAXPES results with a short mean free path revealed occupied 5d states in contrast to the expected insulating behavior, suggesting 5d band conduction. Additionally, our measurements of core-level shifts and lattice expansion indicate increased bi-valency of the Eu site, supporting 5d conduction as the cause of the IMT.

This abstract discusses the concept of the core of a set-valued mapping and its efficient selection algorithms for Lipschitz continuous functions. It then applies these ideas to a specific type of set-valued mapping that maps into a complex vector space and has its image contained within an affine subspace of lower dimension. Under certain conditions, including being Lipschitz continuous and having compact range, such a mapping admits a Lipschitz continuous selection if and only if its projection onto a complementary subspace also admits a Lipschitz continuous selection. Furthermore, it shows that such a mapping always has a continuous selection, especially when its image is contained within a hyperplane.

This paper is driven by a distinct type of likelihood, termed nontransitive likelihood, which defies the conventional transitive likelihood that "A is more likely than B" implies "B is less likely than A." The study of nontransitive likelihood is particularly advantageous in the field of social choice theory due to its ability to formalize cyclic preferences. By establishing a systematic method to derive a cyclic likelihood from a cyclic preference order, the text contributes a cyclic likelihood axiomatization rooted in likelihood's fundamental properties. Additionally, the characterization of the cyclic likelihood is accompanied by an explanation of when a strict preference can be considered a cyclic likelihood.

Certain applications can be dramatically optimized through the strategic use of hardware features via software run-time setups, yet this process often requires in-depth hardware knowledge and is otherwise too complex to compile statically. To address this challenge, this research explored whether a region of setup space can be segmented and moved to compile-time, enabling the benefits of static setup region compilation (SSSRC). Our findings indicate that this is feasible for specific region types, particularly those with dynamic behavior confined to a specific hardware feature subset. Consequently, we developed two novel techniques for identifying such regions, particularly those that adhere to the Little Endian Normal Form (LERNF). Our experiments, conducted on three real-world hardware specialization setups such as network interfaces and memory managers, demonstrated that our methods successfully identified a substantial percentage of setup regions and resulted in a significant increase in the number of compile-time specializations after applying our techniques. Moreover, the use of hardware features at compile-time yielded notable performance improvements, with network managers exhibiting a 1.7x to 4.2x increase in throughput following SSSRR.

Researchers have been primarily focused on using electron displacement from interactions with nuclei in direct dark matter detectors, but in the range of $0.1-10$ MeV, the movement of the nucleus itself moves more than the electron, which could be useful for detecting lighter dark matter particles. A new concept for using this increased motion to detect sub-GeV dark matter particles involves using a simple relationship between the energy an atom gains and how much it moves. By combining this relationship with accurate quantum calculations of how atoms and nuclei store energy, it becomes possible to use calibration data from known particle interactions, like neutron and alpha decay, to set limits on the interaction of dark matter particles and establish detection strategies for future experiments.

This investigation focuses on an elegant modification of the Jaynes-Cummings model, where a two-level atom interacts with a quantum field and an additional two-level atom acts as a mirror, without exchanging levels with the field. The key difference from the original JC model is the inversion of the atom-field interaction term from a raising to a lowering operator. Our study explores the dynamics of electron populations and entanglement generated through atom-atom and atom-field interactions. The presence of the inverted interaction intensifies entanglement and its dependence on the initial state is an important aspect. Additionally, when the initial state of the field is a single-sided traveling wave created by a beam splitter, our analysis indicates that the system can undergo periodic energy transfer between the atom and the field in accordance with the Rabi oscillation principle. Notably, an initial photonic state of the field has the potential to generate strong entanglement among atom and field components even in the presence of an inverted interaction, and under specific conditions, near-permanent entanglement can be achieved.

Nonlinear time series analysis is employed to quantify the complexity of physiological systems. One of its key measures, nonstationary periodicity, is essential for evaluating ECG signals and diagnosing cardiovascular conditions. This approach involves calculating inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from R-R peaks in ECG signals using a novel technique called tangential time delay embedding. While effective, this method often introduces noise that limits its practical application. To address this issue, we have developed a data-driven approach to mitigate noise by embedding IBIs within a high-dimensional space using a tangent hyperplane. This approach facilitates the accurate calculation of IBIs by leveraging a pre-trained multimodal transformer model, particularly the Tiramisu model. Our approach involves three main steps: first, we embed the ECG signal into a high-dimensional space similar to the latent space of the Tiramisu model; second, we construct a tangent hyperplane to the embedded signal at each heartbeat; third, we calculate IBIs based on the distance between these tangent structures. This approach allows us to accurately estimate IBIs and achieve a low root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0406 on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia database.

We explore active matter by analyzing work fluctuations in the Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle model under various protocols, applying the generalized second law of thermodynamics. The model generates time series data for active particles and we use these to calculate work variation, a key concept in understanding active thermodynamics. Our calculations are performed using the full discrete data and an smoothed version, which approximates instantaneous force and displacement. The two approaches yield the same theoretical work variation and align well with the active thermodynamic identity, particularly with the continuous data method. The calculation of heat remains theoretically ambiguous in active thermodynamics, so instead of using an existing definition, we decompose the excess work variation into accessible and inaccessibile components and analyze their ratios. Our results show that the inaccessibile work dominates the excess work and is itself divided into two parts, with the 'entropic' component being more significant than the 'active' component, which is an unexpected finding.

Gesture communication is a natural form of nonverbal communication that is frequently used in everyday life and is essential for effective human-human interaction. To unlock the full potential of this ubiquitous skill, researchers in both computer vision and speech processing fields have incorporated Unspoken Gesture Recognition (UGR) into their domains, although comprehensive studies on this aspect are still relatively scarce compared to speech and facial expression analysis. To establish cutting-edge benchmarks for UGR, we present HUMBI, a large-scale multiview dataset consisting of 9 distinct view combinations and comprising approximately 10,000 annotated gesture sequences representing 127 different gesture classes performed by 58 annotation experts. To evaluate the challenges and foster innovation in robust UGR models, we conduct the first-ever UGR multiview benchmark challenge utilizing the HUMBI dataset. The resulting benchmark outcomes reveal the current state-of-the-art performance levels and pinpoint areas for further improvement, ultimately driving further advancements in this field of UGR. The HUMBI dataset, benchmark code, and related materials are freely available to the research community.

Model-agnostic neural task representations can be combined with transfer learning to achieve cross-lingual translation without the need for task-specific models, as exemplified by using knowledge from multiple languages to train a unified model for natural language tasks. This was demonstrated by achieving a baseline cross-lingual translation between zero and non-related languages with competitive results to existing in-language models, by employing transfer learning and addressing challenges with neural task guidance and data scarcity. Future research in this area is promising and has the potential to surpass current language model abilities.

A cutting-edge two-stage method, known as Video Special Enhanced Super-Resolution (BasicVSR), has gained significant traction in improving video enhancement, leveraging long-term connections. However, its initial stage's video enhancement module still lags behind single-image enhanced super-resolution in quality. Our research addresses this limitation by proposing an upgraded multi-frame system, which is simpler yet more effective than its predecessor. We made key modifications to the alignment and enhancement processes, including incorporating residual high-frequency information and a detailed motion compensation mechanism that leverages frame relationships to accurately restore lost visual data. Experimental evaluations validate the superiority of our design in advanced video enhancement, outperforming 24 related methods in quantitative and qualitative metrics. Our code is publicly available at the following link: https://github.com/j-s-v/BasicVSRPlusPlus.

In order to improve reinforcement learning agents' sample efficiency, researchers have developed multi-task learning. However, these agents often encounter issues learning multiple tasks simultaneously due to parameter sharing, which can result in performance degradation. To overcome this, our study investigates the impact of moduleization on architecture, finding that distinct modules for each task can substantially reduce model overlap and prevent performance decline. We demonstrate this through experimental results in both simple and complex multi-task environments.

Over their operating cycle, heat engines exchange heat with thermal reservoirs of varying temperatures through a controllable working substance.  Studies have used specific forms of the engine's power and efficiency to derive optimal control strategies, but these models often fail to capture the full range of possible engine performance.  To address this gap, we model thermal engines as stochastic control systems and derive the fundamental thermodynamic limits that can be achieved through any control strategy.  The identified limits can be represented as a closed mathematical object, or 'face-set', that completely encloses the achievable states of power and heat flow.  By applying an information-theoretic framework, we show that any desired protocol can be approximated by a protocol that imposes a constant feedback information rate and a time-independent average power and efficiency under the engine's operating conditions.

To examine the capacity of power systems in the United States to withstand and operate during hurricane-induced storm surges, we employed spatial analysis and a custom-developed geospatial software. This approach enables a granular, unit-by-unit assessment of specific power system components affected by storm surges, providing system operators with vital insights for making informed and timely decisions. Moreover, our analysis contributes to the broader goal of enhancing power system resilience by identifying vulnerable components and facilitating long-term operational and planning-based improvements.

This study formulates and proves the Three Balls Conjecture for the eigenfunctions of a Dirac operator within a Clifford algebra framework, extending existing three-ball inequalities to non-Abelian Lie groups with a sub-Laplace operator.

We're analyzing countable Markov partitions of countably piecewise linear automorphisms on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with a finite number of branches, a type of dynamic system introduced by Kloudas in 2008. These systems include invariant Cantor set attractors with a positive measure basin of attraction, often exhibiting non-wandering points outside the attractor's influence. Focusing on a specific type of map with two countable sets of slopes, we derive a countable transition matrix under certain conditions, enabling the development of a unique invariant measure with maximal entropy through an associated random process. This maximal entropy measure is shown to be supported solely by the attractor under specific conditions on the control parameter values. Furthermore, we find that varying these parameters causes the unique invariant measure to gain the influence of points located outside the attractor, illustrating a specific mechanism for the breakdown of entropy accessibility, for which we provide a new dynamic explanation.

Our focus is on expanded scalar sectors, specifically in situations where a single scalar is produced at high-energy colliders through the force of a new, short-range interaction. This occurs at the fundamental level as $\frac{1}{\Lambda^2}$ contact terms, which can arise from new physics at the gap level of $\Lambda$. Our research examines the relationship between the rate of producing these scalars and their coupling to other fundamental fermions, such as SM Higgs or top quark, in the standard model. This means that if we don't detect any evidence of new physics at the gap level of $\Lambda$ in the scalar's decay channels, our data can be used to set a lower bound on the gap level of $\Lambda$ by potentially exceeding existing constraints from indirect methods. The most significant findings are observed in the situation where a new scalar particle is produced in association with a standard model and then decays into invisible particles or pairs of new fermions, such as sterile neutrinos or dark matter. The potential for detecting these scenarios at the LC or future $e^+e^-$ and $e^+e^-$ colliders is significant, with the new scalar having a mass of up to a few hundred GeV and the gap level of $\Lambda$ potentially being as low as a few TeV.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), which uses an expanded convolution neural network structure to efficiently learn pitch-dependent patterns in speech signals. By incorporating a complex quasi-periodic model into the expanded convolution layer, QPNet can automatically adjust its filter kernels based on the signal's pitch, and it outperforms a standard WaveNet model in speech synthesis while being more computationally efficient. Moreover, QPNet's design enables seamless integration with other generative models, such as QPNet-GAN and QPNet-RRM, which demonstrate superior performance in speech synthesis by using a flow-based model and a top-down autoregressive mixture model, respectively. Evaluations reveal that speech synthesized by these models surpasses the QPNet model in the Mean Opinion Score for speech quality. All implemented models have been made available on the GitHub repository for the FastSpeech project.

Current recommender systems still fall short in addressing the complex user preferences needed for personalized recommendations in various real-world contexts. To tackle this, we propose a novel user-based biclustering recommendation framework, building upon existing biclustering techniques and collaborative filtering theory. The framework uses biclusters to capture local user preference patterns, enhancing captured utility and URM density while mitigating the effects of preference subjectivity via the use of normalized score data in BICMAT. We derive the BICMAT algorithm for efficient bicluster identification and develop a novel user-specific bicluster-based recommendation technique that outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score. The proposed approach, with its conceptual clarity and BICMAT effectiveness, provides a sound basis for reliable and versatile personalized recommendations.

To determine how solar magnetic activity affects the precision of exoplanet velocity measurements, we analyzed two years of solar observations from the HARPS-N solar mode. By comparing velocities of disk-integrated solar planets with activity indicators, we discovered that H$\alpha$ central intensity and $g$-factor are most influenced by magnetic activity. However, these indices are susceptible to photospheric phase variations. Our novel activity indicators, magnetically weighted activity indicators (MWIs), show less variation with the solar phase and magnetic activity has a relatively uniform effect across planets. Additionally, MWI8 exhibits a notable positive correlation with all planets, and its impact on velocity measurements is within acceptable limits for planets with orbit periods less than 15 days, and its influence remains below the 1 m/s threshold for planets with orbit periods less than 30 days.

Our suggestion for identifying the Majorana peak involves setting up a tunnel junction with a topological superconductor by creating a tunnel barrier with an ohmic component. This setup results in the Majorana peak standing out as it remains stable and unaffected in contrast to other peaks under adjustments to the tunnel barrier's capacitance and resistance. The tunnel barrier is modeled after an RC circuit, leading to two types of tunneling spectroscopy: DC measurements akin to standard STM experiments and time-resolved measurements following light exposure as in PHSTM. Both methods of analyzing these spectra can confirm the presence of Majorana modes.

The presence of bi-categorical limits allows for the reconstruction of a bi-categorical structure, which in turn enables the definition of shadows as certain bi-categorical limits. Specifically, shadow limits and diagonal limits are two types of bi-categorical limits that generalize corresponding concepts from single-categorical and bisected categories, respectively. Our work demonstrates that a category with shadow limits and a category diagonal can uniquely determine bi-categorical limits, showing that any category with these structures and satisfying specific conditions is equivalent to the bi-categorical limit definition. Furthermore, we show that any functor satisfying the expectations for shadow diagonal functors and functoriality preserves shadow limits. This leads to an established connection between functors preserving both structures and shadow functors between bi-categorical categories.

We've developed a straightforward method to learn a style between image pairs, achieving a seamless transformation between any image in the style of another. This technique employs a straightforward setup of just two images for both the teacher and student. We've applied this style distillation technique to the task of hue shifting and successfully obtained style-learned hue shifting networks that produce high-quality results with minimal computational resources (only 0.000002 GPU hours). Our results show that the learned style mapping achieves a lower L1 loss (0.000002) compared to other methods, such as VIFU (0.00002) and CycleColor (0.00004), and also demonstrates better image preservation as measured by the VIF metric (0.8622 vs. 0.8032 and 0.8314). We've further demonstrated the versatility of our technique by applying it to global hue shifting as well as colorization.

This technical report outlines the methodology and results from the AQTC challenge of the LOVEU competition, which aimed to evaluate water damage localization capabilities in DMV documents using diverse visual presentations. Twenty-one teams participated in the challenge, submitting entries to both the public leaderboards, where data was accessible, and the private leaderboards, which required the development of proprietary models. Various approaches were explored by participants, including the utilization of pre-trained convolutional neural networks, transformation of images into a consistent format, and the application of encoder-decoder architectures for the prediction of damage regions. Our proposed method involved the generation of a grid-based matrix that represented the probability of water damage in each individual grid, which was then compared against the ground truth to calculate the intersection over union (IoU) and determine the final prediction.

This field experiment investigates the atmospheric turbulence and settling dynamics of snow particles in a flat, snow-covered terrain. The study aims to validate the concept of selective sweeping, which suggests that atmospheric turbulence can filter and remove larger snow particles more effectively than smaller ones. This phenomenon potentially offers an explanation for the reversed gravitational settling behavior observed in lab and field studies, where the concentration of snow particles decreases with height regardless of particle size. To gather data, the study utilized selective radar and laser particle counters to measure the size-dependent variability in snow particle concentrations at 1 to 5 cm heights, along with measurements of atmospheric turbulence and surface roughness effects. The study found that at low turbulence levels, the concentration of 1 cm snow particles decreased more rapidly with height than 0.5 cm particles, indicating a roughness effect of less than 1 cm. However, when turbulence exceeded 0.25 m/s, the larger particles showed a lower concentration at equal heights, indicating they were being "swept up" into the atmosphere at higher rates than smaller particles. The observed field results were found to be consistent with a theoretical model that suggests that selective sweeping becomes dominant when turbulence exceeds a critical threshold that depends on particle Reynolds number and radii.

This paper explores a novel approach to autonomous robot navigation using Deep Active Learning prediction (DAL), a technique that selects key training samples for model improvement. Our method integrates DAL with a deep convolutional neural network for object recognition and a set of predefined geometric shapes for orientation on a planar surface. By training the model with only selected samples, we achieve efficient object detection and orientation estimation. Our approach was tested on a physical robot platform within a laboratory setting, and findings indicate that DAL can enhance robotic navigation performance while reducing training time.

At the CERN Touch-PoC experiment, sparsely distributed detectors capture high-energy particle interactions, producing a three-dimensional sparse dataset in the meter range. A typical dataset contains around 100,000 data points per event, resulting in a vast amount of data that will continue to grow with an upcoming upgrade to BICHON. Utilizing a Convolutional AutoEncoder, this research demonstrates that it's possible to efficiently compress 3D sparse data without distorting the underlying data patterns, thereby maintaining crucial particle information. By training the Convolutional AutoEncoder on the entire dataset, it's shown that a vast amount of data can be preprocessed and compressed in a sparse format, with the encoded data then used to train a classification model, namely a Convolutional Neural Network. As a result, the classification model achieves comparable performance to a classification model trained on the full dataset, while training time is significantly reduced due to the smaller, compressed data.

Utilizing the Finzi gravity theory that accounts for information theoretical interactions, we assess the properties of galactic clusters from the statistical perspective. The proposed Finzi gravity model corresponds to a group of non-extensive statistical systems characterized by an unusual additive composition rule for the dimension of the underlying phase space. We derive key statistical parameters, including energy, particle number, and density, as well as the galactic cluster size distribution, when considering non-interacting and interacting galactic clusters under the Finzi gravity theory by applying Combes, Simons, and Holmwood potentials respectively. The outcomes indicate significant parallels between the theoretical predictions and observed galactic cluster data, particularly the frequency distribution of clusters and their density profiles.

A geometric hypergraph can be defined by associating each edge with a point set in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where the edges are referred to as structured. These convex hypergraphs, where the edges are defined by convex shapes such as balls, halfspaces, or convex polygons, are a subset of general hypergraphs and thus retain properties, such as saturation. This paper saturates convex geometric hypergraphs, $\textrm{sat}(\textrm{cx})$, using a refined version of Graham's method, where it is proven that $F_2^k$ can determine the minimum number of vertices, $n$, at which the hypergraph contains either a hypergraph of Graham or its complement, $\overline{G}(n,k)$. To study the structure of compound nuclei formed in alpha-inclusive reactions, 
X-ray probability distributions have been analyzed in the case of 51V + 6Li collisions 
at an energy of 40 MeV/nucleon using high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy. 
This was performed in conjunction with time-of-flight measurements of 6Li and recoil 
particles, which were recorded with the 4$\pi$ detector GRETINA. 
Two distinct gamma-ray bands have been identified and their spin-parity values 
determined via statistical analysis of the X-ray spectra. Furthermore, the two 
observed bands support the validity of the impulsive model for alpha-inclusive 
reactions in the fast regime and allow us to directly compare theoretical and 
experimental cross-sections for specific alpha-inclusive channels.

This research focuses on developing a lamprey-inspired robotic head capable of navigating through narrow and vertical confined spaces. A key aspect of this navigation involves a motile snout, controlled by pacemaker neurons, which detects and grasps surfaces through sensory feedback. We present a two-layer neural network model, similar to the pacemaker system found in the Pacific Lamprey (Ichthyomyons spawnatus), to address the design of a side-climbing mechanism for a robotic head. The open-loop neural network model successfully generates complex wave patterns, including stationary, moving, and reverse tri-chromatic waves, which are also seen in the Pacific Lamprey. A closed-loop system incorporating neural networks for pattern extraction and regression accurately replicates the external sensory patterns, with high precision and robustness. High fidelity of the neural network model, with a low regression error of 0.0066, results in stable and smooth external sensory patterns, with a low standard deviation of 0.0063. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of our neural network model in controlling a lamprey-inspired robotic head to climb the side of a cylindrical surface, with successful simulations of external sensory patterns matching the expected pacemaker neuron output.

This study presents a theoretical framework based on the Fokker-Planck framework to optimize treatments in diseases like colon cancer, with a focus on personalized therapy through the analysis of patient immune system behavior modeled by a stochastic process. Various interventions, such as an immune booster and cancer-inducing factors, modulate the patient's immune response, with only favorable outcomes determining clinical success. To select the ideal therapy timing and dosage over a treatment period, we employ the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs maximum principle, complemented by a rigorous mathematical analysis of the resulting stochastic differential equations and their corresponding probabilistic aspects. Furthermore, we explore various scenarios and provide concrete examples to illustrate the theoretical findings.

A new method of measuring efficiency for information sharing systems has been developed and is now being used in diverse communication networks, emphasizing the freshness of shared data. We explore the effectiveness of Decoding Order and Side information assisted by Multiple measurements (DOSAM) in balancing the Age of Information (AoI) in D2D communication without direct data links. The problem is formulated as an optimization issue, focusing on optimizing two multi-node multi-vector control variables under complex real-world constraints. Due to the issue's non-convex and non-differentiable nature, we introduce an iteration-based decomposition approach, incorporating an auxiliary variable to linearize its effects and applying the Cramer and Dyer theorem to simplify co Channel interference management. The result is reformulated as a job scheduling problem, solved by our proposed Deep Recurrent Q-Networks (DReQN). The Deep Recurrent Q-Networks (DReQN) is trained in two stages: an initial stage of training Recurrent Q-Networks (RQN) to learn the side information and measurement vector, and a second stage of training RQN and Recurrent Q-Network (RN) to produce an optimal decoding order. The performance of DOSAM is demonstrated on a scenario involving 16 D2D nodes with 6 subchannels, where our approach yields a 20.6% improvement in Age of Information (AoI) compared to existing methods such as S-ARQ and DDAM.

This research focuses on verifying that the average helicity of a barotropic, compressible, inviscid fluid remains conserved as it evolves over time according to the Euler equations. The verification is achieved through two methods: by formally demonstrating that the conservation law holds and by employing Deolsary's proven result for helicity conservation. The average helicity is defined as the average of the fluid's velocity field's local helicity over its entire domain and is known to be weakly conserved in inviscid, compressible fluids. The concept of weak conservation implies that the average helicity remains constant as the fluid's domain stays invariant over time.

This research focuses on analyzing reflection spectra of the Davey-Stewartson II equations, and a precise mathematical expression has been derived to calculate the reflection coefficient. The study finds that there is a notable variation in the reflection coefficient as absolute value of wave number k changes, and this variation depends on spatial scale. To investigate this phenomenon, numerical simulations were conducted at various spatial scales, revealing distinct reflection coefficients for different scale values. The results show that the reflection coefficient is nearly negligible at certain high values of absolute value of wave number k, indicating a transition to a different physical regime. The theoretical model of reflection coefficient, derived from partial spectral data, adequately explains the observed significant $|k|$ behavior. Based on these findings, it is proposed that the significant $|k|$ behavior of reflection coefficients may offer valuable insights into the initial conditions of data from gravity wave measurements.

Current gravitational-wave detectors primarily detect inspiralling binary systems through their generated gravitational waves. However, most models used in detector analyses in the frequency range of a few hundred Hz to a few kHz lack the necessary precision in waveform modeling to be fully utilized. By incorporating an accurate eccentricity-inclusive model within this frequency range, we can determine how orbital eccentricity affects the detectability of inspiralling binaries, particularly for less massive binaries where eccentricity effects are more pronounced. Our findings indicate that binary systems detected at the threshold of a detector may retain measurable levels of orbital eccentricity, even if their counterparts in the same system were circular at larger frequencies. For example, an observer may detect binaries with orbital eccentricities as high as 0.3 or 0.6 for specific binary configurations, highlighting the importance of accounting for eccentricity effects in analyzing the signals generated by these systems.

A new concept for an X-ray laser has been developed using free-electron laser technology, involving a coherent X-ray laser that is seeded by a free-electron laser oscillator. This setup encompasses a complex system of components, including an oscillator with multiple mirrors, a main amplification chamber, and a master-attenuated seed laser beam that is combined with the other laser beam for interaction with the electron beam in a subsequent gain medium. Due to free-electron laser technology's inherent instability, it is challenging to achieve the necessary conditions for a coherent X-ray laser, involving both high interaction intensity and precise phase matching. To address these issues, a novel approach involves increasing the photon intensity while maintaining phase stability, by employing intricate electron beam compression techniques and innovative optical designs for the FEL components. These solutions involve a unique arrangement of the oscillator's mirrors for temporal phase matching and a specialized arrangement of the interaction region for spatial phase matching, along with the use of magnetic field configurations that further enhance the coherence of the emitted radiation. This arrangement also facilitates inversion of the energy exchange between the electrons and photons for increased X-ray intensity during the interaction with the electron beam. As an example of the feasibility of this approach, calculations demonstrate that a setup based on existing FEL technology parameters can yield a coherent X-ray laser pulse, with an anticipated output power in the range of 100 GW, with energy of a few nanojoules and pulse duration of a few tens of femtoseconds.

Dynamic graph incidents such as sudden changes in graph structure are detected in graph data analysis. However, most current methods are limited to static graphs and struggle to accurately detect incidents in dynamic graphs due to their inherent instability and varying node features over time. To overcome these challenges, we have developed an deep learning-based method called Incident Detection on Dynamic Graphs (IDDG), which can effectively identify Incidents in dynamic graphs. The IDDG approach involves multiple modules including a graph embedding module, incident detection module, node state prediction module, and a loss function for parameter optimization. Through numerous experiments, we have demonstrated that IDDG outperforms existing methods in accurately detecting Incidents in multiple types of dynamic graphs. The code for our method is publicly available at https://github.com/yourusername/IDDG.

High-energy astrophysical phenomena such as supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and accretion events are significant sources of cosmic rays, often arising from shock waves, particle acceleration, and jet activity. These processes play a vital role in the evolution of supermassive star clusters and active galactic nuclei, influencing both past and present accretion events. Our research examines how an implosion wave interacts with a surrounding medium, taking into account differences in ion and electron temperatures and variations in electron opacity. We observe that when magnetic field aligns with the implosion wave and the surrounding gas consists of fully ionized elements heavier than hydrogen, a pressure anisotropy develops, potentially leading to an adiabatic, low-opacity shock wave that may outlast the implosion phase. However, in other cases, we find that plausibility and self-consistency constraints necessitate the formation of a radiative shock, characterized by an enhanced e-/ion temperature ratio and a more significant e-/magnetic-field energy ratio.

Most current research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its associated risks is centered around **Technical Explainability**, focusing on making complex algorithms more transparent to **Technical stakeholders**. However, **Non-Technical stakeholders** also require the ability to understand and grasp AI systems, as simply increasing the explainability of an algorithm does not necessarily result in true understanding. To address this, this paper will (1) identify the limitations of **Technical Explainability** in helping **Non-Technical stakeholders** understand AI, (2) advocate for **Understanding** as the ultimate goal for **Non-Technical stakeholders** in addition to existing **Explanation** as a goal for **Technical stakeholders**, and (3) explore a new approach to **Understanding** through understanding requirements, utilizing requirements engineering to define and manage **Explainability** for effective communication between **Technical** and **Non-Technical stakeholders**. Ultimately, this paper will support **Understanding** through a user-centric approach where **Explainability** is treated as a manageable set of requirements, facilitating both **Explanation** and **Understanding**.

The UniToPatho dataset consists of 1222 annotated histopathological slides and accompanying color-coded maps generated by our segmentation tools, all depicting colorectal tissue polyps. The UniToPatho dataset comprises 80% training data comprising 968 polyps from 650 patients, 120 normal tissue samples, and corresponding adenoma severity ratings. The remaining data, consisting of 254 polyps from 22 patients, were used for testing. The UniToToPatho dataset has been made publicly available at https://univoto.github.

In the context of zero-error source coding, we consider a source graph where edges represent noiseless communication links between a source and a decoder. The source and decoder share secret information from previous interactions, enabling the source to encode past leakage information into its message. While this shared knowledge doesn't directly contribute to reducing the current transmission length, it's valuable for encoding leakage information from the source's perspective. We define and investigate the asymptotic conditional regular information density (ICRID) and introduce the ICRID graph to analyze ICRID. Furthermore, we establish lower and upper bounds for ICRID based on the ICRID graph's structure and show that in certain graph structures, the ICRID upper bound is tight, whereas the gap between the two bounds can be arbitrarily large.

Deep learning methods have made significant advancements in synthesizing Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) images. However, most approaches are limited by their reliance on raster-based models and homogeneous architectures, which do not fully capture the inherent multiscale and hierarchical nature of SAR imagery. To address these shortcomings, this paper presents a novel Hierarchical Generative SAR Prior (HGP) model, comprising multiple layers, with higher levels modeling abstract features and lower levels generating high-frequency details. Building upon the success of the SAR Attention Refined Prior (SARP) attention module, which enhances the description of object features through the attention of regional areas, the refined SARP (rSARP) module is introduced to capture local details in image patches while minimizing computational costs via the pyramid operator. The integration of rSARP with HGP yields the MrSARP model, which is evaluated in terms of its image generation quality and sharpness, demonstrating superior performance over the baseline SARP approach.

A well-designed algorithm known as the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) targets discrete optimization issues, yet determining the ideal parameters for QAOA remains a difficult task, often requiring an exhaustive search of the parameter space. To facilitate this, a novel approach utilizes Bayesian optimization to determine the optimal parameters efficiently. By modeling and capturing correlations between data points in the parameter space, this method can accurately predict untested parameter sets. Furthermore, a rapid assessment technique has been developed to quickly identify the most promising regions in the parameter space by analyzing the approximate quantum state without the need for full state reconstruction. Using a limited number of data points in various QAOA test cases, this method outperforms conventional approaches in finding the optimal parameters, and when applied to solve a real-world issue involving a minimum vertex cover on a specific graph, it yields a more accurate result with fewer data points compared to state-of-the-art methods.

A formula has been developed for determining the overlapping area of two ellipses, 
where one ellipse is positioned at the origin, and the other is defined by its 
translation, rotation, and dimensions. To achieve this, an existing method is adapted 
for this specific scenario, and then further modified to accommodate ellipses with 
varied sizes and shapes.

This paper explores the continuous time equivalent of q-Learning by examining the limit as the interval size approaches zero for q-Policy Iteration. We demonstrate that q-Policy Iteration performs trajectory rolling out with a fixed q-factor bias and that it converges to a unique fixed point in the limit. Furthermore, we prove that this fixed point corresponds to a unique stationary Nash equilibrium in a continuous duration game with compact action spaces and concave reward functions. We also establish the existence of this Nash equilibrium and its relationship to the fixed point of trajectory convergence. Additionally, we show that q-Policy Iteration converges linearly to this fixed point and that it can be viewed as a gradient ascent method on the entropy regularized Bellman operator when q is less than one.

Quantum computer simulations using a unique triangular lattice Hubbard model have been developed and utilized to investigate magnetic properties at an temperature of near zero. A detailed examination of the ground state at a magnetic stake of 1/3 has yielded an ordered state with a D3 symmetry, characterized by a unique spiral pattern of magnetic moments. When analyzing the anti-tripolar state at a stake of 1/3, our model exhibits a disorder of magnetic moments, as indicated by an increased disorder factor compared to previous simulations using a different model. However, utilizing neural network states to represent the magnetic moments allows us to discover new ordered states at an temperature of near zero, as well as an increased disorder factor when transitioning to finite temperatures. Furthermore, magnetic spiral patterns are shown to be unstable when the stake is 1/3, yet they remain stable when the stake is increased to 1/2, resulting in a magnetic state with high symmetry at this stake. Lastly, we have created a comprehensive chart illustrating the phase transitions of this model across a wide range of stake temperatures.

In automatic medical diagnosis, accurately localizing and identifying vertebral bodies in spine CT images is a crucial task. This paper presents an innovative approach that rectifies the spine to a 2D plane and then leverages deep learning and anatomically-constrained optimization to pinpoint each vertebra. By transforming the spine into a standardized view, our method eliminates the need for complex multi-task models and achieves superior localization and identification results. Furthermore, our method demonstrates impressive generalizability, allowing it to effectively adapt to new datasets with different anatomical variations and image styles through a process of few-shot adaptation. As a result, our model outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions, achieving impressive accuracy in the Challenge 2020 of the Medical Image Computing Challenge.

In stochastic thermodynamics, electric currents are often modeled as deterministic quantities under the assumption of fixed parameters, which excludes fluctuations from the analysis. However, when a Markovian system reaches equilibrium under periodic conditions, electric currents can be viewed as random variables subject to fluctuations, which can be studied using Fokker-Planck equations. This line of research has yielded important results regarding the statistical behavior of electric currents and their cumulants. A recent development has further established that the probability distribution functions and all higher-order cumulants of these currents are gauge invariant, meaning they remain unaffected by transformations of the vector potential. This is the first part of a two-part study that also investigates the thermodynamic properties, such as efficiency and entropy production, of electric currents under periodic conditions, which are shown to be gauge invariant as well, thereby aligning with the principles of stochastic thermodynamics.

We examine relative quantum cohomology for dominant morphisms q: X -> Y, 
where X and Y are projective varieties with an ample line bundle L that respects 
the quotient morphism q. The study focuses on the rational q-cohomology ring 
R = C(q), defined by direct summands of the cohomology ring of X and 
connections with q*OL's sections. We define and study key aspects of the 
relative quantum cohomology ring, including its axiomatic properties, 
identifies specific substructures within it, and with those components, 
establishes a rational quantum product. Additionally, we investigate and 
characterize the symmetry group of the quantum product and with that, 
formulate and explore a W-equivalence relation.

This research focuses on nonexponential energy transmission between two piezoelectric crystals through the surrounding medium by utilizing an inverted spectral density. This goal is accomplished through optimization of the inter-crystal separation and piezoelectric orientation. Study of the magnesium fluoride molecule reveals that an accelerated transmission of acoustic vibrations between the constituent atoms can be achieved, particularly when located very closely and with specific piezoelectric orientations - either polarized radially or tangentially. Calculations indicate that fast atomic transmission can occur at fast atomic distances and with certain orientation conditions. Additionally, the possibility of nonexponential heat transfer between heat reservoirs through piezoelectric crystals with polars aligned tangentially to the interatomic gap has been considered. This outcome signifies that to manipulate heat transfer between materials, one must consider their piezoelectric properties and geometric configuration.

A new field called reservoir photonics has emerged for studying complex open quantum systems, where a reservoir of particles, called an exciton-polariton condensate, forms as a result of strong interactions and a finite population of an underlying charged component, called a charged reservoir, which is responsible for generating and scatters photons from a chip-based cavity. The coupling of photons with this charged reservoir leads to a rich array of phenomena such as the random lasing effect, modulation of statistical properties of the emitted photons, and the emergence of topological photon states. To illustrate this research area, various approaches for manipulating the exciton-polariton condensate and associated photons are presented, along with an overview of recent experimental achievements, ultimately pointing towards potential applications for novel light sources and engineering of complex light-matter systems.

The presence of exoplanetary dust disks beyond known gas giants poses intriguing queries about planetary evolution and material loss rates from terrestrial to massive worlds.  Several small hot Jupiter and super-Earth systems display signs of dust leakage from their atmospheres or disrupted remnants, predominantly particles under 10 micrometers in size.  However, a substellar remnant has been discovered leaking dust around the mini-hot Jupiter K2-22b.  Leveraging the Low-Frequency Array by Terrestrial Technology (LBT) Adaptive Optics System with a coronagraph, scientists detected dust around the system, yielding an estimated size of a few micrometers for the dust and a size distribution resembling astrophysical molecular clouds.  Dust leakage estimates yielded a mass loss rate of on the order of 10^19 to 10^20 grams per second, roughly a million times greater than that of other partially disrupted disks or other leaking dust systems.  Such massive dust production by a disrupted satellite or remnant offers valuable insights into the final stages of massive planetary cores and super-Earths eroding under the intense heat of their host stars.

We establish a strong form of the strong continuity theorem for Milnor fibers in terms of critical loci, specifically that the Milnor fiber at a smooth point can be defined as the algebraic fiber over that point on the complement of the critical hypersurface defined by the Jacobian ideal. This is equivalent to stating that this complement is a flat document. As a consequence, the topological type of the Milnor fiber at a singular point is guaranteed to be the same as the typical Milnor fiber, and the topological type of the typical Milnor fiber is guaranteed to be stable under small perturbations of the defining polynomial. Furthermore, this connection provides an algebraic approach to studying the stability of the typical Milnor fiber at singular points.



This study argues that during the scientific revolution, mathematics was seen as a way to connect reason with observation, rather than a link between mathematical thought and observational data. Observations played a key role in shaping scientific advancements, as demonstrated by Galileo's work, in which empirical data guided theoretical developments. By analyzing Galileo's reasoning processes and references to modern physics, this research aims to provide a realistic account of the evolution of the theory of falling bodies. Furthermore, the study positions Galileo's mathematics within a broader mathematical context of his time and explores the diverse functions of mathematical reasoning within modern physics.

To examine the universe's early distribution of matter, we studied the 3-D and time-dependent density probability of the cosmos, considering both hydrogen's ionization and the changing rate of expansion. This study focused on the density's 3-D distribution and its evolution over time and across the cosmos, with various models of hydrogen ionization and expansion rates. We discovered that hydrogen recombination significantly impacts the universe's 3-D matter density and led to space-time variance $\frac{\sigma^2/k_s-t^2}{\bar{\rho}_s-t} > 2$ in some situations, indicating non-Gaussian behavior in the cosmos's early density distribution.

A programmer's assistant, known as a co-pilot, has been around for some time, but its co-author, a programmer's co-helper or programmer's trainee, known as an assistant, is relatively new to the scene. Although co-pilots and assistants are similar in many ways, they differ in one key aspect: how they are triggered. Co-pilots tend to be activated on demand by a programmer, whereas assistants proactively offer their help by analyzing a programmer's code and anticipating their needs. This paper delves into a novel in-asside tool designed to make a programmer's assistant more intelligent by giving it the ability to learn from examples and execute complex tasks, such as multiple-line text edits, similar to a more advanced co-pilot.
